MODULES.title: LLM Fundamentals
MODULES.tag: Tokens, context, effort and sampling, model families: the vocabulary layer
MODULES.why: Every AI system you'll oversee sits on top of an LLM API. If you aren't fluent in tokens, context windows, sampling, and model families, you can't make a sound call on cost, latency, or quality.
MODULES.mental: An LLM is a function call to a stateless, slow, expensive, probabilistic, context-bounded text-completion service. Every architectural decision flows from those five adjectives. Stateless means you pass the history yourself. Slow means latency budgets and streaming. Expensive means cost discipline. Probabilistic means evals and guardrails. Context-bounded means retrieval and compression.
concepts: Token

The unit an LLM processes, roughly ¾ of an English word (~4 characters) on most tokenizers. Pricing, context limits, and latency are all measured in tokens. Code and non-Latin scripts need more tokens per word, and tokenizers differ: Claude's newer one (Opus 4.7 and later) produces ~30% more tokens for the same text.
Context window

Max tokens per call: input + output, thinking included. 1M tokens on most current frontier models (Claude Fable 5.1 / Opus 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5, the GPT-6 family at 1.05M, Gemini 3.1 Pro and 3.8 Flash); exceptions include Grok 4.7 (500K) and Claude Haiku 4.5 (200K). Filling 1M tokens costs real money (about $0.20 on GPT-6 Luna to $20 on GPT-6 Astra, roughly 100×, long-context surcharges included), and long context still degrades: 'lost in the middle' didn't disappear.
Input vs output tokens

Priced separately; output tokens cost several times input (5× on the current Claude and GPT-6 lineups, roughly 3–8× across vendors) and are where latency comes from (generated one token at a time). Thinking tokens bill as output.
Sampling

temperature (randomness), top_p (nucleus), top_k, plus max_tokens and stop sequences. On Claude 4.7+ models (every current Claude model except Haiku 4.5) non-default temperature/top_p/top_k return a 400, and the Anthropic Python SDK v1.0+ drops them; many reasoning models fix or ignore sampling (OpenAI's GPT-6 models accept it only at reasoning effort 'none'; Google says to keep Gemini 3 at temperature 1.0), so steer with effort, max_tokens and structured outputs. Where the knob still exists (Haiku 4.5, open weights, older models), T=0 reduces randomness but is NOT deterministic across calls.
Model families (October 2026)

Closed: Claude Fable 5.1 / Opus 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5 / Haiku 4.5, GPT-6 (Astra / 6.1 Sol / Luna), Gemini 3.1 Pro / 3.8 Flash, Grok 4.7, Meta's API-only Muse Spark. Open weights: DeepSeek V4, Qwen3.8, GLM-5.3, Kimi K3, MiniMax M3, Gemma 4, Muse Glimmer. Reasoning is now an effort setting on one model rather than a separate SKU, and it burns extra thinking tokens (billed as output) on harder tasks.
Reasoning effort & thinking tokens

One model, an effort dial: Claude's output_config.effort (low, medium, high, xhigh, max; Opus 5.5 defaults to medium, Fable 5.1 and Sonnet 5.5 to high; Haiku 4.5 has no effort and still uses a manual budget_tokens), OpenAI's reasoning.effort, Gemini's thinking_level, Grok's reasoning_effort. With adaptive thinking the model decides how much to think within that level, and on easy inputs it may skip thinking entirely. Thinking tokens bill as output and are generated before the visible answer, so they add cost and latency; max_tokens caps thinking plus answer, and on Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 thinking can't be turned off, so effort is the only control. Raise effort for hard reasoning and agentic coding, lower it for chat, extraction and classification, and decide with cost per completed task on your own evals.
Latency anatomy

TTFT (time to first token) + output tokens ÷ TPS (tokens per second), thinking included. Streaming cuts perceived latency to roughly TTFT but not total time, and hidden thinking delays the first visible token.
Prompt caching

Cache the static prefix (system prompt, tool definitions, reference docs). Cached input reads bill at ~10% of the base input price on most models (5% on Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, 2.5% on Fable 5.1) and cut TTFT; writes can cost a premium (1.25×–2×). One of the biggest cost levers after model choice and effort.
Batch API
~50% off at Anthropic, OpenAI (Batch/Flex) and Google (Batch/Flex) for async work that can wait. Ideal for nightly evals and bulk classification.
mistakes: Assuming identical inputs give identical outputs: temperature=0 never guaranteed it, and most current flagships don't accept a temperature setting at all
Underestimating output token cost: output, thinking included, dominates the bill
Using premium models for trivial routing/classification
No fallback when the provider has an outage
Not re-counting tokens when porting prompts or upgrading models: the same text can cost ~30% more tokens on a different tokenizer (Claude Opus 4.7 and later vs earlier Claude models, for one)
Assuming a 1M window means you should fill it, cost and quality both degrade
Leaving effort at the default on every route: high-effort thinking on easy traffic bills output tokens for nothing
flags: "We're using the flagship model for everything", nobody right-sized
"We don't track token usage per feature", no cost discipline
"We just call the SDK directly", no gateway → no fallback, caching, observability, or model swap
"We don't version our prompts", every change is a silent prod incident
ask: What's our cost per request, broken into input/output tokens?
Why this model and not the next tier down?
What happens when the provider rate-limits or 5xx's?
What % of our prompt tokens hit the cache?
What effort level does each route run at, and who chose it?

MODULES.title: Prompt Engineering
MODULES.tag: The cheapest, fastest quality lever you own
MODULES.why: Prompt changes are free, instant, and routinely worth 10–30 points of task accuracy. Pull this lever first, before you fine-tune, switch models, or add complexity.
MODULES.mental: A prompt is a program written in natural language, executed by a probabilistic interpreter. Like any program, it needs structure, examples, explicit output contracts, and version control. Unlike any program, it fails silently and gradually, so it needs regression tests (evals).
concepts: System vs user messages
System prompt sets persistent behavior, constraints, and persona; user messages carry the task. Models weight system instructions heavily, put non-negotiables there.
Few-shot examples
A few diverse input→output examples (3–5 is the usual sweet spot) beat paragraphs of instruction. Examples define format, tone, and edge-case handling implicitly.
Chain of thought

On non-reasoning models, 'think step by step' or a reasoning field before the answer measurably improves hard-task accuracy. Current flagships think natively, steered by an effort or thinking-level setting: raise the dial instead of scaffolding the prompt, and don't double-prompt them to reason.
Structured output

First-class in the major APIs: Claude's output_config.format (a JSON schema) and strict: true tools, OpenAI's Structured Outputs (json_schema with strict). Both constrain decoding, so off-schema output can't be sampled; plain JSON mode only guarantees valid JSON, not your schema. Always prefer schema enforcement over 'please respond in JSON', and on current Claude models over the old forced-tool-call trick, which they now reject.
Validation & schema design

Constrained decoding guarantees shape, not truth: still validate business rules in code (ranges, cross-field logic, IDs that must exist), check the stop reason, and retry once with the validator's error in the prompt; for providers or open models without a grammar, validate-and-retry is the whole defense. Keep schemas small and flat with enums for categories, and give reasoning-heavy tasks room to think before the structured answer (thinking on reasoning models, or a required reasoning field listed first, since required properties keep their schema order). Forcing a hard task straight into a rigid format can cost answer quality, so measure it on your evals.
XML/markdown sectioning
Delimit context, instructions, examples, and data with clear tags. Models parse structure far more reliably than prose blobs.
Prompt versioning
Prompts are code: version-controlled, code-reviewed, eval-gated before deploy. A prompt change without an eval run is a blind deploy.
Negative instructions
Models follow 'do X' far better than 'don't do Y'. Reframe prohibitions as positive instructions with examples.
mistakes: Iterating on vibes, changing prompts without an eval set is guessing
One mega-prompt doing five jobs, decompose into focused calls
Stuffing instructions in the user turn that belong in system
Begging for JSON instead of enforcing schema
Prompting reasoning models with elaborate CoT scaffolding they no longer need
Prefilling the assistant turn to force JSON or skip a preamble: current Claude models reject prefill, so use structured outputs or a direct instruction
flags: "The prompt is in the codebase somewhere", unversioned, untested
"We tweaked the prompt and shipped it Friday", no regression gate
"Our prompt is 6,000 tokens", likely doing too many jobs, and every edit to it invalidates a large cached prefix
ask: Where does this prompt live, and what gates a change to it?
What eval set runs before a prompt change deploys?
Which parts of the prompt are static (cacheable) vs dynamic?

MODULES.title: Context Engineering
MODULES.tag: Curating what the model sees: the discipline that ate prompt engineering
MODULES.why: The 2025–26 consensus is that managing WHAT goes into the window matters more than wordsmithing instructions. Agents, RAG, memory, and harnesses are all context engineering problems. Prompt engineering isn't irrelevant; clear instructions still matter. But in agentic systems, what the model sees outweighs how it's phrased. Prompt engineering designs the instructions. Context engineering decides what else is in the room when the model reads them.
MODULES.mental: Treat the context window as RAM, and yourself as the operating system. You decide what gets loaded, what gets paged out, what gets compressed, and what gets fetched on demand. The model only knows what's in RAM right now.
concepts: Context budget
Allocate the window deliberately: system prompt + tools + retrieved docs + history + scratchpad + output reserve. Track utilization like a memory profiler.
Lost in the middle

Models attend best to the start and end of context. Keep non-negotiable rules in the system prompt, put long documents above the question, and ask the question last (Anthropic reports up to 30% better answers with the query at the end); don't bury key facts mid-window.
Compaction / summarization

When history exceeds budget, summarize older turns into a compact state. This is how agent harnesses (e.g. Claude Code) run long sessions, and provider APIs now offer it server-side too (Anthropic's compaction API, in beta); compaction is lossy, critical state must live in files or structured notes, not only in the summary.
Just-in-time retrieval
Don't preload everything, give the model tools to fetch what it needs (file reads, search) when it needs it. Agentic search often beats one-shot RAG stuffing.
Context rot

Recall and quality degrade as the token count grows (Anthropic's definition), and faster when the window fills with stale tool output, dead ends, and repetition. Prune aggressively; a clean 30K context beats a noisy 200K one.
Cache-aware layout
Order context stable→volatile: system prompt and tool defs first (cached), per-request data last. Reordering breaks the cache prefix.
Sub-agent isolation
Spin off a fresh-context sub-agent for a noisy subtask (e.g. broad search), return only the conclusion. Keeps the main context clean.
Platform context primitives

The APIs now ship this module's techniques as features. On Claude: server-side compaction (beta) summarizes older turns for you; context editing (beta) clears old tool results or thinking blocks once input passes a threshold (100K tokens by default, keeping the 3 most recent tool uses); the memory tool lets the model read and write files under /memories that your application stores; tool search with defer_loading keeps a large tool catalog out of the window until the model looks for what it needs (designing that catalog is covered in Tool / Function Calling). OpenAI's Responses API has its own compact endpoint. Learn the pattern, then use the primitive instead of rebuilding it.
Append-only history

On Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 each thinking block is bound to the exact history before it: edit or delete an earlier turn and the thinking after it fails the API's history check (a 400 by default for accounts created on or after August 31, 2026, or silently dropped if you opt into that). Design harnesses to append rather than rewrite: add instructions as mid-conversation system messages instead of editing the system prompt, let compaction and context editing do the rewriting, and if you must rewrite yourself, drop thinking from the turns you keep.
mistakes: Stuffing the window because it fits, cost and accuracy both suffer
Letting raw tool output accumulate unpruned
Putting volatile data before stable data (kills prompt caching)
Relying on compaction alone for critical state, write it to durable artifacts
Preloading 50 documents when the agent could fetch the 2 it needs
Rewriting or deleting earlier turns in a session that carries thinking blocks instead of appending: the API rejects or drops the stale thinking
flags: "Our average request uses 150K context", almost certainly unpruned noise
"We lose track of what the agent did earlier in long sessions", no compaction strategy, no progress files
"Cache hit rate is near zero", context layout is volatile-first
ask: What's our context budget breakdown for a typical request?
How do we handle conversations that outgrow the window?
What's our prompt cache hit rate, and what breaks it?

MODULES.title: 2026 Model Landscape
MODULES.tag: Who's who as of October 2026, and how to choose
MODULES.why: Model choice is the highest-impact cost and quality decision on any AI project. The lineup shifts quarterly. The decision framework doesn't.
MODULES.mental: Models are interchangeable commodities behind a gateway; your moat is the harness, evals, and data. Pick per-task tiers, re-benchmark quarterly on YOUR evals (not leaderboards), and keep switching cost near zero.
concepts: Current flagships (October 2026)

September 2026 alone brought new top models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI. Anthropic: Claude Fable 5.1 (Sept 1) is the top tier, Opus 5.5 (Sept 22) the recommended default, Sonnet 5.5 (Sept 28) the fast workhorse. OpenAI: GPT-6 Astra (Sept 3) is the flagship, GPT-6.1 Sol (Sept 29) comes close at a fifth of Astra's per-token price, and GPT-6 Luna is the budget tier. Google: Gemini 3.8 Flash (Sept 2) is its most intelligent Flash model, Gemini 3.1 Pro (still in preview) remains the Pro tier, and Gemini 4 Argon is restricted to vetted cyber defenders for now. xAI (now part of SpaceX): Grok 4.7 (Sept 21) at mid-tier prices. Meta's frontier model is now the API-only Muse Spark.
Pricing reality

Per M tokens, input/output: Claude Fable 5.1 $10/$50, Opus 5.5 $4/$20, Sonnet 5.5 $2/$10, Haiku 4.5 $1/$5. GPT-6 Astra $10/$50, GPT-6.1 Sol $2/$10, GPT-6 Luna $0.10/$0.50. Gemini 3.1 Pro $2/$12; Gemini 3.8 Flash $0.75/$3.75 (introductory through December 31, 2026, then $1.50/$7.50). Grok 4.7 $2/$6. DeepSeek V4.1-Flash $0.30/$1.20 at peak, half that off-peak. Long prompts can cost more: OpenAI bills GPT-6 prompts over 272K tokens at 2× input and 1.5× output, Gemini 3.1 Pro ($4/$18) and Grok 4.7 ($4/$12) have a higher tier above 200K, and Claude 4.6+ has none. Cached input reads bill at ~10% of the base input price on most models (5% on Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, 2.5% on Fable 5.1), and Batch is ~50% off at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. Filling the same 1M window costs about $0.20 on GPT-6 Luna and $20 on GPT-6 Astra, roughly 100× inside one vendor's lineup. Re-read these off the provider pages before you model with them, the ratios age far better than the numbers.
1M+ context is table stakes

Most hosted frontier models ship 1M-class windows (Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 at 1M; the GPT-6 family at 1.05M; Gemini 3.1 Pro and 3.8 Flash at 1M; DeepSeek V4.1-Flash, plus open-weight Kimi K3 and MiniMax M3, at 1M too), though not all: Grok 4.7 caps at 500K and Haiku 4.5 at 200K. The differentiator is no longer window size, it's effective recall across the window, cost to fill it, and latency.
Reasoning as a dial, not a model

Every flagship now exposes reasoning depth as a per-request effort setting on one model rather than a separate SKU: Anthropic's effort (low to max; thinking is always on for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5), OpenAI's reasoning.effort (none to max on GPT-6 Sol and Luna, low to max on Astra and 6.1 Sol), Gemini's thinking_level, Grok's reasoning_effort. Defaults differ (medium on Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol), and thinking bills as output, so spend it on hard tasks only and pin the level per route. LLM Fundamentals covers the mechanism.
Open weights are frontier-adjacent

DeepSeek's V4 family, Qwen3.8 (its 2.4T-parameter flagship's weights are open), GLM-5.3, Kimi K3 and MiniMax M3 are credible for high-volume, cost-sensitive, or data-residency-bound workloads, if you can fund the MLOps (Serving & Self-Hosting Open Models covers the build); Google's Gemma 4 and Meta's 30B Muse Glimmer (both Apache-2.0) cover local and edge work. Read the license of the exact checkpoint before you ship: terms range from permissive (Apache-2.0, MIT) to custom ones with commercial thresholds, like the Kimi K3 License (a model-as-a-service business above $20M in revenue over 12 months needs a separate agreement).
Release cadence & deprecations

Frontier releases now land every few weeks, and retirements run on fixed clocks: Claude Sonnet 4.5 retires November 30, 2026, OpenAI shuts down its GPT-5 and o3 families on December 11, 2026, and the Assistants API has been gone since August 26, 2026. Upgrades also ship API changes, not just new weights. Pin model IDs, keep the eval suite ready, and budget one migration per quarter.
Tiering strategy

Cheap/fast tier (Haiku 4.5, GPT-6 Luna, Gemini Flash-Lite) for triage, classification, extraction; mid tier (Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 3.8 Flash) for the workhorse; a flagship at high effort for the hardest 5% of calls. Route on model AND effort, don't default.
Benchmarks lie (a little)

Leaderboard deltas compress in practice, and harness quality (plus the effort setting a score was run at) swamps model deltas on agentic tasks. Your own eval suite on your own data is the only score that matters.
mistakes: Hard-coding one provider's SDK everywhere, no gateway means no leverage
Chasing every release, re-benchmark quarterly, not weekly
Choosing by leaderboard rather than your own evals
Ignoring open-weight options at scale (10–50× unit cost difference)
Buying the flagship for workloads a small model handles at equal accuracy
Comparing models at mismatched effort levels and calling the result a model comparison
flags: "We can't switch models, too much rework", vendor lock-in by architecture
"We picked it because it tops Arena (ex-LMArena)", nobody validated on real traffic
"All traffic goes to one model", no tiering, no routing
ask: What would it take to swap providers next week?
When did we last re-benchmark our top 3 routes?
What fraction of calls actually need flagship-tier quality?

MODULES.title: RAG Systems & Pipelines
MODULES.tag: The dominant production pattern for grounding models in your data
MODULES.why: RAG is still the best way to make a model answer from YOUR knowledge with citations, freshness, and access control. Fine-tuning and long context alone give you none of those.
MODULES.mental: RAG is a search problem wearing an AI costume. Retrieval quality caps answer quality. If the right passage never gets retrieved, no prompt or model will save you. Get search relevance right first, then worry about generation.
concepts: The pipeline
Ingest → chunk → embed → index → (query) retrieve → rerank → assemble context → generate → cite. Every stage has failure modes; instrument each.
Chunking & contextual retrieval

Split on document structure (headings, paragraphs), not fixed character counts; typical chunks run 200–800 tokens (chunking strategies and index lifecycle are covered in Data Engineering for AI Systems). Then fix orphaned chunks: contextual retrieval has an LLM write 50–100 tokens of chunk-specific context ('This chunk is from ACME's Q2 2023 SEC filing…') and prepends it before embedding and BM25 indexing. Anthropic measured top-20 retrieval failures falling 35% with contextual embeddings, 49% adding contextual BM25, 67% adding a reranker; its cost estimate was $1.02 per million document tokens, one-time, with prompt caching (800-token chunks, 8K-token documents, 100 tokens of context per chunk).
Hybrid retrieval

Dense vectors (semantic) + BM25/keyword (exact terms, IDs, names) + metadata filters. Pure vector search misses part numbers, names, and acronyms. Hybrid + rerank is the floor of a 2026 stack; one-shot vector top-k is no longer a default.
Reranking

A cross-encoder re-scores the top 50–100 candidates and keeps the best 5–10 your context budget allows. Cheap, large quality win, the most under-used stage. Options: hosted rerank APIs (Cohere's rerank-v4.0-pro, Voyage's rerankers) or open-weight cross-encoders you self-host (Qwen3-Reranker, bge-reranker-v2-m3). An LLM can rerank too, at a multiple of the latency and cost; measure before paying for it.
Query transformation
Rewrite the user's question for retrieval: expansion, decomposition into sub-queries, HyDE. Conversational queries especially need rewriting with history context.
Agentic search & deep research

Retrieval becomes tools the model calls in a loop: search, grep, open, read, decide what's missing, search again. That's how coding agents and deep-research features work. It beats a static index on small, structured or fast-changing corpora (code, tickets, the live web) and on multi-hop questions; it loses on latency, cost per answer and permission control. Deep research adds a planner, notes, a step or token budget and a cited report, so evaluate citation faithfulness (does each cited source support its claim?), not just the answer.
RAG vs long context

Long context handles 'analyze this one document'; RAG handles 'answer from a corpus too large/dynamic/permissioned to send'. They compose: retrieve broadly, then load full docs JIT. Cached prefixes bill at a fraction of input, so stuffing wins for small corpora or low volume; the worked example prices the break-even.
Citations & grounding
Force answers to cite retrieved chunk IDs; reject or flag answers with no supporting chunk. Your main hallucination defense.
Beyond hybrid: GraphRAG & late interaction

GraphRAG runs an LLM over every chunk to extract entities and relationships, clusters them into communities and summarizes each, so it can answer corpus-wide questions ('what themes recur across 40,000 tickets?') that no top-k of chunks can. That costs at least one LLM call per chunk before the first query plus re-runs on refresh; Microsoft's own README warns indexing 'can be an expensive operation'. Late interaction keeps one vector per token (ColBERT) or per page-image patch (ColPali, which retrieves charts, tables and scans without OCR) and scores token by token, for sharper matches at many times the storage. Adopt either only when hybrid + rerank measurably fails on your golden set.
mistakes: Evaluating only the final answer, not retrieval (recall@k) separately
Fixed-size chunking that splits tables and sentences mid-thought
Vector-only search, fails on exact identifiers
No reranker, top-k raw vector hits go straight into context
Ignoring document permissions in retrieval (data leak via RAG)
Skipping freshness: stale index serving deleted/edited docs
Reaching for GraphRAG, late interaction or agentic loops before hybrid + rerank has been measured on the golden set
flags: "Our RAG answers are bad" with no retrieval metrics, they're debugging blind
"We chunk at 500 characters", arbitrary, format-blind
"Everyone searches the same index", permission model missing
ask: What's retrieval recall@10 on our golden set?
How do we know when retrieval, not generation, failed?
How fast does an edited document reach the index?
How are document ACLs enforced at query time?
Which question types does our traffic hold: lookups, multi-hop questions, or corpus-wide themes?

MODULES.title: Embeddings
MODULES.tag: Meaning as geometry: the substrate under retrieval
MODULES.why: Embeddings power retrieval, dedup, clustering, recommendation, and semantic caching. Choosing them well and running them well is the foundation under every RAG and memory system.
MODULES.mental: An embedding model is a lossy compression of meaning into a point in space, where distance is roughly semantic similarity. Like any lossy codec, it's tuned for a domain, and mixing codecs corrupts the archive. Vectors from different models don't compare, unless a vendor deliberately trained a model family into one shared space.
concepts: What they are
Dense vectors (typically 256–4096 dims) from a dedicated embedding model (not your chat LLM). Similar meaning → nearby vectors (cosine similarity).
Model choice

Voyage 4 family, OpenAI text-embedding-3, Cohere Embed v4, Google Gemini Embedding (v2 is natively multimodal); open-weight Qwen3-Embedding, BGE-M3, voyage-4-nano. Multi-vector (late-interaction) models such as ColBERT and ColPali keep one vector per token or page patch when one vector per chunk loses too much (see RAG). Check the MTEB leaderboard but validate on YOUR retrieval task, domain match beats benchmark rank.
Dimensions tradeoff
Bigger = better quality, more storage/latency/cost. Matryoshka embeddings let you truncate dims with graceful degradation, store big, query small.
One model rule

Query and documents MUST share one embedding space: the same model and version, or siblings of a family trained into a shared space (Voyage 4 lets you embed the corpus with voyage-4-large and queries with the open-weight voyage-4-nano, at the same dimension). A model upgrade means re-embedding the whole corpus, plan migration like a schema change.
Asymmetric embedding
Queries and documents are different text types; modern models accept input_type hints (query vs document). Use them.
Beyond retrieval
Semantic cache (skip duplicate LLM calls), near-dup detection, clustering for topic discovery, anomaly detection on drift.
Fine-tuned embeddings
For specialized jargon (legal, medical, internal codenames), fine-tuning the embedder lifts recall far more cheaply than fine-tuning the LLM.
mistakes: Comparing vectors from different models/versions, silent garbage results
Embedding entire documents in one vector, chunk first
Forgetting to re-embed after a model upgrade
Cosine similarity on unnormalized vectors when the index expects normalized
Treating 0.8 similarity as universally 'similar', thresholds are model- and domain-specific
flags: "We upgraded the embedding model last sprint" + no re-embedding ticket, the index is corrupted
"Why is similarity weird?", usually mixed models or missing input_type
Storage bill growing linearly with docs at 3072 dims, nobody considered truncation
ask: Which embedding model and version, and where is that pinned?
What's our re-embedding plan for a model upgrade?
Did we evaluate against our domain or just trust MTEB?

MODULES.title: Vector Databases
MODULES.tag: Approximate search at scale, and when you don't need one
MODULES.why: The vector DB you pick locks in cost, latency, scale ceiling, and operational burden for every retrieval-backed feature. Getting it wrong hurts both ways: overkill wastes money, underkill caps you.
MODULES.mental: A vector DB is a search index, not a database of record. It answers 'what's nearby?' fast by being approximately right (ANN). Your source of truth lives elsewhere. The index is rebuildable, disposable infrastructure.
concepts: ANN algorithms

HNSW (graph, fast queries, RAM-heavy), IVF (cluster-based), ScaNN (clusters + quantization), DiskANN (graph on SSD, billion-scale). All trade recall for speed, tune ef_search/nprobe and MEASURE recall.
The landscape

Dedicated: Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus. Bolt-on: pgvector (Postgres), OpenSearch/Elastic, Redis. Embedded: LanceDB, Chroma, FAISS. Bolt-on wins below ~10M vectors if you already run that infra.
pgvector first
If you run Postgres and have <5–10M vectors, pgvector with HNSW is usually the right answer: one less system, transactions, joins with your relational data, real ACLs.
Metadata filtering

Pre-filter vs post-filter matters: post-filtering after top-k can return zero results for selective filters. Check how your engine handles filtered ANN: pgvector's HNSW post-filters by default, and its iterative scans (0.8+) fix most of that.
Quantization

Scalar (4×), binary (32×) or product quantization (up to ~64×) cuts memory; rescoring a shortlist at full precision recovers most of the lost recall. The difference between a $400 and a $4,000 monthly bill at scale.
Freshness & deletes
Upserts and deletes in ANN indexes are messy (tombstones, segment merges). Know your engine's consistency lag, it's your stale-answer window.
Multi-tenancy
Namespace-per-tenant or partition keys; never rely on 'the filter in the prompt' for isolation. Tenant leakage via vector search is a real incident class.
mistakes: Buying a dedicated vector DB for 200K vectors that fit in pgvector
Never measuring recall of the ANN index against exact search
Post-filtering selective metadata → empty result sets
Treating the vector DB as source of truth, no rebuild path
Ignoring index rebuild/merge windows in latency SLOs
flags: "We chose it because it was on Hacker News", no requirements analysis
"Recall? It returns 10 results, so it works", accuracy never measured
"Rebuilding the index takes a week and we're scared", no automation
ask: How many vectors now, and at 10× growth?
What's measured ANN recall vs exact search?
How long until an updated doc is searchable?
Could pgvector do this and remove a system?

MODULES.title: Memory Systems
MODULES.tag: State across the stateless: sessions, users, agents
MODULES.why: The model forgets everything between calls. Every product experience of 'it remembers me', and every agent that survives a long task, is a memory system you engineered and own.
MODULES.mental: Memory is a write-path problem disguised as a read-path problem. Anyone can retrieve notes. The hard part is deciding what's worth writing, updating, or deleting without poisoning future behavior.
concepts: Memory taxonomy
Working memory (current context), episodic (past conversations/events), semantic (facts about user/domain), procedural (learned how-tos, feedback). Different storage and retrieval for each.
Short-term: history management
Sliding window + progressive summarization of older turns. Compaction summaries are lossy, pin durable facts elsewhere.
Long-term: extract-then-store
After conversations, extract candidate facts ('user is vegetarian'), dedupe against existing memory, store with provenance and timestamps. Retrieval-inject relevant memories per request.
File-based agent memory
The 2026 agent pattern: memory as plain files the agent reads/writes (progress notes, MEMORY.md indexes, scratchpads). Durable, inspectable, harness-portable, and it survives compaction.
Memory as a tool (API primitives)

Memory now ships as API features. Claude's memory tool (memory_20250818) lets the model view, create, edit, rename and delete files under /memories through tool calls, while your handler owns the storage and must reject path traversal. Hosted agent runtimes add managed stores: Claude Managed Agents memory stores (beta) mount versioned, auditable files into each session; OpenAI's Agents API (beta) includes memory; the AWS and Google agent platforms sell managed memory services. The write-path discipline (provenance, supersede, untrusted on read) doesn't change.
Memory hygiene
Update beats append: contradictions must overwrite, not coexist. TTLs and decay for stale facts. User-visible and editable memory is both a trust and a correctness feature.
Memory poisoning
Bad writes compound: one wrong extracted 'fact' or an injected instruction stored as memory corrupts every future session. Validate writes; treat memory content as untrusted input on read.
Tooling

Libraries: Mem0, Zep (built on its Graphiti temporal graph), Letta, LangMem, or an in-house extract + vector store, alone or on top of the API primitives above. Whichever you pick, the design decisions (what to write, when to forget, what needs confirmation) stay yours.
mistakes: Appending forever, context bloat and contradiction soup
Storing raw transcripts as 'memory' instead of extracted facts
No provenance, can't debug why the agent 'believes' something
Letting retrieved memory carry instructions (injection via memory)
No user visibility/control over what's remembered
flags: "The agent remembers wrong things and we can't fix it", no update/delete path
"Memory is the last 50 messages", that's history, not memory
"We store everything users say", privacy incident pending
ask: What decides whether something gets written to memory?
How do contradictions get resolved?
Can a user see and edit what's remembered?
Is memory content sanitized before re-entering context?

MODULES.title: AI Agents
MODULES.tag: LLMs in a loop with tools: capable, over-applied, and dependent on the harness
MODULES.why: Agents are the pattern everyone reaches for right now, and the one people misuse most. Knowing when a plain workflow beats an agent, and what actually makes agents reliable, is senior-level judgment.
MODULES.mental: An agent is an LLM in a while-loop with tools and a goal. The model decides, acts via a tool, observes the result, and repeats. Reliability comes from how you engineer that loop (the harness), not from the model being clever. Error compounds at every step: 95% per-step success works out to roughly 36% over 20 steps.
concepts: Workflow vs agent

Workflow: predefined steps with LLM calls inside (predictable, debuggable, cheap). Agent: model chooses the path (flexible, expensive, harder to bound). Default to workflows; earn your way to agents when paths can't be enumerated.
The agentic loop
Gather context → plan → act (tool call) → observe → verify → repeat or finish. Verification (tests, checks, self-review) is what separates demos from production.
Error compounding
Per-step reliability is everything. Mitigations: fewer steps, verification gates, checkpoints/rollback, human approval on irreversible actions.
Stopping conditions
Max iterations, budget caps, goal tests, and 'declare victory' detection. Agents fail both ways: giving up early and declaring premature success.
Granular tools beat clever prompts
Agents improve more from better tool design (clear names, descriptions, narrow scopes, good error messages) than from prompt tuning.
Human-in-the-loop
Approval gates on destructive/irreversible actions (sends, deletes, payments). Autonomy is a dial set per action class, not a switch.
Durable execution & hosted runtimes

When a run must survive crashes and deploys, or wait days for an approval, don't hold it in a process. Durable-execution engines (Temporal, DBOS, Restate, Inngest, LangGraph checkpointers, Microsoft Agent Framework's durable extension) record every model output and tool result and resume by replaying the record, never by re-asking the model. Replay stays safe only if side effects happen inside recorded steps, orchestration code avoids wall-clock time and randomness, tools are idempotent (see Tool / Function Calling), and an approval is a durable wait with a timeout and an escalation owner. Hosted runtimes (Claude Managed Agents, OpenAI's Agents API, both in beta) run the loop for you; MCP's Tasks extension covers long-running tool calls.
Observability
Full traces of every step: model calls, tool I/O, decisions. Without traces, agent debugging is archaeology.
mistakes: Building an agent where a 5-step workflow would do
No iteration/budget caps, runaway loops burn real money
Letting agents take irreversible actions without gates
20 vague tools instead of 8 sharp ones
No verification step, trusting the model's claim of success
Debugging from final output instead of traces
Holding a days-long approval wait in a live process, or re-asking the model on resume instead of replaying what it already said
flags: "It works in the demo", n=1, happy path
"The agent decides everything", autonomy without bounds or audit
"We can't reproduce failures", no tracing
ask: Why an agent and not a workflow here?
What bounds the loop, iterations, budget, time?
Which actions require human approval?
Show me the trace of the last failure.
If the process dies mid-run, what replays, and which tools could act twice?

MODULES.title: Tool / Function Calling
MODULES.tag: The hands of the model: API design for a probabilistic caller
MODULES.why: Tool calling is how models reach into the world. Most so-called agent bugs are really tool-design bugs: vague descriptions, leaky abstractions, errors that explain nothing.
MODULES.mental: Writing tool definitions is API design where the client is a probabilistic intern: brilliant, but easily confused. Use crisp names, unambiguous parameters, examples inside the descriptions, and error messages that teach. The model rereads your docs on every single call.
concepts: Mechanics

You send tool schemas (name, description, JSON params) with the request; model returns a structured tool_use call; YOUR code executes it; you return the result; model continues. Server tools (web search, code execution) run on the provider's side instead, but the rule holds: the model never executes anything, it only asks. Computer-use and browser toolsets are client tools too; they get their own module, Computer-Use & Browser Agents.
Description quality
The description is a mini-prompt. Say what the tool does, when to use it, when NOT to, units/formats, and give an example. Most tool-selection errors trace to vague descriptions.
Tool scope
Match granularity to intent: a search_flights tool, not raw_sql_query. Too broad invites misuse; too narrow forces long chains. Consolidate related operations.
Error returns
Errors go back INTO context, make them instructive: 'date must be YYYY-MM-DD' beats 'Error 400'. The model self-corrects from good errors and flails on bad ones.
Parallel & forced calls

Independent calls batch in one turn (parallel) for latency wins. tool_choice can force a specific tool on models that allow it, but Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1 reject forced choice with a 400: for a guaranteed shape, use strict tool use or structured outputs instead.
MCP

Model Context Protocol: the open standard for exposing tools, resources and prompts to any model; write a server once and every compliant harness can use it. Vendor-neutral since December 2025 (the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation). The 2026-07-28 revision made the core stateless: no initialize handshake and no sessions, each request carries its protocol version and capabilities in _meta, and a server that needs state hands out an explicit handle the model passes back as an argument. Streamable HTTP requests carry Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers so gateways can route and meter without parsing bodies. A server that needs user input mid-call returns input_required and the client retries with the answers (Multi Round-Trip Requests). Roots, Sampling and Logging are deprecated (they keep working for at least 12 months); Tasks (long-running calls) and MCP Apps (interactive UI) are official extensions; the Tier-1 SDKs are TypeScript, Python, Go and C#. The USB-C of tool calling.
MCP authorization & remote servers

Remote servers use OAuth. The client finds the authorization server through the MCP server's Protected Resource Metadata, runs the code flow with PKCE, identifies itself with a Client ID Metadata Document (Dynamic Client Registration is deprecated), and validates the issuer (RFC 9207). Tokens are audience-bound: the client names the target server in the resource parameter, and the server must reject tokens issued for anyone else. The server must never pass the client's token through to downstream APIs; it calls them with its own credential and the user's delegated scopes. Identity comes from the token, never from model arguments.
Large tool surfaces

Selection accuracy drops past roughly 30–50 tools, and definitions eat the window long before that, so Anthropic suggests tool search from about 10 tools or 10K tokens of definitions (the token-budget side is in Context Engineering). Tool search with deferred loading keeps the catalog out of context until the model searches it; programmatic tool calling lets the model write code in the code-execution sandbox that calls your tools in a loop, so 20 lookups take one script instead of 20 model round trips and the intermediate results never enter context; namespaced names (github_list_prs, slack_send_message) let one search find a whole service's tools. Strict tools keep the arguments schema-valid either way.
Safe side effects

Agents and durable engines retry and replay by design, so every mutating tool takes an idempotency key that names the intended effect (run + step), never a fresh value per attempt, and the downstream must honour it: a retry then returns the first result instead of acting twice. When the downstream ignores keys, read before retrying (did the refund land?). An effect you can neither dedupe nor look up gets a compensating action or a human gate.
Security
Tool calls are attacker-reachable surface: validate args server-side, enforce authz per call (the MODEL is not a principal), idempotency keys on mutations, allowlists over open-ended execution.
mistakes: Descriptions written for humans who already know the system
Returning raw stack traces or empty errors to the model
Trusting model-supplied args without server-side validation
One mega-tool with a 'command' string param, un-promptable
Ignoring parallel calls, serial latency stacks
Generating a fresh idempotency key per attempt, so every retry looks like a brand-new request
Forwarding the user's OAuth token from an MCP server to downstream APIs
flags: "The model keeps picking the wrong tool", read your descriptions aloud
"We pass user_id as a tool parameter", model-supplied identity = privilege escalation
"Adding a tool means redeploying everything", consider MCP
"Our MCP server just forwards the user's token to the API", token passthrough, which the spec forbids
ask: Could a new hire pick the right tool from these descriptions alone?
Where is authorization enforced, the tool boundary or model side?
Which tools mutate state, and what makes them safe to retry?
Which mutating tools carry an idempotency key, and how is that key derived?

MODULES.title: Agent Harnesses
MODULES.tag: The scaffolding around the model: 2026's defining layer
MODULES.why: The same model scores wildly differently depending on its harness. In December 2025, Princeton's HAL leaderboard team reported Claude Opus 4.5 scoring 78% on CORE-Bench in Claude Code's harness versus 42% in the generic CORE-Agent scaffold, a 36-point gap from the same model. Anthropic's Opus 4.8 release (May 2026) builds the lesson into its method: it ran every model's Terminal-Bench 2.1 score on one public harness, noting GPT-5.5's separately reported 83.4% in OpenAI's own Codex CLI. In 2026, harness engineering is AI engineering. It's where capability actually comes from.
MODULES.mental: If the model is the CPU, the harness is the operating system. It curates context (RAM), runs the boot sequence (system prompt, hooks), provides drivers (tools, skills), schedules work (loops, sub-agents), and handles persistence (memory, compaction). Same CPU, different OS, wildly different machine.
concepts: What a harness is

Everything wrapping the model call in an agentic system: system prompt assembly, tool registry, the loop, context management (compaction, pruning), permissions/approvals, tracing, error recovery, checkpoints/resume. The model proposes; the harness disposes.
The 2026 landscape

Claude Code / Claude Agent SDK (the harness behind Claude Code, opened up for custom agents), OpenAI Agents SDK (April 2026 upgrade: model-native harness with Codex-style file tools + native sandbox execution), LangGraph (explicit graph orchestration with checkpointed state), plus lighter frameworks (CrewAI, Strands, Smolagents). The 2026 newcomer is the hosted harness: Claude Managed Agents ($0.08 per session-hour plus tokens) and OpenAI's Agents API (both in beta) run the loop and the sandbox for you.
Harness > model deltas

On multi-step tasks, harness quality swamps model differences. Benchmark results are model+harness results. When comparing models, hold the harness constant; when buying capability, evaluate the harness first.
Context management core

The harness's main job: what enters the window each turn. Compaction of old turns, pruning stale tool output, JIT retrieval, sub-agents with fresh windows for noisy subtasks, cache-friendly stable→volatile layout.
Long-running agents

Work spans many context windows; each session 'wakes up' amnesiac. Anthropic's proven pattern: an initializer agent sets up the environment (init script, feature list as structured JSON, initial commit), then each coding session reads progress notes + git log, picks ONE feature, verifies end-to-end, commits, updates the progress file. Artifacts on disk bridge the amnesia.
Failure modes harnesses fix

One-shotting (doing too much, dying mid-task with undocumented state) → incremental feature-at-a-time. Premature victory ('looks done!') → explicit pass/fail feature checklist the agent may only flip after verification. Broken-state handoffs → commit clean, log progress, boot-check before new work.
Hooks, permissions, sandboxing

Production harnesses expose hooks (pre/post tool-call interception), permission tiers per tool/action, and sandboxed execution (filesystem/network isolation) so the agent can act boldly inside a safe boundary.
Agent Skills (open format)

A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md (required name and description frontmatter, then instructions) plus optional scripts, references and assets. Progressive disclosure keeps a big library cheap: only names and descriptions sit in context until a task matches, then the full SKILL.md loads, and bundled files load only when used. Anthropic launched skills in October 2025 and published the format as an open standard in December 2025; GitHub Copilot and an official MCP extension load them too, and the Skills API is GA on the Claude API. Skills are code plus instructions, so review third-party ones like dependencies. With MCP servers and sub-agent definitions, they make capability configuration rather than a code change.
Coding agents in the team workflow

Treat coding agents as team members with a process. Repo instruction files give every agent the same context: AGENTS.md (an open format and an Agentic AI Foundation founding project) next to vendor files such as CLAUDE.md, short and versioned. The loop is plan, implement, test, with the test suite as the oracle and small reviewable diffs; parallel agents work in separate worktrees or sandboxes; background agents in CI open PRs with read-only tokens and declared outputs (GitHub Agentic Workflows calls them safe outputs). Review agent PRs like a junior's, check every new dependency (hallucinated package names are an attack vector, see AI Security & Adversarial Robustness), keep secrets out of agent CI (MITRE ATLAS documents a leak through an agent's GitHub Action), and measure cycle time and escaped defects, not lines generated.
Build vs adopt

Adopt a proven harness (Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph), or rent a hosted one, unless you have hard requirements they can't meet. In-house harnesses recreate years of loop/compaction/permission engineering, usually badly.
mistakes: Evaluating models without controlling for harness, you benchmarked the scaffolding
Prompting 'build the whole app' instead of structuring incremental, verifiable units
Letting agents mark work done without an end-to-end verification step
Relying on compaction alone for long-task state instead of durable artifacts (progress files, git)
Building a bespoke harness for problems the Agent SDK solved in 2025
No resume capability, a crash at hour 6 restarts at hour 0
Letting agent PRs merge without repo instructions, tests as the oracle, or human review
flags: "We wrote our own agent loop in a weekend", wait for the compaction, permissions, and resume bugs
"The agent says it finished", does anything verify that claim?
"Long tasks mysteriously degrade", context rot, no pruning/compaction strategy
"We switched models and everything broke", harness was overfit to one provider
ask: What's our harness, and why this one?
How does state survive a context-window boundary or crash?
What verifies a step before the agent moves on?
Which actions are sandboxed vs gated on human approval?
If the model improves 20%, what in our harness captures that gain?
What do AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md tell an agent about this repo, and who keeps them current?

MODULES.title: Computer-Use & Browser Agents
MODULES.tag: When there is no API: agents that read screens and drive browsers, and how to keep them on a leash
MODULES.why: Every major lab now ships an agent that drives a screen: Anthropic took computer use out of beta and added a browser toolset in August 2026, OpenAI's Responses API has a GA computer tool, and Google's Gemini API has one too. They reach what no API does: legacy desktop apps, vendor portals, long-tail web chores. They are also slow, error-prone and built to read attacker-writable pages; Anthropic's November 2025 tests still saw about 1% of an adaptive attacker's injections land on its hardened browser agent. The craft is limiting what a hijacked one can reach.
MODULES.mental: A computer-use agent is a new hire operating your software over a video call: slow, literal, and easily misled by whatever is on the screen, including notes an attacker left there. So you hand it the narrowest machine, the shortest list of sites and no keys, and you stay on the call for anything that can't be undone.
concepts: The action-surface ladder

Take the highest rung that can do the job: a direct API, MCP server or CLI; then browser automation over the DOM and accessibility tree; then pixel-level computer use. Each step down adds steps, tokens, latency and attack surface, so justify it in writing. GitHub's Copilot docs agree: a tool that can do the task directly gives more structured information and more predictable results. Pixels are for legacy desktops, canvas UIs and portals with no integration.
The perception-action loop

Observe (screenshot or accessibility tree), act (click, type, key, scroll), let the UI settle, then observe and verify. On Claude, one toolset entry declares a family of member tools: 17 in computer_toolset_20260801, 31 in browser_toolset_20260801 (four off by default). A turn often carries a batch: run the calls in order, stop at the first failure, answer every block. Coordinates are in the pixel space of the screenshots you return: resize once, scale clicks back.
Browser-native agents

A browser toolset reads the page as structure: read_page returns the accessibility tree with element references such as [ref_3] that later clicks, form_input and scroll_to can target, plus tabs, page text and downloads. References survive the layout shifts that break pixel coordinates, and a tree read often costs fewer tokens than a screenshot; screenshots stay for canvas, video and visual layout. Microsoft's Playwright MCP server takes the same approach from any MCP client.
Sandboxing

The sandbox from Agent Harnesses, made concrete: one throwaway VM, container or browser profile per task, with minimal privileges, no host mounts, no ambient secrets, no saved logins or autofill, and a snapshot to roll back to. Egress is an allow-list enforced at the network layer and re-checked after redirects, with loopback, link-local and private ranges blocked. The agent loop, API key and policy code live outside the box the model drives.
Credentials & confirmation gates

The model never holds a secret: give it a pre-authenticated session for one dedicated low-privilege account, or have your executor fill a known login form from a vault. Consequential actions (purchases, sends, account changes, accepting terms or cookies) need a human yes, checked in the executor before each block runs, because one batch can click, type and submit. A GUI has no idempotency key, so after a timeout on Submit, read the order list before retrying (see Safe side effects in Tool / Function Calling). CAPTCHAs and MFA go to a person.
Injection exposure

Every page, ad, email, tab title and file name the agent reads is attacker-writable, and some of it is invisible to the humans supervising (white-on-white text, off-screen elements). A logged-in browser that can click and type holds all three legs of the lethal trifecta (taxonomy in AI Security & Adversarial Robustness). MITRE ATLAS records real hijacks, from "AI ClickFix" attacks on computer-use agents to data destruction via injection against Claude computer use. Classifiers help; design so a successful injection finds nothing to steal and nowhere to send it.
Reliability & evals

Long UI tasks compound errors exactly as AI Agents showed, so verify mid-run and judge success by the end state (order exists, field changed), never the transcript. Test in environments you can reset, such as a VM snapshot or a self-hosted copy of the portal, running each task k times and grading with code. Public suites (OSWorld: desktop tasks in real VMs, graded on the resulting files and app state; WebArena: self-hosted web apps) build literacy, but scores move with harness, resolution and effort.
Cost & latency

Screenshots bill as image input at ⌈width ÷ 28⌉ × ⌈height ÷ 28⌉ visual tokens (1280×800 is 1,334). Keep every screenshot and step n re-sends n of them, so cost grows with the square of the step count. Each request also carries the toolset definition: about 4,500 input tokens for computer use, 6,600 for browser use. Levers: climb the ladder, fix one screenshot size, cache the stable prefix, clear old screenshots server-side. Every step is slow, so run these as background jobs, not behind a spinner.
mistakes: Reaching for pixels when an API, MCP server, export or the DOM would do the job
Running the agent in an everyday browser profile with saved logins and an autofilled card
Allow-listing sites in the prompt, or with a string-prefix check, instead of a parsed host check backed by the egress proxy
Asking for approval after the batch has run, when the 'Place order' click already happened
Sending native-resolution screenshots, then blaming the model for missed clicks
Calling a run done because the agent said so instead of checking the app's end state
Deleting old screenshots client-side on Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5 instead of clearing them server-side
flags: "It can use the buyer's browser, it's already logged in": and so is anyone who hijacks it
"The prompt tells it to stay on approved sites": that is a request, not an allow-list
"Each click is 95% reliable": that is about 21% over a 30-click task
"Approval kicks in above $1,000": attackers split orders, so gate the action, not the amount
ask: Is there an API, MCP server, export or DOM path that makes pixels unnecessary?
If a page hijacks this agent, what can it reach: which sessions, files, networks and payment methods?
Where does the human approval run, and can a single batch get past it?
What end state can code check to prove a run succeeded?
What do our stored screenshots contain, and who can read them?

MODULES.title: Multi-Agent Systems
MODULES.tag: When one context window isn't enough, and the coordination tax that follows
MODULES.why: Multi-agent works well for parallelizable, context-heavy jobs and wastes money everywhere else. The skill is telling the two apart and paying the coordination tax only when it buys you something.
MODULES.mental: Multi-agent is an org chart for context windows. You hire another agent for the same reason you hire another person: the work is too big for one head. And like any org, every added agent brings communication overhead, drift risk, and cost. Headcount has to justify itself.
concepts: Why split
Context isolation (a noisy subtask pollutes the main window), parallelism (independent subtasks fan out), specialization (different tools/prompts per role). NOT because it sounds sophisticated.
Orchestrator–worker
The proven pattern: a lead agent decomposes the task, spawns workers with focused briefs and fresh contexts, integrates results. Workers return conclusions, not transcripts.
Handoff quality
Agents communicate through text briefs. Vague briefs → drifted work, duplicated effort. The orchestrator's brief-writing quality is the system's bottleneck, same as human delegation.
Sub-agents as context tools
The most defensible 2026 use: spawn a fresh-window sub-agent to do a broad noisy search/analysis and return a tight summary. Pure context hygiene.
A2A (Agent2Agent)

For delegating to agents you don't own. A2A is a Linux Foundation protocol (v1.0 in March 2026, v1.0.1 in May 2026): a remote agent publishes an Agent Card (skills, endpoint, auth; v1.0 cards can be signed), and you hand it tasks with a lifecycle over JSON-RPC, gRPC or HTTP/REST, with modernized OAuth (PKCE, device code). Use it for opaque cross-vendor or cross-org agents; keep your own workers as sub-agents in your harness, and give agents tools through MCP. Treat whatever a remote agent returns as untrusted input.
Cost multiplier

In Anthropic's research system, a single agent used about 4× the tokens of a chat and the multi-agent setup about 15×, so budget roughly 4× a single agent. Reserve it for tasks where the value or parallelism justifies that bill.
Shared state
Filesystem/artifacts beat message-passing for cross-agent state (durable, inspectable). Concurrent writes need ownership rules, last-write-wins eats work.
Debugging
One bad handoff cascades. Trace per-agent AND cross-agent; evaluate the system end-to-end, not just each agent in isolation.
mistakes: Five agents role-playing a company to do one agent's job
Workers inheriting the orchestrator's entire context, no isolation benefit
Two agents editing the same artifact without ownership rules
Evaluating agents individually, never the integrated outcome
Ignoring the token bill until finance asks
Wrapping your own in-process workers in A2A, adding network hops, auth and failure modes for nothing
flags: "We have a researcher, writer, critic, editor, and manager agent" for a task one good prompt handles
"Results vary wildly run to run", handoff briefs too vague
"It costs $4 per request", coordination tax nobody priced
ask: What does splitting buy here, isolation, parallelism, or specialization?
What exactly does a worker receive in its brief?
What's the token cost multiple vs single-agent?
How do we evaluate the end-to-end output?
Do we own both agents? If so, why is this a protocol and not a sub-agent?

MODULES.title: AI System Design
MODULES.tag: The full production stack around the model call
MODULES.why: The model call is 5% of the system. Gateways, caching, queues, fallbacks, observability, and cost controls are the other 95%, and they're what page you at 3am.
MODULES.mental: Design AI systems like distributed systems with a flaky, expensive, slow dependency at the core. Every classic pattern applies (timeouts, retries, fallbacks, circuit breakers, queues, caches), plus new ones: token budgets, eval gates, and semantic caching.
concepts: LLM gateway

Single choke point for all model traffic: routing, fallback, retries, rate limiting, caching, cost attribution, key management. LiteLLM, Portkey, Kong AI Gateway, or in-house. Non-negotiable beyond one team.
Fallback chains
Primary model → secondary provider → degraded mode (cached/templated response). Providers have multi-hour outages regularly; design for it.
Caching layers
Prompt caching (provider-side prefix), exact-match response cache, semantic cache (embedding-similarity hit on paraphrases). Order-of-magnitude cost/latency wins on repetitive traffic.
Async by default
Anything not interactive goes through queues + batch APIs (50% discount). Reserve synchronous capacity for user-facing paths; stream everything interactive.
Cost architecture

Token metering per feature/user/route, budgets with alerts, tier routing (cheap model first, escalate on need), max_tokens caps everywhere. Cost is a first-class SLO. Price per completed task, not per call (agents and reasoning multiply tokens), and set the dials per route: reasoning effort, speed tiers (Claude fast mode and OpenAI Fast mode cost about 2× standard) versus Batch and Flex (about 50% off), long-context surcharges (GPT-6 Astra bills prompts over 272K tokens at 2× input; Claude has none), and data residency (Claude US-only inference costs 1.1×).
Observability
Traces for every call (prompt, params, tokens, latency, cost), eval scores on sampled production traffic, drift dashboards. LangSmith, Langfuse, Braintrust, Arize Phoenix, or OTel GenAI conventions.
Guardrail placement

Input rails (injection screens, PII redaction, topic filters) → model → output rails (schema validation, grounding checks, safety filters). Rails are cheap small-model or rule passes, not flagship calls.
Versioned everything
Prompts, model IDs, tool schemas, eval sets, pinned and versioned together. 'The model updated and behavior changed' should be a deliberate event, not a surprise.
mistakes: Calling provider SDKs directly from app code, no gateway
Synchronous calls for batch-shaped work at 2× the price
No per-feature cost attribution until the bill doubles
Retrying non-idempotent agent actions blindly
Pinning nothing, silent model/prompt drift
One global rate limit shared by interactive and batch traffic
flags: "The AI bill surprised us", no metering or budgets
"Provider outage = our outage", no fallback chain
"We found out from users", no eval sampling on prod traffic
ask: What happens, step by step, when the primary provider goes down?
What's cost per request by route, and who watches it?
What % of traffic could move to batch/async?
Where are the guardrails, and what do they catch monthly?

MODULES.title: Evaluation & Eval Harnesses
MODULES.tag: The discipline that separates shipping from guessing
MODULES.why: Probabilistic systems can't be unit-tested into correctness. Evals are how you know quality went up, catch regressions before users do, and ship prompt or model changes with evidence. Teams without evals are flying IFR with no instruments.
MODULES.mental: Evals are the test suite for behavior: golden datasets are your fixtures, scorers are your assertions, the eval harness is your CI. No eval, no deploy, exactly like no tests, no merge.
concepts: The eval stack

Golden dataset (curated input→expected pairs, grown from real failures) → scorers (exact match, rubric, model-graded) → harness (runs the suite, reports, gates CI) → production sampling (online evals on live traffic).
LLM-as-judge

A model grades outputs against a rubric. Now standard practice, near-human agreement when configured well. Rules: binary judgments beat 1–10 scales, one criterion per judge call, calibrate against human labels periodically, and never let the generating model grade itself ungated.
Judge bias & agreement

Judges have systematic biases: position (pairwise judges favor one slot, so run both orders), length (longer reads as better, so control for it) and self-preference (a model family rates its own outputs higher, so judge with another family). Measure agreement per class or as Cohen's κ, which discounts chance: a judge that says PASS to everything scores 90% raw agreement on a 90%-pass set, and κ = 0. Re-calibrate whenever the judge model changes.
Eval tooling landscape (2026)

Inspect (open-source, from the UK AI Security Institute, built for agent and sandboxed evals), promptfoo (MIT-licensed CLI with red-teaming, now part of OpenAI), Braintrust (hosted experiments and logging, PR comments with score deltas), Langfuse (open-source tracing and evals, part of ClickHouse since January 2026), MLflow 3, LangSmith, DeepEval, Arize Phoenix. Owners change, so keep the exit path open: datasets and judge prompts in your repo as JSONL and YAML, traces in OpenTelemetry. Pick one that gates releases; evals that don't block ships are decoration.
Agentic evals

Agents are evaluated in environments, not on strings: each trial starts from a seeded, resettable sandbox (repo, database, mock APIs, a simulated user when the task is a conversation), the agent runs under its production harness, and graders check the end state (tests pass, ticket resolved, no forbidden action) and the trajectory (sensible tools, recovery, stopping). Code graders first, a judge only for what code can't check. Cost, steps and latency per task are eval outputs too.
pass^k: reliability across runs

Run each task k times. pass@k counts a task solved if any run succeeds; pass^k only if every run does. With independent runs at per-run success p, pass^k = p^k: an agent at 70% per run passes all three of three runs 0.7³ ≈ 34% of the time, while its pass@3 looks like 97% (1 − 0.3³). Use pass@k when a human picks the best attempt; gate autonomous routes on pass^k.
Component + end-to-end
RAG: eval retrieval (recall@k) separately from generation (faithfulness, relevance). Agents: per-step success AND task completion. Component evals localize blame; end-to-end evals tell the truth.
Online evals
Sample production traffic, score asynchronously (cheap judge model), alert on drift. Your eval set is always stale; production is the real distribution.
Failure-driven datasets
Every production failure becomes an eval case. The golden set should grow weekly. 50 hard, real cases beat 5,000 synthetic ones.
Red-teaming
Adversarial evals: injection attempts, jailbreaks, PII extraction, off-policy requests. promptfoo and dedicated suites automate this; run it like security scanning, on schedule.
mistakes: Vibes-driven iteration, 'it seems better' is not a metric
1–10 judge scales (noisy) instead of binary/categorical rubrics
Eval set frozen at launch while traffic distribution moves
Testing only happy paths, no adversarial or edge cases
Evals exist but don't gate deploys
Same model generates and judges with no calibration check
flags: "How do you know the new prompt is better?" → silence
"We eval before big releases", should be every change, in CI
"Our success metric is thumbs-up rate", biased, sparse, lagging
ask: Show me the eval run for the last prompt change.
How many cases, and when did the golden set last grow?
What's judge agreement with human labels?
What samples production, and what alerted last month?

MODULES.title: Hallucination & Guardrails
MODULES.tag: Confidently wrong: engineering around the failure mode that erodes trust
MODULES.why: Hallucination is intrinsic to next-token prediction. The model is rewarded for sounding fluent, not for being true. One confidently wrong answer in a legal, medical, or financial flow can erase the product's credibility. You can't eliminate it, so you have to engineer around it.
MODULES.mental: Treat every model output as a claim from a brilliant, eager intern with no fear of being wrong. Trust grows only through grounding (citations to sources), verification (checks against truth), and constraint (schemas, allowed values). The system, not the model, is what makes answers trustworthy.
concepts: Why models hallucinate
Next-token training optimizes plausibility, not truth; the model has no internal fact/fiction boundary. Worst in: niche facts, citations, numbers, recent events, and anything beyond its data.
Grounding via RAG

Force answers from retrieved sources with chunk-level citations. 'Answer only from the provided context; say I don't know otherwise', then VERIFY citations exist and support the claim (entailment check).
Faithfulness scoring
An LLM-judge or NLI model checks: is each claim in the answer entailed by the retrieved context? Gate or flag low-faithfulness answers. This is the workhorse production defense.
Structured constraint
Schemas, enums, and allowed-value lists shrink the hallucination surface: a model can't invent a product ID if output is constrained to retrieved IDs.
Abstention design
'I don't know' must be an acceptable, rewarded output path, in prompts, in UX, in evals. Systems that punish abstention manufacture hallucinations.
Prompt injection

The other trust failure: instructions hidden in retrieved docs, emails, or web pages hijack the model. Treat ALL external content as untrusted data: delimit it, instruct the model it's data-not-commands, strip suspicious patterns, and never let injected content trigger privileged tool calls without checks. An agent that holds private data, reads untrusted content and can send data out has all three legs of the lethal trifecta (see AI Security & Adversarial Robustness): assume it can be made to leak.
Layered guardrails
Input rails (injection screens, PII, topic) → grounded generation → output rails (schema, faithfulness, safety, allowed-claims). Each layer cheap; defense in depth.
UX honesty

Show sources, confidence cues, and easy escalation to humans. Calibrated trust beats blind trust, design for verification, not authority. Disclose that users are talking to an AI unless it's obvious (an EU AI Act duty since August 2026), and attach an ai_generated label to every answer so each surface that shows it can label it; provenance marks on generated media are covered in Multimodal Systems & Document Intelligence. Resist sycophancy: agreeing with a wrong user feels helpful and is still wrong.
mistakes: Asking the model 'are you sure?' as the verification strategy
Citations displayed but never validated against content
Prompts that forbid 'I don't know', abstention punished
Retrieved/email/web content concatenated raw into context (injection highway)
Guardrails only on output, input rails missing
Treating low hallucination on a benchmark as product safety
Optimizing for thumbs-up, which trains agreement, not accuracy
flags: "The model cited a case/paper that doesn't exist" and nothing caught it
"Users found the wrong answers", no faithfulness gate
"An email told the agent to forward the inbox and it did", no injection defense on tool-using agents
ask: What checks an answer's claims against its sources?
What happens when the model should say 'I don't know'?
How is retrieved/external content sanitized before the model sees it?
Which guardrail fired most last month, and on what?

MODULES.title: Leadership Playbook
MODULES.tag: Judgment, communication, and the meta-skill of staying current
MODULES.why: Past senior level, your value comes from decisions and narratives: which bets to make, what to tell executives, how to grow a team's AI judgment. Technical depth is the entry fee. This is the differentiator.
MODULES.mental: Your job is portfolio management of irreversibility. Let teams move fast on reversible decisions (prompts, models behind a gateway, retrieval tuning), and slow down hard on one-way doors: data contracts, vendor lock-in, trust-destroying launches, harness rewrites.
concepts: Build/buy/wait

Buy commodity (gateways, vector DBs, eval platforms, harnesses), build differentiation (domain evals, data pipelines, product UX), wait on hype (most multi-agent, most fine-tuning). Revisit quarterly, 'wait' answers expire.
The demo-to-prod gap
Demos are the happy path at n=1. Production is adversarial users, edge cases, cost at scale, and 99.5% reliability targets. Budget 3–10× the demo effort; say this out loud at kickoff.
Executive translation

Frame AI work in risk/cost/revenue, not architecture. 'Faithfulness gating cut wrong-answer escalations 40%' lands; 'we added an NLI entailment check' doesn't. Always pair capability claims with their failure modes.
ROI discipline
Cost per task × volume vs human-time saved or revenue created, tracked post-launch, not just projected. Kill features whose unit economics never close.
Team capability

Grow evals-first culture: every engineer writes eval cases; failures become test cases; demos require eval scores. Hire for systems thinking and judgment over framework familiarity, frameworks churn quarterly. When agents write much of the code, measure delivery, not output: cycle time, defect escape rate and review load, never lines generated or self-reported speed-ups.
Responsible deployment
Know your obligations: data residency, PII handling, provenance/disclosure of AI content, human override on consequential decisions, audit trails. Governance done early is cheap; retrofitted, brutal.
Compliance engineering (2026)

Obligations you build, not just know. Know your role: under the EU AI Act a provider carries more duties than a deployer, and substantially modifying a model or shipping it under your name can make you the provider. Transparency duties apply now: disclose that people are talking to an AI unless it's obvious, mark synthetic content in a machine-readable way, label deepfakes. High-risk duties (logging, human oversight) phase in from December 2027. Expect auditors to ask for ISO/IEC 42001 or NIST AI RMF evidence. Where each control gets built: disclosure in Hallucination & Guardrails and Voice & Realtime Agents, marking and provenance in Multimodal Systems & Document Intelligence, audit logs and record-keeping in AI Observability & Production Reliability.
Staying current sustainably

The field turns over quarterly. Protocol: one deep re-implementation per month beats ten skimmed posts; maintain your own eval set to test new models in an afternoon; follow primary sources (provider engineering blogs, model cards) over commentary.
mistakes: Letting teams build agents before evals exist, backwards
Announcing capabilities to execs without failure modes attached
Treating model choice as permanent (it's a gateway config) while treating data contracts as casual (they're forever)
Hiring framework experts over systems thinkers
Measuring activity (features shipped) over outcomes (task success, unit economics)
Treating the EU AI Act as a 2027 problem: transparency duties already apply
flags: "We don't have time for evals this quarter", you don't have time NOT to
"The vendor says it's 99% accurate", on whose data?
"We'll add governance after launch", translation: after the incident
ask: Which of our current decisions are one-way doors?
What would falsify our success claim for this feature?
If the flagship model gets 30% better next quarter, what do we delete?
Who on the team can challenge a vendor benchmark with our own numbers?
Are we the provider or the deployer for this feature, and who decided?

MODULES.title: Fine-Tuning & Alignment Mechanics
MODULES.tag: When to reshape weights vs when to reshape prompts, and how not to wreck the model
MODULES.why: At volume, fine-tuning buys you unit economics and behavioral consistency that prompting can't reach. A mis-scoped fine-tune does the opposite: it destroys general capabilities, quietly inflates eval scores, and costs you weeks to recover from. Staff-level judgment is knowing when the math works, and knowing when to stop before the damage compounds.
MODULES.mental: Fine-tuning is surgery on the weight space; prompting is clothing. Both change outputs, but surgery is permanent. You can re-dress a model in 30 seconds. You cannot un-train it on bad data. The decision rule: if a prompted baseline with good few-shot examples hits acceptable quality, skip the surgery. Reach for fine-tuning only when you have a volume, latency, or consistency problem that prompting can't solve, a clean labeled dataset, and a regression suite ready to run the moment training finishes.
concepts: When fine-tuning beats prompting

Four specific signals: (1) volume, few-shot tokens at 500K req/day cost more than amortized training, even after prompt caching makes re-reads of a static few-shot prefix ~90% cheaper; (2) latency, eliminating a 2K-token few-shot block cuts TTFT materially; (3) consistency, behavioral style the model drifts from under prompt variation; (4) capability gap, an output format or skill the model genuinely doesn't have. Absent at least one, stop and improve prompts.
LoRA mechanics

Low-rank decomposition: freeze W (d×k), learn ΔW = A×B where A is d×r and B is r×k, r << min(d,k). Trainable params ≈ 0.1–1% of the full model, depending on rank and which layers you adapt (r=16 on every linear layer of a 7B model is ~40M, about 0.6%). Rank r=8–16 for style tasks; r=32–64 for new capabilities. Adapt all linear layers, attention and MLP: the QLoRA paper found all-layer adapters were needed to match full fine-tuning, and Thinking Machines' 2025 'LoRA Without Regret' study found attention-only LoRA underperforms even at higher rank. The key insight: model behavior lives in low-rank subspaces, you reshape the behavior without touching the knowledge-bearing full-rank weights. Alternatives worth knowing: DoRA (Weight-Decomposed LoRA) splits each update into magnitude and direction and typically beats plain LoRA at the same rank; IA3 learns small vectors that rescale attention and feed-forward activations, lighter still and fine for style-only adaptation; full fine-tuning stays the ceiling when your dataset outgrows the adapter's capacity.
QLoRA

LoRA + a 4-bit NF4-quantized, frozen base model. A 7B base drops from ~14GB of bf16 weights to ~4GB, so a QLoRA fine-tune fits a single consumer GPU; 16-bit LoRA needs a 24GB-class card; full fine-tuning carries ~16 bytes per parameter of weights, gradients and Adam state, over 100GB for a 7B (the paper's headline: a 65B model fine-tuned on one 48GB GPU). Quality: the QLoRA paper matched 16-bit full fine-tuning on its benchmarks; in practice gaps are small and task-dependent, and steps run slower because weights are dequantized on the fly. The practical gate to fine-tuning without an A100/H100 budget.
DPO vs PPO/RLHF

DPO (Direct Preference Optimization): offline, labeled preference pairs (winner/loser), no reward model, no rollouts, trains directly on a Bradley-Terry objective. Simpler, often matches PPO on helpfulness. PPO: train a reward model on preferences, use RL to update the policy against it. Use PPO when your preference signal is complex, conditional, or must generalize to unseen domains; use DPO otherwise. Both learn from preferences; when a program can check the answer instead, RL fine-tuning with graders (next) is the better signal.
RL fine-tuning with graders (RFT, RLVR)

Supervised fine-tuning imitates answers you wrote; RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) optimizes against a grader you wrote. Each step samples several completions per prompt, scores them with a programmatic check (unit tests pass, exact match, the SQL result set equals the gold one) or a rubric-following model grader, and shifts probability toward the above-average ones. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) scores each completion against its own group's mean and spread, so it needs no separate value model; GRPO-family algorithms are the standard way to train reasoning models with RL.
