Recipes warm-start with SFT: DeepSeek reports that R1-Zero, trained by RL alone, suffered endless repetition and poor readability, and R1 fixed that with cold-start supervised data before RL; NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Ultra recipe reads 'Pretrain → SFT → RLVR'. Tooling: TRL's GRPOTrainer for open models; OpenAI's fine-tuning API calls it reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT), method.type reinforcement with string-check, text-similarity, Python, score-model or multi graders. Reach for it when you can check an answer but can't cheaply write the ideal one. The failure mode is reward hacking: the policy optimizes the grader, not your intent (a test that only checks format, a judge that rewards length), so read high-reward samples and keep a held-out eval the grader never touches.
Distillation (teacher to student)

Use a strong teacher model to label your real prompt distribution (final answers, plus reasoning traces where the task needs them), filter the outputs with your eval or a grader, then SFT a small student on the survivors. DeepSeek's R1-Distill models are the public template: six Qwen2.5 and Llama checkpoints from 1.5B to 70B, fine-tuned on samples generated by R1, and DeepSeek reports that distilling R1's reasoning into small models beat running RL on the small models directly. It pays on narrow, high-volume tasks where the student runs on hardware you keep busy (Serving & Self-Hosting Open Models covers that side). Two gates first. Terms: provider terms often forbid training competing models on their outputs (Anthropic's commercial terms bar using the services 'to build a competing product or service, including to train competing AI models'), and MITRE ATLAS records distillation campaigns against Claude as a threat (AML.CS0056), so read the terms or pick a teacher whose license allows it (DeepSeek-R1's MIT license explicitly permits distillation). Ceiling: the student inherits the teacher's mistakes, so filter on correctness, not just format, and compare student against teacher on held-out data.
What RLHF changes in production

RLHF shapes the behavioral envelope, refusal tone, calibrated hedging, helpfulness style, not raw capability. Capability comes from pretraining. In production, RLHF-tuned models can be LESS capable on specific tasks where safety filters or refusal tendencies fire. Fine-tuning on top of an instruct model without instruction-following examples can erode RLHF alignment.
Catastrophic forgetting

Continuous fine-tuning overwrites pretraining weight patterns. Mitigations: conservative learning rate for LoRA (1e-4–2e-4 is the standard LoRA range; never use the default Adam lr of 1e-3 with LoRA, it's too high and causes instability); small, clean dataset (less gradient signal); LoRA itself (base frozen by construction); replay (mix 5–10% general pretraining-style samples into the fine-tune batch).
Base vs instruct model selection

Instruct model: add a new capability while keeping alignment, the common case. Base model: run a full preference pipeline (SFT → RM → PPO or SFT → DPO) from scratch, or when you need raw next-token completion behavior. Wrong choice: fine-tuning an instruct model on base-style text (no system/user role markup) strips the role-delimiter alignment it was built on.
Eval methodology for fine-tuned models

Hold-out test split must be drawn BEFORE any labeling or training work, contamination is invisible in loss curves and undetectable after the fact. Contamination signal: near-zero training loss plus a gain far beyond the usual 5–15 points over the prompted baseline (25+ is a red flag). Additionally: run a regression suite on 3–5 general tasks (instruction following, summarization, Q&A) before calling the fine-tune done.
The data quality bar

1,000–5,000 high-quality, consistent, edge-case-covering examples beat 100,000 noisy ones. Quality checklist: format consistency (same schema across all examples), factual accuracy (domain expert review), correct task behavior on hard cases, coverage of the failure modes you're trying to fix. Manual review of at least 200 examples is not optional, loss curves cannot catch systematic label errors. Synthetic examples, including a teacher model's outputs for distillation, can fill coverage gaps only after the same review and filtering (Data Engineering for AI Systems covers generate, filter, mix).
mistakes: Starting fine-tuning before prompt engineering is fully exhausted, almost always the wrong sequence
Training on a dataset nobody has manually reviewed, systematic label errors are invisible in training loss
Using the default Adam learning rate (1e-3) with LoRA, it is 5–10× too high for adapter training and causes instability and catastrophic forgetting; the correct LoRA range is 1e-4 to 2e-4
No held-out test set defined before training begins, contamination is undetectable after the fact
Measuring loss improvement instead of task metric improvement, the model can memorize format and score zero on content
Deploying without a general-capability regression suite, RLHF alignment damage often shows up in adjacent tasks
No version control for the fine-tuned model artifacts alongside the training data and eval set
Trusting a rising reward curve: RL against a weak grader learns its blind spots (format-only tests, a judge that likes long answers), so read high-reward samples before believing the curve
flags: "We fine-tuned it and the loss went to near-zero", memorized the training set, not learned the task
"We're using all our production data as training data", no held-out split, contaminated eval
"We just need to fine-tune it a bit" before any eval set or labeled data exists
"Fine-tuning fixed the style" without testing whether it broke anything else
"We trained for 10 epochs to be safe", overfit; 2–3 epochs on clean data is almost always better
"The reward keeps going up", and nobody has read the high-reward samples
ask: What would a zero-shot or few-shot prompted baseline achieve, and what specific gap justifies fine-tuning?
What is in the training data, and who reviewed it manually?
Was the test split defined and frozen before any data labeling began?
What general-capability regression tests run after training, and what do they show?
What's the off-ramp plan if the fine-tuned model degrades on production metrics?
Can a program check the answer? If so, why are we writing ideal outputs by hand instead of training against that check?

MODULES.title: Serving & Self-Hosting Open Models
MODULES.tag: Inference engines, GPU memory math and quantization: what running the weights yourself actually takes
MODULES.why: Open-weight models are frontier-adjacent (2026 Model Landscape has the lineup), and some workloads have to run on GPUs you control: data that can't leave your network or region, sustained volume where per-token margins add up, fine-tuned adapters, offline and edge deployments. The moment you self-host, the bill stops being tokens and becomes GPU-hours, and what each hour buys is set by memory and utilization. Teams that skip that arithmetic often pay more per token than the API they left.
MODULES.mental: A GPU is a memory budget with a compute engine attached. The weights are rent: a fixed slab you pay for whether one user is talking or a hundred. The KV cache is the variable cost: every conversation in flight claims memory in proportion to its length. The inference engine's whole job is to keep that memory full of useful work, and your job is to keep the GPU busy enough that the rent is worth paying.
concepts: When self-hosting pays (and when it doesn't)

Good reasons: residency or sovereignty an API's regional endpoints can't satisfy, sustained high volume, fine-tuned adapters, offline or edge deployment, end-to-end latency control. What you take on: GPUs that bill while idle, on-call, an engine-and-model upgrade treadmill, and the safety filtering a provider used to run for you. The deciding number is utilization: $/MTok = GPU $ per hour ÷ millions of tokens served per hour, where tokens served is load-tested throughput at your latency target times the share of the week you're actually busy. Compare per request, at your real input/output mix, against the cheapest API tier that passes the same evals, not the flagship. Own-versus-rent across a whole fleet is an architecture call made from demand forecasts; this module supplies its per-GPU inputs.
GPU memory math: weights, KV cache, overhead

Weights = parameters × bytes per parameter: 2 for BF16, 1 for FP8, a little over 0.5 for 4-bit formats once their scales are counted (MXFP4 is 4.25 bits), so a dense 32B model is ~64 GB, ~32 GB or ~17 GB. KV cache per token = 2 (K and V) × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes, times context × requests in flight. That second term, not the parameter count, usually binds. Architecture moves it more than size does: grouped-query attention shares KV heads (gpt-oss: 64 query heads, 8 KV heads), sliding-window layers cap their cache, and latent or linear attention (DeepSeek's MLA, Kimi K3's linear and MLA layers) compresses it. Add a few GiB per GPU for activations and CUDA graphs. In MoE models, total parameters set the memory and active parameters set the compute per token.
Inference engines

vLLM and SGLang are the default open-source servers: continuous batching, paged KV, prefix caching (SGLang calls it RadixAttention), FP8 and 4-bit formats, speculative decoding, multi-LoRA and tensor parallelism on NVIDIA, AMD and TPU hardware, behind an OpenAI-compatible API, so gateway and client code don't change. TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA's own engine, NVIDIA-only. llama.cpp (GGUF files, 1.5- to 8-bit quantization, CPU plus GPU, Apple silicon) and Ollama suit laptops, edge boxes and single-user tools, not multi-tenant serving. Hugging Face TGI is in maintenance mode. NVIDIA Dynamo and llm-d sit above the engines for multi-node routing, disaggregation and autoscaling; Dynamo's own README says one model on one GPU doesn't need it. Choose by hardware and model support (read the model's recipe), then benchmark two engines on your traffic.
Continuous batching, paged KV and prefix caching

At small batch sizes decode spends most of each step waiting on memory, so engines pack every request the KV cache can hold into each step. Continuous batching re-forms the batch every step, refilling a finished request's slot at once instead of waiting for the slowest request. Paged KV (vLLM's PagedAttention) hands out cache memory in fixed-size blocks as a request grows, so nothing is reserved for a length it may never reach. Chunked prefill slices long prompts between decode steps so they don't stall everyone's next token. Prefix caching reuses the KV of a shared prefix (system prompt, tool definitions, earlier turns): the self-hosted twin of provider prompt caching. vLLM turns on both of the last two by default. When memory runs out, the engine preempts a request and recomputes it later, so preemptions are your KV-pressure alarm.
Quantization: trade bits, then measure

FP8 weights halve memory versus BF16 and are usually the safe first step; full-speed FP8 needs recent GPUs (vLLM's FP8 W8A8 path runs on Ada, Hopper and AMD). 4-bit cuts weights to about a quarter: AWQ and GPTQ (integer, weight-only), MXFP4 and NVFP4 (4-bit floating point with shared scales), GGUF k-quants for llama.cpp. When 4-bit hurts, it tends to be on reasoning, code, long context and less common languages, where generic benchmarks look least. Native beats post-hoc: gpt-oss was post-trained and evaluated in MXFP4, and Kimi K3 trains in it from SFT onward; quantizing a BF16 checkpoint yourself makes a new model you must evaluate. An FP8 KV cache halves the variable cost: calibrate its scales (vLLM's uncalibrated default is 1.0) and watch sliding-window layers, which are more sensitive to it.
Speculative decoding and disaggregation

Speculative decoding spends spare compute to cut latency: a cheap drafter (an EAGLE head, n-gram matches against the prompt, a small draft model) proposes several tokens and the big model verifies them in one forward pass, keeping the accepted run, so the output matches what the big model alone would produce. Gains track the acceptance rate (high when output copies input: edits, extraction, RAG answers that quote sources) and fade under load, since a full batch has no spare compute; vLLM positions it for medium-to-low QPS. Prefill/decode disaggregation runs the two phases on separate GPU pools and ships the KV cache between them, so TTFT and inter-token latency are tuned independently. It is a multi-node technique (experimental in vLLM, orchestrated by llm-d and Dynamo); on a single node, start with chunked prefill.
Serving fine-tuned adapters

A LoRA adapter (Fine-Tuning & Alignment Mechanics) is tens to hundreds of MB riding on a base of tens of GB, so one GPU can serve many tunes. vLLM (--enable-lora --lora-modules name=path) and SGLang (--lora-paths) batch requests for different adapters together; the client picks one by passing its name as model. Check the caps: vLLM allows one adapter per batch (--max-loras) and rank 16 (--max-lora-rank) until you raise them; SGLang defaults to 8 per batch. Merge for a plain checkpoint with no adapter overhead, at one model footprint and one redeploy per tune; hot-swap (serve unmerged) to share one base across every tune at a small per-token cost. A QLoRA adapter learned against a 4-bit base, so a BF16 or FP8 base shifts its outputs (usually slightly), and merging into an already-quantized base is unsupported or lossy for several formats: merge into BF16 and quantize the result, or serve unmerged, then evaluate that exact configuration. Keep runtime adapter loading off in production.
Operating the endpoint

Track four numbers: TTFT (queue wait plus prefill), inter-token latency (the decode speed users feel), output tokens/s per GPU at your SLO (the unit-cost input) and preemptions (KV pressure). vLLM exports them at /metrics, along with vllm:num_requests_waiting and vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc, the signals to autoscale on; never scale on CPU or on nvidia-smi's GPU utilization, which only says a kernel was running. Cold starts take minutes, so keep a warm floor. Run the engine behind your gateway like any other provider, with an API fallback route, and canary engine upgrades behind the eval suite: they change kernels, numerics and defaults (vLLM's default memory fraction went from 0.90 to 0.92 between releases 0.10 and 0.20).
Model supply chain and licenses

Weights are code you run next to your data: pickle checkpoints can execute code on load (safetensors exists to stop that), trust_remote_code runs the repository's Python (off by default in vLLM; pin a reviewed commit if you enable it), GGUF chat templates can be poisoned (MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0064), and a deleted publisher's model name can be re-registered by someone else (AML.CS0065). So: safetensors only, --revision pinned to a commit hash, checksums verified, an internal mirror. 'Open-weight' isn't 'open source', and the license is per checkpoint: gpt-oss is Apache-2.0; the Kimi K3 License requires a separate agreement for a model-as-a-service business above $20M revenue over 12 months and a 'Kimi K3' display for products above 100M monthly users or $20M monthly revenue, with internal use exempt; the Llama 4 Community License adds its own terms and an acceptable-use policy. A downloaded fine-tune carries its base model's terms too.
mistakes: Sizing by parameter count ('it fits on one GPU') and discovering at launch that the KV cache for real concurrency doesn't
Quoting $/MTok at 100% utilization: a week of real traffic, nights and weekends included, is the denominator that counts
Comparing self-hosted cost with a flagship's list price instead of the cheapest API tier that passes the same evals
Shipping an FP8 or 4-bit conversion, or a merged adapter, without re-running the eval suite on the exact serving configuration
Autoscaling on CPU or GPU-utilization percent instead of queue depth, KV-cache usage and TTFT
Load-testing one request at a time, or with synthetic prompt lengths, and extrapolating to production concurrency
Exposing the engine port directly because it has an API key: vLLM's --api-key covers only its /v1-style paths
flags: "It fits on one GPU", that's the weights; nobody has sized the KV cache for peak concurrency
"Self-hosting is 10× cheaper", at what utilization, against which API tier, and who is on call?
"We'll run the 4-bit GGUF in production", a local-runner format on a multi-tenant GPU server, with no eval run
"The model server is internal, so it doesn't need auth", until a scanner finds the endpoints the API key doesn't cover
ask: What output tokens/s per GPU did we measure at our p95 TTFT target, with our real prompt mix?
What is our average utilization over a full week, and what $/MTok does that imply?
Which API tier passes the same eval suite, and what does it cost per request at our input/output mix?
What happens when the GPU pool is saturated or down: queue, shed, or spill to an API route?
Who pinned the checkpoint's revision, reviewed its license, and signed off its quantization on our evals?

MODULES.title: AI Security & Adversarial Robustness
MODULES.tag: New attack surfaces, new attack classes: engineering a system that holds under adversarial pressure
MODULES.why: Every LLM feature you ship is a new attack surface. Prompt injection, jailbreaks, and supply-chain attacks buried in tool results are production incident classes, not theoretical worries. The threat model, the pre-launch red-team, and the defense architecture all land on the staff engineer, because no amount of vendor alignment makes a system safe without the structural controls you design yourself.
MODULES.mental: Your AI system is a trusted executive who reads every email, including the ones from attackers. Design as if the model cannot be made adversarially robust, because no model resists a sufficiently crafted attack. The controls that actually hold are structural: external content framed as untrusted data, privileged actions gated independently of anything the model read, and defense-in-depth that never relies on the model's judgment as the last line.
concepts: Direct and indirect prompt injection

Direct: the user's own message carries instructions that override system behavior, the classic 'ignore prior instructions' family. Indirect: attacker-controlled content arrives through the environment (retrieved documents, emails, web pages, tool results) while the agent does a legitimate task, so no malicious user is needed; it is the higher-severity case for agents, because whatever the agent reads can steer what it does next. Mechanically both work the same way: the model has no instruction/data boundary in token space, so a well-crafted payload looks like any other instruction. Classifiers and narrow role framing ('your only job is X') reduce exposure; no prompt wording eliminates it. OWASP files both under LLM01:2026 Prompt Injection; MITRE ATLAS under AML.T0051 LLM Prompt Injection, with sub-techniques .000 Direct and .001 Indirect.
Multi-hop and multi-modal injection

Multi-hop: a payload planted in memory, a tool result, or an agent handoff activates in a later context. Multi-modal: hidden text in images (white-on-white, adversarial pixels encoding text, image metadata), instructions embedded in audio, or injections in retrieved documents containing figure OCR text. Agents that read screens and web pages meet the same attack through pixels and page text; Computer-Use & Browser Agents covers that surface.
The lethal trifecta

Simon Willison's test for any agent: does it combine access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and a way to communicate externally? If all three meet in one agent, assume an injected instruction can read the data and send it out. Filters lower the odds; only cutting a leg removes the condition, and egress is usually the cheapest leg to cut. The outbound channel is wider than a send_email tool: a markdown image or link whose URL carries the data and that the client renders automatically (MITRE ATLAS AML.T0077, LLM Response Rendering), any tool call that writes outward (HTTP, email, an issue comment, a BCC line), DNS lookups, URL parameters, logs. EchoLeak (ATLAS AML.CS0059) is the reference case: one email, zero clicks, and Microsoft 365 Copilot sent data to attacker-controlled URLs past its injection classifier and link redaction. Meta's Agents Rule of Two, which OWASP LLM01:2026 adopts as a floor, turns the test into a budget: an agent may hold at most two of untrusted input, sensitive data or systems, and the ability to change state or communicate externally; all three require per-action human approval. Render model output defensively too: no auto-loaded remote images or link unfurls, allow-listed link domains, invisible Unicode stripped at render as well as at ingest.
Injection-resistant agent designs

Patterns that make injection harmless by construction instead of unlikely. Action-selector: the model maps a request to one of a fixed set of actions and never reads their results, so nothing it reads can redirect it. Plan-then-execute: the model commits to a plan (which tools, in what order) from the trusted request before it touches untrusted data; injected text can still corrupt a step's arguments but cannot add actions. Dual LLM: a privileged model plans and calls tools but never sees untrusted text; a quarantined model with no tools reads that text and returns results as opaque variables the privileged side passes along unread. CaMeL (Google, Google DeepMind and ETH Zurich) hardens the dual-LLM idea: the privileged model writes a small program from the user's query, a custom interpreter runs it, values derived from untrusted data carry capability labels, and policies stop them from flowing into sensitive tool arguments; the released code is a research artifact, not a product. The shared price is flexibility: each design gives up open-ended 'read this, then decide what to do next' autonomy, which is exactly the capability an attacker hijacks. Pair them with egress allow-lists and the rendering controls above.
Agent identity and authorization

Decide whose authority each tool call runs under. Delegated (on behalf of a signed-in user, via OAuth): the agent can never exceed that user's permissions, and the audit trail names a real person. Shared service account: one identity for everyone, so any user, or any injected instruction, can reach everything the account can. Prefer delegated, narrowly scoped, short-lived tokens issued per task. Credentials never enter the context window: the model asks for an action, trusted code attaches the token, and identity comes from the authenticated session, never from model output (ATLAS lists harvesting credentials through agent tools as AML.T0098). Remote MCP servers use the protocol's OAuth-based authorization with audience-bound tokens and no token passthrough (Tool / Function Calling covers it). Make every consequential action attributable: user, agent and version, tool and arguments, approval and approver, joined by one trace ID (AI Observability & Production Reliability covers the audit log).
Jailbreak pattern families

(1) Prompt wrapping: role-play framing ('pretend you have no restrictions'), fiction laundering ('write a story where a character explains…'); (2) Multi-turn escalation (Crescendo-style): start benign and ratchet toward harmful across a long conversation, each step small enough to pass; (3) Encoding attacks: base64, ROT13, leetspeak, invisible Unicode to bypass keyword classifiers; (4) Many-shot jailbreaking: pack dozens to hundreds of faux dialogues showing compliance into one prompt before the harmful request, exploiting in-context learning to override alignment (Anthropic, 2024).
Structured red-team methodology

Threat model first: actor (curious user, external attacker, malicious insider, compromised upstream), motive, capability, entry point. Attack surface enumeration: every channel that feeds external content to the model. Manual probing (human red-teamers are more creative than any fuzzer). Automated sweep: promptfoo red-team mode with injection, jailbreak, and PII-extraction test suites. Run pre-launch and on schedule (quarterly minimum). Test against adaptive attackers who know your defenses: OWASP's 2026 LLM01 entry cites research in which most of 12 recent defenses held up against static attack sets but fell to adaptive attacks more than 90% of the time. Write findings in a shared vocabulary: MITRE ATLAS (v2026.09) catalogs AI attack techniques and real incidents (AML.T0051 LLM Prompt Injection, AML.T0054 LLM Jailbreak, AML.T0110 AI Agent Tool Poisoning, AML.T0086 Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation), so the threat model, the red-team report and the incident ticket point at the same IDs.
OWASP LLM Top 10 (2026) as a review checklist

The 2026 edition, published August 2026 and the first weighted by real incident data: LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, LLM03 Excessive Agency (the agent takes consequential actions without gates), LLM04 Supply Chain (models, adapters, MCP servers, hallucinated package names), LLM05 Data and Model Poisoning, LLM06 Unbounded Consumption (cost and denial-of-service abuse), LLM07 Misinformation, LLM08 Hidden Context Exposure (system prompts and tool schemas are discoverable, so never put secrets or authorization logic in them), LLM09 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, LLM10 Improper Output Handling (trusting model output downstream). The numbers moved in 2025 and again in 2026, so cite them with the year (LLM03:2026). For agents, pair it with the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack through ASI10 Rogue Agents). Walk both lists before any feature launches.
Agent supply chain

Everything an agent loads is code you didn't write: MCP servers, tool packages, skills and rules files, plugins, model weights and adapters, and the packages it installs. Tool poisoning: instructions hidden in a tool's description or schema, which the model reads as trusted (ATLAS AML.T0110). Rug pull: a tool changes after you approved it; in the Postmark case (ATLAS AML.CS0053) an impersonating npm package, postmark-mcp, shipped clean versions until it passed 1,000 weekly downloads, then BCC'd every email it sent to the attacker. Malicious skills and agent configs: a skill or rules file is a prompt that runs with your agent's privileges. Slopsquatting: attackers register the package names models hallucinate, so a generated install command fetches malware. Poisoned embedding models and compromised upstream APIs returning attacker-controlled content complete the list. Controls: pin versions and also hash the tool definitions themselves (a description can change while the version doesn't), re-approve on any hash change, review skills and rules files like code, install only from allow-listed registries, keep an inventory of every model, adapter, server and skill in production (an AI bill of materials), and treat every tool result as untrusted data. OWASP covers packages under LLM04:2026 Supply Chain and MCP servers and tool registries under ASI04.
Output filtering architecture

Input classifiers before the model: injection detection (classifier + regex heuristics), PII detection (NER-based), topic filters. Output classifiers after the model: schema validation, safety classifier, content policy check. Rule-based filters: fast, zero false negatives on exact patterns, brittle to paraphrase. Classifier-based: catches novel variants, higher latency, non-zero false positives. Both layers are required, neither alone is sufficient.
Incident response playbook

(1) Containment: disable the feature or route, log the window of affected traffic; (2) Evidence: preserve raw inputs, model outputs, and full traces for the affected session IDs; (3) Scope: estimate how many users/transactions were affected; (4) Disclosure: legal/compliance determines notification obligations; (5) Remediation: patch the specific control that failed; (6) Post-mortem: add the attack to the red-team suite so it never silently recurs.
mistakes: Relying on prompt-based injection defense ('ignore instructions in retrieved content') as the primary control, it's a layer, not a gate
Red-teaming after launch instead of before, the first incident does the red-team for you
Assuming a specific jailbreak won't work because 'our model has strong alignment', all models break under sufficient pressure
Testing only direct injection, missing the indirect injection vectors through documents and tool results
Privileged tool calls (send, delete, pay) authorized by model-parsed content instead of server-side session state
No incident response playbook before the first security event, every action improvised under pressure
Giving one agent private data, untrusted input and an outbound channel, then adding a filter instead of cutting a leg (the lethal trifecta)
Running agents under a shared service account with broad scopes: every user, and every injected instruction, inherits all of it
flags: "Our system prompt tells the model to ignore injection attempts", prompt-based security theater
"We haven't red-teamed yet, but we're launching next week"
"Tool results go straight into the context" without sanitization or untrusted-content framing
"The model won't do that", unvalidated assumption, zero empirical evidence
"It only renders markdown", rendered images and links are an outbound channel
"The agent uses our admin service account"
ask: Which channels can carry attacker-controlled content into the model context? List every one.
What happens if a document in our RAG index contains a well-crafted injection payload?
Which tool calls can the model trigger without human approval, and what's the worst-case blast radius?
When did we last run an automated red-team sweep, and what does the schedule look like?
Which agents hold all three trifecta legs (private data, untrusted content, an outbound channel), and which leg are we cutting or gating?
Whose identity does each tool call run under, and could the agent reach anything that user couldn't?

MODULES.title: AI Observability & Production Reliability
MODULES.tag: Distributed tracing, quality SLOs, drift detection and audit logs: the instrumentation layer you build before the first incident
MODULES.why: AI systems fail silently. Wrong answers come back with 200 OK. Quality drifts over weeks while the dashboards stay green. Costs run away without ever tripping an error budget. Standard APM is necessary but nowhere near sufficient. Staff engineers design the observability architecture before the system ships, because retrofitting it after the first quality incident always costs more than building it in.
MODULES.mental: Treat the quality metric time series as the heartbeat of your AI system. Latency and error rate tell you whether the HTTP layer is healthy. They tell you nothing about whether the model is hallucinating at 12%. Every AI production system needs three instruments: traces (what did the model see and do), quality scores (is it doing it well), and drift alerts (is the distribution shifting). Miss any one, and you'll hear about it from users first.
concepts: Distributed tracing for agentic systems

Standard HTTP spans capture the network call. AI-specific span attributes come from the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (still marked Development, so pin the version you emit): gen_ai.operation.name, gen_ai.provider.name (it replaced the older gen_ai.system), gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.response.model (the snapshot that actually answered, which is how you catch a moving alias), gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens; agent loops get invoke_agent and execute_tool spans with gen_ai.tool.name. The session key this module calls trajectory_id (shared across all turns in one agent session) maps to gen_ai.conversation.id. Still custom: cost_usd (the conventions record tokens, not prices) and loop_iteration. Every tool call is a child span; sub-agent invocations are linked traces. Without a trajectory ID, debugging a multi-turn agent failure is archaeology.
SLOs for probabilistic systems

Latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99) work unchanged. Quality SLOs require a measurable metric: faithfulness_rate (from async online eval scoring), task_success_rate, abstention_rate. Define error budget as: X% of traffic allowed below the quality threshold per rolling week. The discipline of writing down 'we will alert if faithfulness_rate drops below 82% on a 7-day rolling window' forces you to define what quality means before shipping.
Online eval sampling pipelines

Sample 2–5% of production traffic into an async queue. Score each sample with a cheap judge model (different family from the generator). Write scores + trace IDs to a time-series store. Alert on rolling-average regression (7-day window, threshold drift > 3 points from 30-day baseline). This is the only instrument that catches quality degradation before users do.
Agent quality signals in production

An agent can return 200 OK on every call and still fail the task, so measure per task, not per call: task success rate (a deterministic checker where one exists, a judge on a sample otherwise), steps and tool calls per task (the GenAI conventions define gen_ai.invoke_agent.tool_calls and gen_ai.invoke_agent.inference_calls histograms per agent invocation), tool error and retry rates per tool, budget stops (runs cut off by a step or cost cap), human escalation and override rates, and cost per successful task rather than cost per call. Run a small fixed canary suite against production on a schedule, several runs per task, and alert on pass^k, the share of tasks that pass every run (Evaluation & Eval Harnesses covers the method); one run per task hides the flakiness users feel. A rising steps-per-task curve is often the first sign of a degraded tool or a confused prompt, days before success rate moves.
Behavioral drift vs data distribution drift vs performance drift

Behavioral drift: model output distribution changed, detect via semantic embedding shift in sampled responses (KL divergence or drift distance on response embedding centroids). Data distribution drift: incoming query distribution shifted, detect via embedding shift in input queries. Performance drift: quality metric dropped, detect via online eval score series. These have different causes and different responses: performance drift is the alert to action; behavioral and data drift are the diagnosis.
Canary and shadow deployment for AI

Canary: route 5% of traffic to the new version, score both canary and control via async evals, auto-rollback if canary quality score drops more than N points vs control. The AI difference from standard software canaries: error rates alone won't catch a prompt regression that answers confidently but wrongly. Shadow: route 100% of traffic to both versions, compare quality scores offline without serving shadow responses. Use shadow for high-risk changes.
Incident playbooks for AI-specific failure modes

Hallucination spike: faithfulness_rate alert triggers, sample 50 affected traces, check if a model alias auto-upgraded or prompt changed, disable feature if rate > 2× baseline. Cost runaway: per-route budget alert, check output token growth and cache hit rate drop, identify the route. Prompt injection event: quarantine affected session IDs, identify what was served to whom, evidence preservation before remediation. Each playbook should exist before the incident, not be written during it.
Audit logs and record-keeping

Traces are for debugging and get sampled, redacted and expired; an audit log is evidence and must be complete for the actions it covers. Record every consequential AI action: timestamp, trace ID (so the record joins the full trace), user and tenant, the model ID as served plus the prompt or bundle version, tool calls with arguments and result status, approvals with approver and decision, and inputs and outputs either redacted or stored as content hashes (redact before anything persists). Make it tamper-evident: append-only or object-lock (WORM) storage, each record carrying the hash of the previous one, and the newest hash anchored in a separate system so an edit, a deletion or a truncated tail shows. Set retention per data class (security events, decisions about people, raw content), reconcile it with erasure requests (IDs and hashes can outlive the content they point to), and build the export before an auditor or a customer asks for it. Which rules demand this, such as EU AI Act record-keeping for high-risk systems (phasing in from December 2027) and sector rules, is covered in Leadership Playbook.
AI-ready monitoring vs bolt-on APM

Standard APM: requests/errors/latency, necessary but not sufficient. AI-ready adds: (1) quality metric time series from async eval scoring; (2) per-route cost metrics (USD/request with alert thresholds); (3) semantic drift dashboards for inputs and outputs; (4) model version and prompt version tracking; (5) a token breakdown per route: input and output, cache reads and writes (gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.cache_write.input_tokens) and reasoning tokens (gen_ai.usage.reasoning.output_tokens), each a subset of its total. Together they explain most cost surprises: a cache hit rate that collapsed after a prompt edit, an effort change that multiplied reasoning tokens. Providers count differently (OpenAI's input total already includes cached tokens; Anthropic reports cache reads and writes separately, and the conventions say to add them in), so normalize before you compare. Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, and Braintrust all provide this; OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions let you build it yourself into any OTEL backend.
mistakes: Monitoring only latency and error rate, correct latency with wrong answers is undetected by both
SLOs defined exclusively on infrastructure metrics; quality SLOs not written down before launch
Detecting quality degradation from support tickets rather than from monitoring, users are a lagging, biased instrument
Canary deployments that check error rates without checking quality scores on canary vs control traffic
No trajectory IDs in traces, multi-turn agent failures can't be reconstructed from individual span logs
Retrofitting observability after the first quality incident, treating it as optional infrastructure
Measuring agents per call instead of per task: every call succeeds while the task fails, and cost per call hides cost per successful task
Treating sampled, short-retention traces as the audit trail: when a regulator or customer asks what the agent did and who approved it, a 3% sample is not an answer
flags: "The dashboards look green" when only latency and error rate are on the dashboard
"We found out from support tickets that quality dropped", no quality monitoring
"We can't trace what the agent did on that specific request", no trajectory IDs
"We deploy AI prompt changes the same way as API bug fixes", no quality canary
"It's in the traces somewhere", as the answer to who approved an action
ask: What is the quality metric for this feature, and what value triggers an alert?
Can you pull a complete trace for any specific user interaction, including every model call and tool result?
What percentage of production traffic is scored asynchronously for quality, and how often?
What does the on-call playbook say to do when the faithfulness rate alert fires?
For a consequential action last quarter, can we show who asked, which model and prompt version ran, what the tools did and who approved it, and prove the record was not edited?

MODULES.title: Data Engineering for AI Systems
MODULES.tag: The pipeline that sets your retrieval ceiling: chunking, embedding lifecycle, and the data flywheel
MODULES.why: The model and the retrieval system are only as good as the data pipeline feeding them. Bad chunking, mixed embedding versions, stale ACLs, and missing re-indexing triggers quietly cap quality at 60–70% before you write a single prompt. Staff engineers design the data architecture so the retrieval system improves on its own over time, instead of needing a manual tune-up every quarter.
MODULES.mental: The data pipeline is the invisible quality ceiling. Every downstream optimization (better models, better prompts, better rerankers) operates on whatever your pipeline hands them. A table split across two chunks, a stale document served as current, or an embedding model mismatch produces plausible-looking garbage with no error signal. Design the pipeline as if retrieval quality is a function of pipeline correctness first and model quality second.
concepts: Document preprocessing pipelines

OCR quality gates: Tesseract fails on low-resolution, handwritten, and complex-layout scanned docs; commercial APIs (AWS Textract, Azure AI Document Intelligence, formerly Form Recognizer; Reducto.ai) handle structured layouts but bill per page. Score OCR confidence per page and quarantine low-confidence pages for human review rather than silently ingesting garbage. Structure extraction: a layout-aware parser (Docling, Unstructured) or a table-structure model (Microsoft's Table Transformer) locates tables, headers, and figures before chunking. Check model licenses before production: LayoutLMv3's weights, for one, are CC BY-NC-SA (non-commercial). Normalization: Unicode normalization, header deduplication, whitespace and formatting artifact removal. For visually rich pages (charts, slides, scanned tables) you can skip OCR for retrieval altogether and index page images with a late-interaction model such as ColPali (RAG Systems & Pipelines covers it).
Chunking strategy design

Fixed-size (e.g. 512 tokens / 50-token overlap): fast, breaks semantic units, catastrophically fragments tables. Never the default for structured documents (tables, clauses, numbered lists); on clean prose the gap to smarter chunkers is often small, so measure it before paying for one. Semantic chunking: split at low-similarity sentence transitions (sentence-transformers to detect boundary points). Hierarchical: parent (section, ~1500 tokens) + child (paragraph, ~400 tokens); retrieve on child granularity, return parent for generation context, balances retrieval precision with generation context richness. Late chunking: embed the full document, pool sub-embeddings from full-context representations; preserves inter-chunk context ('the regulation described above') in the embedding itself.
Parent-child retrieval

Retrieve at child granularity (precise vector match), serve parent context to the model (full section with surrounding material). LangChain's ParentDocumentRetriever (now in langchain-classic) and LlamaIndex's AutoMergingRetriever implement it. The concrete win: a 400-token child chunk retrieves with high precision; the 1500-token parent gives the model the surrounding context it needs to answer correctly. Without this, precision and recall trade off with a single chunk size.
Embedding pipeline reliability

Version the embedding model as a first-class artifact, store model ID + version in index metadata, raise a hard error on startup if the deployed embedder mismatches the index. Re-embedding triggers: model upgrade (always), significant format change, domain shift detected via recall regression. Blue-green migration: build the new index while the old one serves, run recall comparison on the golden query set, atomic alias swap. Never mix versions in the same index.
Data flywheel design

Production failures → labeling queue → eval cases → (eventually) training signal. Pipeline: failure detection (low faithfulness score, user thumbs-down, empty retrieval result) → automatic sampling into a labeling queue → human labeling with a rubric → permanent eval case added to the golden set → quarterly review for training signal. The flywheel means the system gets measurably better every week without a dedicated improvement sprint.
Synthetic data generation

Safe for: expanding eval coverage of rare but real query types; generating diverse phrasings of documented facts (backtranslation: answer → question generation). Creates false confidence when used for: training data on factual domains, the generator hallucinates facts into training examples. Adversarial filtering: generate a large pool, filter with a binary judge (factually grounded? diverse from existing set?), keep the top 20%. Never use raw model-generated synthetic data as training data without this filter. Distillation is the same move at model scale: a teacher model's filtered outputs become a smaller student's training set (Fine-Tuning & Alignment Mechanics covers it).
Knowledge graph integration

Entity extraction (spaCy, custom NER) → graph construction (Neo4j, or in-process with networkx). Hybrid retrieval: vector for semantic similarity, graph for multi-hop relationships ('find the manager's direct reports' cannot be answered by cosine similarity alone). Entity disambiguation: 'Apple' in 'Apple vs Samsung' is AAPL; in 'apple allergy' it's the fruit, graphs store canonical entities and their context. Use graph traversal when queries require relationship chains that span multiple documents.
Data quality dimensions for RAG

Freshness: track last-modified timestamp per chunk; alert when chunks exceed the freshness SLA (e.g. >72 hours behind source). Access control propagation: when source document permissions change, the change must propagate to all derived chunks within a defined window, stale ACLs leak restricted content. Deduplication: SimHash or MinHash LSH at ingestion to avoid duplicate chunks boosting a single source's retrieval weight; deduplicate top-k results before reranking.
Event-driven freshness (CDC)

Batch re-ingestion makes freshness a schedule; change data capture (CDC) makes it an event. Read the source's change stream instead of polling it: Debezium tails database transaction logs (Postgres logical decoding, the MySQL binlog) and emits one ordered event per inserted, updated or deleted row through Kafka Connect or Debezium Server, and SaaS sources send webhooks. The indexer applies each event idempotently: chunks keyed by document ID and content version with deterministic point IDs, the new version upserted before the old one is deleted so search never goes empty, and a delete treated as 'remove every derived chunk', because a missed delete is a data leak, not just staleness. Permission changes travel the same pipe and patch chunk ACLs without re-embedding, under a tighter SLA than content edits. Events still get lost (connector restarts, log retention gaps, table truncates), so run a periodic full diff of source IDs and versions against the index.
mistakes: Fixed-size chunking as the production default, splits tables, clauses, and numbered lists at arbitrary boundaries
No version tracking on the embedding model used to build each index, silent quality collapse on any dependency update
Tables ingested as raw text, losing row/column relationships entirely
No freshness tracking, stale documents served as current with no staleness signal to the model or user
Synthetic training data generated without adversarial filtering, hallucinations baked into training signal
ACL propagation not implemented, permissions change on the source, chunks remain accessible to unauthorized users
Index updates that handle creates and updates but drop deletes: the document is gone at the source and still answers questions
flags: "We chunk at 512 characters", arbitrary, format-blind, table-destroying
"We ingested all our documents at launch and re-ingest monthly"
"The embedding model is just a dependency in requirements.txt", not pinned as an artifact with index metadata
"Tables aren't really a problem for us", hasn't looked at what the pipeline actually produces for tables
"We'll pick up deletions on the next full re-index"
ask: How are table structures preserved through the chunking pipeline? Show me a table from a real document post-chunking.
What triggers a document chunk to be re-indexed after the source document is updated?
How does the chunk's access control map to the source document's permissions, and what's the propagation latency?
What is the pipeline from a production retrieval failure to a permanent eval case?
When a document is deleted at the source, what removes its chunks, and within what time?

MODULES.title: Multimodal Systems & Document Intelligence
MODULES.tag: Vision-language pipelines, document ingestion at scale, and when to pay for vision vs when to skip it
MODULES.why: Enterprise document workflows (insurance claims, legal filings, financial reports, technical manuals) are full of tables, figures, and scanned content that text-only pipelines handle badly. Building multimodal document intelligence that stays reliable at scale means knowing when vision adds real value, when it's expensive theater, and how to route by document type instead of treating everything the same.
MODULES.mental: Vision-language models are an expensive retrieval upgrade for content your text pipeline can't see. The question is never 'can the model handle images?' It can. The question is whether the value of what vision recovers (a table structure, a figure's data, handwritten annotations) justifies 3–5× the cost and latency over text extraction. For digital-native PDFs with clean text layers, the answer is almost always no. Route first, vision second.
concepts: Vision-language model selection in 2026

Frontier proprietary (Claude Opus 5.5 / GPT-6.1 Sol class): best for complex mixed-layout documents, structured data extraction from tables, figure understanding. Gemini (3.1 Pro, still in preview; 3.8 Flash): strong native image, video and audio input at competitive pricing. Open-weight (Qwen, natively vision-language since Qwen3.5; Gemma, which has taken images since Gemma 3; InternVL): viable for high-volume, cost-sensitive, or data-residency-bound workloads with self-hosting budget. Cost profile: image tokens bill at the model's normal input rate; Claude charges ⌈width/28⌉×⌈height/28⌉ tokens, so a 1000×1000 page is 1,296 tokens (other vendors publish their own formulas and detail settings). The bigger bill is usually the output: paying a model to write out a page whose text layer pdfminer extracts for free.
PDF and document ingestion pipeline design

Digital-native PDFs: pdfminer.six or pypdf for text extraction, fast, free, accurate. Don't send these to a vision model unless the query targets a figure. Scanned PDFs: AWS Textract, Azure AI Document Intelligence (formerly Form Recognizer), or Google Document AI for production; Tesseract for low-budget. Score OCR confidence per page; quarantine pages below 0.7 confidence for human review. Layout detection: a layout-aware parser (Docling, Unstructured) locates tables, headers and figures before extracting; check model licenses (LayoutLMv3's weights are non-commercial). Table extraction: a table-structure model (Microsoft's Table Transformer, TATR, or Docling's built-in one) locates table regions, then recovers structure with row/column relationships preserved; TATR's repo was archived in 2026, so Docling is the maintained open option. Camelot (rule-based) works only on digital-native, fails on scanned.
Audio input patterns

Transcribe first (open-weight Whisper large-v3 or turbo self-hosted, or a hosted speech-to-text API; low single-digit WER on clean speech): enables all text-side processing, chunking, retrieval, structured extraction. Best for most use cases. Speaker labels belong on this path too: diarization comes from pyannote-audio on top of Whisper or from a diarizing transcription model (OpenAI ships gpt-4o-transcribe-diarize). Pass raw audio to an audio-native model: necessary when the task depends on prosodic cues (emotion, emphasis, hesitation), interruptions, or acoustic environment, and for realtime speech-to-speech agents. Cost: audio-native calls cost far more per minute than transcription + a text call. The routing decision: does the task require how it was said, or just what was said? Realtime voice agents (streaming speech in and out, turn-taking, interruptions) have their own module, Voice & Realtime Agents.
Structured data as context

NL2SQL: include the relevant table schemas (not all 500 tables) in context alongside the user question; retrieve relevant tables first via schema embedding similarity. For large databases (>50 tables), schema filtering is mandatory, attention can't find the right JOIN across 500 schemas. CSV in context: tables under ~150 rows can be included directly; larger tables need code execution (pandas) or NL2SQL. Schema-in-context tradeoffs: full schema enables flexible queries but consumes context budget; filtered schema is cheaper but may miss needed tables.
Cross-modal eval design

End-to-end task accuracy is insufficient, it hides which modality failed. Separate metrics: (1) OCR accuracy: character error rate on a held-out set of scanned documents; (2) Table extraction precision: % of cells correctly extracted with correct row/column assignment; (3) Figure understanding accuracy: key data points correctly identified from charts; (4) Answer faithfulness: standard RAG faithfulness metric on the final answers. Component metrics localize failures; end-to-end tells the user's truth.
When multimodal beats text-only

Complex tables where structure is visual (spanning cells, nested headers), text extraction loses relationships. Figures and charts where the data is not present in the surrounding text. Handwritten annotations. Scanned documents where OCR quality is insufficient for precise extraction but a VLM can tolerate some noise. Mixed-layout documents where column detection matters (newspapers, product catalogs). Multimodal is NOT better for: digital-native PDFs with clean text, simple tabular data where Camelot works, any document where pdfminer extracts clean structured text.
Latency and cost profile of vision calls

A 50-page PDF at 1000×1000px per page: ~65K image tokens on Claude (1,296 a page), about $0.50 per pass at this module's ~$0.01/page vision anchor, vs about $0.10 for the text path (pdfminer is free; the text-model call is ~$0.002/page). Small per document, decisive at a million pages a month. Native PDF input doesn't escape the math: Claude, for one, processes each PDF page as extracted text plus a page image and bills both. Short-circuit logic: detect if a PDF has a text layer (pdfminer returns non-empty text) → use text pipeline; no text layer → route to vision. Cache document analyses aggressively: if the same document is processed repeatedly (common in enterprise), extract once, cache the structured output, skip all future vision calls for that document version.
Generation APIs (image, video, speech)

Generating media is a different workload from reading it. Images come back from a synchronous call in seconds to tens of seconds, priced per image or per image token and higher for larger, higher-quality outputs, so cap resolution per use case. Video takes minutes: submit a job, poll or take a webhook, store the result, and design the UX around waiting and retries; budget per second of output. Speech (text-to-speech) is billed per character or per audio token and should stream, so playback starts before synthesis ends. These endpoints churn faster than chat models: OpenAI shipped GPT Image 2.5 (gpt-image-2.5-flare, gpt-image-2.5-sunburst) in September 2026 and marked its Sora video APIs deprecated in Python SDK 3.1.0; Google's SDK added deprecation warnings to its Imagen methods and to parts of its video-generation call, while Gemini-native image models carry on and Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS covers speech; open weights include Qwen-Image-2.1 for images and MiniMax-H3 for video with native audio. Put generation behind your own interface so a model swap is a config change. Three controls ship with the feature: refusals from provider safety filters handled as a product state rather than an error, likeness and rights rules (no real person's face or voice without consent, no trademarked characters), and provenance marking on every output (next concept).
Provenance and labeling

If you ship generated media, plan to mark it, in two layers. Content credentials (C2PA) attach a signed manifest saying what made the file and how it was edited; the open c2pa-python library reads, validates and signs them. Many uploads and re-encodes strip that metadata, so treat a missing credential as 'unknown', not 'human-made'. Invisible watermarks live in the pixels, audio or text itself and survive more processing; Google's SynthID is the best-known family, and its text variant is open (Apache 2.0) with a production implementation in Hugging Face Transformers for open models you serve. Text watermarking now runs on frontier models: since September 2026, text from Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 carries Anthropic's watermark (code less, since it must stay exact), and supported image, video and audio files that Claude produces through the code execution tool carry C2PA credentials when you retrieve them through the Files API. Anthropic offers detection through an API in private preview for regulators, researchers and similar groups, and its announcement notes an EU transition period for models launched before August 2, 2026. Text marks are the weakest layer, since heavy paraphrase or translation can wash them out. In the EU, Article 50 requires providers of generative systems to mark synthetic audio, images, video and text in a machine-readable, detectable way (Leadership Playbook covers who owes what). For you that means keeping vendor marks intact through your pipeline and signing credentials onto what you generate after your last transformation.
mistakes: Running vision model calls on digital-native PDFs with extractable text, ~5× cost overhead (at this module's $0.01 vs $0.002 per-page anchors) for no quality improvement
Not scoring OCR confidence and serving low-confidence extractions as ground truth
Using fixed-size chunking on tables, produces cell fragments the model can't interpret
Including the full database schema in NL2SQL context for a 200-table database
No separate evaluation metrics for table, figure, and text modalities, end-to-end accuracy hides which component is failing
No caching for processed documents in high-volume pipelines, vision calls run on every request
Stripping metadata in your own resize or format-conversion step, which silently removes the content credentials your vendor or your pipeline attached
flags: "We use vision on all our PDFs", no short-circuit for digital-native documents
"OCR quality is fine" without any measured character error rate
"We include the whole database schema" for NL2SQL
"We can't evaluate figure understanding", that means the pipeline is untested on its hardest cases
"We don't need to label generated images, users know they're AI"
ask: What fraction of documents are digital-native vs scanned, and how does the pipeline route between them?
What is our measured OCR character error rate on a sample of real production documents?
How do we handle a document whose critical data is only in figures, not in the surrounding text?
What is the end-to-end latency and cost for processing a 100-page PDF, broken down by stage?
Which outputs do we generate, and how is each one marked (credentials, watermark) and kept marked through resizing and re-encoding?

MODULES.title: Voice & Realtime Agents
MODULES.tag: Speech in, speech out, inside a one-second budget: pipelines, turn-taking, telephony and disclosure
MODULES.why: Voice is where LLM features meet the phone line: support, scheduling, intake and outbound calls. Speech-to-speech models now ship as production APIs, and open frameworks wire speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech together in an afternoon. The demo is easy. Production is a real-time systems problem: a one-second budget, callers who interrupt, 8 kHz phone audio, tools that take three seconds, and disclosure and recording rules a chat window never triggered.
MODULES.mental: A voice agent is a real-time system with a human on the other end who will not wait. Every stage streams, every stage has a millisecond budget, and the caller can interrupt at any moment. Text agents are judged on their answers; voice agents are judged on timing first: a correct answer after two seconds of dead air sounds broken, and an agent that keeps talking over the caller sounds rude. Engineer the turn (when to speak, when to stop, what the caller actually heard) before you tune the prompt.
concepts: Cascaded vs speech-to-speech

Cascaded: speech-to-text (STT) → a text LLM → text-to-speech (TTS), each streaming into the next. You get text at every hop (logs, guardrails, any LLM including your best tool-caller, best-of-breed STT and TTS) at the price of more hops and lost prosody: the LLM never hears tone. Speech-to-speech: one model hears audio and speaks audio (OpenAI's gpt-realtime-2.1, Google's Gemini Live API, Amazon Nova Sonic and others), with built-in turn detection and usually the lowest latency, but a short model menu, harder mid-sentence inspection, and audio tokens that pile up in context. Hybrid: a fast voice layer holds the conversation and delegates hard reasoning or tool work to a stronger text model. Choose per route on evals, not on the demo.
The voice latency budget

Measure voice-to-voice: from the moment the caller stops speaking to the first audio they hear. It is a sum of stages: end-of-turn detection (often the biggest), STT finalization, LLM time to first token, TTS time to first audio, and network plus the phone leg. Budget each stage as a parameter (this module's example: 250 + 150 + 250 + 150 + 150 = 950 ms against a 1,000 ms target) and stream everything. Generation outruns speech by more than an order of magnitude (a model streaming 100 tokens a second writes about 75 words a second; people speak about 2.5), so only the time to the first sentence counts: start TTS on it, and the rest of the reply is generated while the caller listens.
Turn-taking & barge-in

A VAD (voice activity detection) model labels each short audio frame as speech or silence; endpointing decides the turn is over. A silence timeout alone trades speed for cut-offs: OpenAI's realtime server VAD waits for 500 ms of silence by default, and its docs warn that shorter values may jump in on short pauses. Semantic end-of-turn models (Smart Turn, LiveKit's turn detector, OpenAI's semantic_vad) judge whether the utterance sounds finished, so the agent can answer fast after 'That's all, thanks' and wait after 'My account number is'. Barge-in: when the caller talks over the agent, stop generation, flush audio already queued downstream, and make the model's context match what was actually heard. Don't stop for backchannels ('mm-hmm') or the agent's own echo.
Transport & telephony

WebRTC for browsers and mobile apps: UDP media with jitter buffers, echo cancellation and packet-loss concealment built in. WebSocket for server-to-server legs (your backend to a model API, a phone provider's media stream to your backend); it runs over TCP, so one lost packet stalls everything behind it, fine inside a data center and poor on a shaky mobile network. SIP and the phone network (PSTN) for phone numbers: a carrier or SIP trunk delivers the call, transfers to humans often use SIP REFER, keypad presses arrive as DTMF, and some speech-to-speech APIs accept SIP directly (OpenAI's realtime API can accept, transfer and hang up calls). Phone audio usually arrives as 8 kHz G.711 (μ-law in North America and Japan, A-law in most other countries) while models want 16–24 kHz PCM; resampling can't restore what the phone network cut, so test STT on real call audio.
Tools and delegation in voice

Every second a tool runs is dead air. Play a short acknowledgment the moment the model calls a tool ('Let me pull that up'), owned by your orchestrator and pre-synthesized rather than left to the model, add a progress line if the tool passes a few seconds, and enforce timeouts with a spoken fallback. Prefetch at call start (look up the account tied to the caller ID while greeting; caller ID is a lookup hint, never authentication). Keep the voice-layer model fast: reasoning before the first token is silence, so run low effort (on Claude Sonnet 5.5, thinking: {type: "between_tools"} turns off up-front thinking) and hand slow reasoning to a stronger model in the background. Read back names, dates and amounts before any irreversible action.
STT and TTS choices

STT: streaming with interim results (start work early, commit on the final transcript), custom vocabulary or keyword boosting for product names, and an honest look at entities: a 5% word error rate reads fine in a meeting summary and is fatal when the misheard word is a digit of an account number. Confirm entities by reading them back, and take card numbers and PINs by keypad (DTMF). TTS: time to first audio, streaming text input, a voice that fits the brand, and pronunciation control for names and jargon. Above all, write for the ear: one or two short sentences a turn, no markdown, lists or URLs, numbers and dates as people say them. A 200-word answer is 80 seconds of audio nobody can skim.
Evaluating voice agents

Score four layers separately. Recognition: word error rate and entity accuracy (names, numbers, emails) on your own 8 kHz call audio, with your callers' accents and background noise. Timing: p50 and p95 voice-to-voice per turn, time to silence after a barge-in, false barge-ins (the agent stops for a cough) and missed ones (it talks over the caller). Task: simulated callers (an LLM persona speaking through TTS, with noise, interruptions and long pauses) scored on the transcript and tool calls; LiveKit Agents, for one, ships a test framework with judges. Production: containment (resolved without a human), transfer rate, repeat-call rate and sampled call reviews. A text-only eval misses the failures callers hang up on.
Cost per minute

Voice bills by the minute: telephony + STT on the caller's audio + TTS on the agent's speech + LLM tokens (or audio tokens on a speech-to-speech model). The LLM line hides a trap: every turn re-sends the whole conversation, so input tokens grow with the square of the turn count, and a 12-minute call costs more per minute than a 6-minute one ($0.048 vs $0.043 in this module's example). Cache the stable prefix (system prompt, tool schemas) and cap or summarize history; OpenAI's realtime truncation setting drops the oldest turns to control cost, at the price of a cache miss on the next turn. In the example, audio services are about two-thirds of the bill, so price them before you swap models.
Disclosure & consent

Say it in the first sentence ('I'm an AI assistant for Acme') and offer a human on request. In the EU, AI Act Article 50 transparency duties apply from August 2026: people must be told they are interacting with an AI system unless it's obvious, and on a phone call it never is (the Leadership Playbook module covers your role and the other duties). Recording needs its own notice and, in some jurisdictions, every party's consent. In the US, robocall rules treat AI-generated voices as artificial voices, so automated outbound calls need the prior consent a prerecorded call would. Clone a voice only with its owner's documented consent, and never accept a voice as proof of identity: cloning has made voices forgeable.
mistakes: Measuring latency at the server (model time to first token) instead of voice-to-voice at the caller's ear, where end-of-turn detection, TTS and the phone leg often add more than the model does
Canceling TTS on barge-in without flushing audio already queued in the client or phone provider, so the agent keeps talking over the caller
Leaving the whole reply in context after an interruption, so the agent later says 'as I mentioned' about words the caller never heard
Feeding text written for the eye to TTS: markdown, bullet lists, URLs and '$1,250.00' read aloud
Silence while a tool runs, then a duplicate answer when the caller's 'hello?' starts a second turn
Testing on clean wideband recordings, then shipping on 8 kHz phone lines with speakerphones and street noise
Taking card numbers and PINs by voice, which writes them into transcripts, traces and the model's context
flags: "Our latency is 400 ms", measured as model time to first token, not from the end of the caller's speech to first audio
"Callers keep saying hello?", dead air during tool calls or an overlong silence timeout
"It talks over people", barge-in that stops generation but not playback
"We'll add the AI disclosure in v2", it belongs in the first sentence of v1
ask: What is our p95 voice-to-voice latency, measured from the end of the caller's speech to first agent audio, and which stage owns the tail?
When a caller interrupts, how many milliseconds until our audio stops, and what does the model believe it said?
What does the caller hear during a three-second tool call?
What is our error rate on names and numbers in real 8 kHz call audio?
Where do we disclose the AI and the recording, and whose consent rules apply to the places we call?

llm.q: A chatbot's monthly bill doubled while traffic stayed flat. Two weeks ago the team shipped 'more detailed answers.' Which lever do you investigate FIRST?
o: Input token growth as longer conversation histories accumulate and re-send on every turn
A prompt cache hit-rate regression triggered by the new prompt invalidating the cached prefix
Output tokens per response, detail means longer completions at several times input price
A quiet provider price increase on the model tier you're running, applied without notice
llm.exp: All four can move a bill, but the timing points at the change: 'more detail' = longer outputs, and output is both the priciest token class and the latency driver. History growth and a cache regression are real effects worth checking second, but they don't double a bill in two weeks the way doubled completion length does, and a quiet price change would hit every route, not just the one that changed.

llm.q: On a model that still accepts temperature (Haiku 4.5, say), a team sets temperature=0, gets slightly different outputs on identical requests, and files a provider bug. The accurate assessment?
o: It's a genuine bug, greedy decoding is deterministic by definition, so any drift proves the stack is misconfigured somewhere
Expected: providers don't guarantee bitwise reproducibility (batching, hardware variance); enforce determinism at the application layer
You also need top_p=0 and a fixed seed, since temperature=0 alone only partially reduces sampling randomness
The drift comes from prompt cache hits returning slightly stale completions across otherwise identical calls
llm.exp: Greedy decoding is deterministic in theory (the logic behind the 'genuine bug' option), but real serving stacks batch requests and vary across hardware, so providers explicitly don't guarantee reproducibility. Seeds help on some APIs but carry no guarantee, and prompt caching reuses computation, not completions. Most current flagships don't accept temperature at all, so determinism was never going to come from a sampling knob: cache by input hash and canonicalize outputs at the application layer.

llm.q: On your eval, a Haiku-class model scores within 1% of the flagship for a classification route. An engineer argues for the flagship anyway: 'headroom for harder future cases.' Strongest counter?
o: Agree, but negotiate a volume discount on the flagship to make the headroom argument cheaper to honor
Run both in production 50/50 for a quarter and let live quality metrics settle the disagreement
Fine-tune the small model first to close the remaining 1% gap, then revisit the tiering decision
Route to the small model now; add an escalation path for the hard slice when it actually appears
llm.exp: 'Headroom' means paying 4× today (Opus 5.5 at $4/$20 against Haiku 4.5 at $1/$5), or 10× against Fable 5.1, for cases that don't exist yet. Tier-and-escalate gets you the savings now and a designed path for hard cases later. The 50/50 production test burns half the savings to learn what the eval already told you; fine-tuning adds work before capturing free wins; a volume discount shrinks the premium without removing it.

llm.q: Your request has a 5K-token static block (system prompt + tool definitions) and ~1K of per-request data. Which layout maximizes prompt-cache savings?
o: Static block first and byte-stable; per-request data appended last
Per-request data first so it's freshest, with the static block placed after it
Interleave static and dynamic sections so partial segments still cache-match
Static block moved into the first user message, with the system kept minimal
llm.exp: Caching matches the leading prefix byte-for-byte: a stable-first layout caches the 5K block (~90% off reads on most models); any volatile content before it, or one edited byte inside it, invalidates everything after. Putting per-request data first optimizes for a recency concern that end placement already serves; interleaving guarantees misses; moving the block into the first user message can still cache if it stays first and byte-stable, but trades away the system role's weight for no gain.

llm.q: A colleague claims 1M-token windows have made RAG obsolete: 'just send everything.' The strongest technical counter is:
o: Models can't actually attend past ~200K tokens regardless of the advertised window size, so the larger numbers are pure marketing spec-sheet padding
Filling 1M tokens costs about $0.20–$20 per call, adds serious latency, degrades mid-window recall, and bypasses per-user access control
Long-context windows will be deprecated soon as providers shift to retrieval-native model architectures anyway
RAG remains strictly cheaper to build and operate than long-context prompting at essentially any workload scale
llm.exp: The correct option stacks the four real arguments: per-call economics, latency, lost-in-the-middle (reduced, not solved), and ACL enforcement, which requires retrieval-time filtering. The '~200K attention ceiling' claim overstates (long-window recall is degraded, not zero); the deprecation prediction is invented; 'RAG is strictly cheaper' is false in general, since RAG pipelines carry real engineering cost.

llm.q: You sweep effort on two routes. A ticket classifier scores 94% at low, 94% at medium and 95% at high effort; an agentic coding route scores 61% at low, 72% at medium and 80% at high. The sound default per route:
o: Classifier at low effort and coding at high, then re-run the sweep after every model upgrade
Both routes at high effort, since the classifier still gains a point and one setting is simpler
Both routes at low effort, adding retries on the coding route until its pass rate reaches 80%
Both routes at medium effort, the documented middle ground for balancing cost against quality
llm.exp: Effort is a per-route decision. One point on a classifier rarely pays for high-effort thinking on every request, while the coding route gains 19 points from low to high (61% to 80%), exactly the hard, multistep work effort exists for. Uniform high pays thinking tokens on easy traffic; uniform low plus retries multiplies calls where depth was needed, so cost per completed task rises; uniform medium leaves 8 points (72% vs 80%) on the route that needs them. Defaults also move between model versions (Opus 5.5 defaults to medium), so re-sweep after upgrades.

llm.q: After a route moves from Claude Haiku 4.5 to Claude Opus 5.5, every request fails with a 400 because the code still sends temperature=0.2. The right fix:
o: Drop the sampling parameter and steer with the prompt, effort level, max_tokens and structured outputs
Send temperature=0 instead, because a fully deterministic setting is accepted on every current model
Pass top_p=0.9 in its place, which the newest Claude models accept as the documented substitute knob
Pin the route back to Haiku 4.5 permanently, since only it can still produce consistent formatted output
llm.exp: Claude 4.7-and-later models reject non-default temperature, top_p and top_k with a 400, and the Anthropic Python SDK v1.0+ removes them from its request types entirely, so the parameter has to go; control now comes from instructions, the effort level, max_tokens and schema-enforced output. Temperature 0 and a custom top_p are still non-default sampling values, and T=0 never guaranteed identical outputs anyway. Pinning back to Haiku 4.5 gives up the upgrade to keep a knob the new model doesn't need.

prompt.q: A teammate improved a support prompt's tone Friday; by Monday, refund-eligibility answers (same prompt) regressed 12%. The ROOT failure to fix is:
o: No regression gate: a multi-behavior prompt changed without an eval suite covering all its behaviors
No version pinning: an older prompt variant shipped alongside the new one and served some traffic
Tone and policy instructions inherently conflict, so they have to live in two separate models
No human QA: the change should have run against 50 real transcripts before it reached production
prompt.exp: The systemic fix is treating prompts as code: eval coverage spanning every behavior the prompt serves, gating every change. Hand-checking 50 transcripts is a weaker, non-repeating version of the same idea; version pinning addresses a different failure class; splitting tone and policy into separate models overreacts, since separation of concerns means decomposed prompts, not separate models.

prompt.q: You need machine-parseable JSON from a model on every call. The production-grade approach is:
o: Few-shot prompting with five well-chosen JSON examples that cover the known edge cases
Temperature 0 plus an explicit 'respond ONLY with valid JSON' instruction in the system prompt
Schema-enforced structured output, so invalid JSON is unsamplable by construction
A tolerant parser with automatic repair logic and a single retry whenever parsing fails
prompt.exp: Constrained decoding masks invalid tokens during generation, so the failure class is removed, not reduced (check the stop reason for cut-offs). Few-shot examples and a 'JSON only' instruction lower the error rate; repair-and-retry is a reasonable backstop, but as the primary strategy it means owning a parser and a tail of weird failures forever.

prompt.q: A model keeps using bullet points despite 'Do NOT use bullet points' in the system prompt. The highest-yield fix:
o: Repeat the prohibition at both the start and the end of the system prompt for emphasis
Add a frequency penalty during decoding to suppress the list-marker tokens it keeps emitting
Move the rule into the user turn instead, where it sits closest to the point of generation
Rephrase positively with a short example of the desired prose format the model should follow
prompt.exp: Models follow 'do X, like this' far better than 'don't do Y': prohibitions name the wrong thing without showing the right one. Repeating the rule or moving it into the user turn buys marginal gains; a frequency penalty is a blunt instrument that damages legitimate text.

prompt.q: You're moving a hard analytical task to a native reasoning model. Your old prompt has elaborate 'think step-by-step: first…, then…, finally…' scaffolding. You should:
o: Keep the scaffolding, since explicit step-by-step structure can only help a reasoning model arrive at a more reliable answer
Strip it: state the task and quality bar plainly; the model reasons internally and double-scaffolding can degrade output
Keep it, but relocate it into a dedicated scratchpad field the model fills in before it answers
Convert the scaffold into a few-shot example showing a full worked reasoning chain end to end
