prompt.exp: Reasoning models internalized chain-of-thought during training; imposed scaffolds waste tokens and can fight the model's own decomposition. Keeping the scaffold, or moving it into a scratchpad field, feels safe but micromanages; a worked-chain example pays example tokens on every call for reasoning the model already does. Spend the effort on task clarity, output contracts, and the effort setting itself.

prompt.q: Which observation most strongly indicates a prompt is doing too many jobs?
o: It exceeds 2,000 tokens and packs both detailed instructions and several few-shot examples together
It depends on both a system section and per-request user content in order to produce a result
Editing it for one intent keeps regressing unrelated intents that happen to share the same prompt
It relies on XML tags to delimit more than five visually distinct sections within the prompt body
prompt.exp: Coupling under change is the tell, same as a god-class in code. Length, a system-plus-user structure, and XML sectioning are all compatible with a well-scoped prompt; non-local regressions are not. The fix is decomposition: a router plus focused prompts, each separately evaluable.

prompt.q: Your extractor uses JSON mode, and the team adds a required field priority with three allowed values. A week later, some outputs omit priority or invent values like 'urgent-ish'. The durable fix:
o: Switch to schema-enforced output with priority as a required enum, so off-schema values can't be sampled
Add three few-shot examples that show priority, and keep relying on JSON mode to hold the output format
Lower the temperature and repeat the three allowed values in the system prompt to cut invented values
Post-process with a regex that maps any unknown priority string onto the closest of the three values
prompt.exp: JSON mode guarantees valid JSON, not your schema: a missing key or an invented enum value is still valid JSON. Schema-enforced output (Claude's output_config.format or a strict tool, OpenAI's Structured Outputs) makes the field required and the enum closed at decoding time. Few-shot examples and repeated instructions only lower the error rate (and current Claude models reject temperature changes anyway); regex repair guesses meaning and hides the drift your evals should catch.

context.q: An agent's output quality degrades noticeably around turn 40, yet the context window is only half full. Most likely cause?
o: Provider-side KV-cache eviction kicking in once a long-running session passes a hidden duration limit
Positional encoding quality degrading sharply once turns push past the model's original training length
Context rot: accumulated stale tool output, dead ends, and repetition conditioning the model toward noise
The system prompt's steering influence decaying steadily as each new turn grows its distance from it
context.exp: The window isn't full, it's polluted. Models are pattern completers, and 40 turns of unpruned tool dumps and abandoned reasoning actively condition worse output. Cache eviction and positional-encoding limits sound mechanical but don't apply at half capacity; system-prompt 'decay' has a grain of truth (recency effects) but isn't the dominant failure here. Prune and compact.

context.q: Critical compliance rules sit at ~token 60K of a 120K prompt and get intermittently ignored. The mechanism at fault:
o: Lost-in-the-middle: attention is strongest at the start and end of context; mid-window content gets the weakest coverage
The rules blew past the model's instruction-following budget, which tops out around a few dozen directives
The rules sit in the user turn, but compliance content has to be in the system role to bind reliably
120K tokens exceeds the model's reliable attention span, so the call needs to be split into two passes
context.exp: Position, not count or role, is the failure: U-shaped attention is a well-documented empirical property. Move non-negotiables to the start, keep the live question at the end. An 'instruction budget' isn't the binding constraint here; system-role placement matters but doesn't explain position-dependent failures; splitting the call gives up a workable window.

context.q: Your agent occasionally needs content from a 300-page manual. The best context strategy:
o: Embed the full manual in the system prompt once and lean on prompt caching to keep each call cheap
Maintain a hand-built 2-page summary of the manual and include it in every single request you send
Give the agent search/read tools to fetch relevant sections just-in-time
Fine-tune the model directly on the manual so the content lives in weights and needs no context at all
context.exp: JIT retrieval keeps the window clean and adapts to what each task needs. Embedding the manual and leaning on caching softens cost but not the accuracy hit of a stuffed window, and 'occasionally needs' means most calls pay for nothing. A hand-built summary loses exactly the detail that makes a manual useful; fine-tuning is slow, expensive, and bad at verbatim recall.

context.q: A long-running agent relies on compaction summaries to carry key decisions across sessions, and decisions keep getting lost. The durable fix:
o: Raise the compaction threshold so that many more raw turns survive fully untouched before each summarization pass is finally allowed to run
Persist critical decisions to durable artifacts (progress files, structured notes) that each session reads at boot
Run compaction more frequently so every individual summary covers less and therefore loses less
Pin each decision into the system prompt the moment it's made so it can never be summarized away
context.exp: Compaction is lossy by design: raising the threshold or compacting more often just moves which information dies. The harness lesson: state that must survive lives outside the context, in files/git the next session reads. Pinning decisions into the system prompt works briefly, then becomes its own unbounded context problem (and every edit to it invalidates the cached prefix).

context.q: Why spawn a sub-agent for a broad codebase search rather than running it in the main loop?
o: A sub-agent can run on a cheaper model, which cuts the raw cost of doing the broad search itself
Several parallel sub-agents return their results faster than one sequential in-loop search would
Tool-output size limits in the main loop would otherwise truncate the broad search's raw results
A fresh-context sub-agent absorbs the noisy intermediate output and returns only the conclusion
context.exp: The point is context hygiene: broad searches dump thousands of noisy tokens that would rot the main window for the rest of the session. Cheaper models and parallelism are nice side benefits, not the reason; output-size truncation is a symptom you'd work around, not the design rationale.

context.q: Your agent connects to five MCP servers and loads every tool definition on every call, about 55K tokens before the user speaks, and wrong-tool calls are rising. The best first fix:
o: Defer most tools behind tool search so only the few each task needs load, keeping 3–5 core tools loaded
Cache the 55K tokens of definitions so they bill at the cache-read rate, and keep every tool loaded
Trim every tool description to a single line so the whole catalog fits in far fewer tokens per call
Rewrite the tool definitions as prose in the system prompt so the model reads them as instructions
context.exp: There are two problems and one fix: the definitions tax every call, and tool selection degrades past 30–50 tools. Tool search with defer_loading loads the 3–5 relevant tools on demand (typically cutting definition tokens by over 85 percent) and leaves the cached prefix untouched. Caching cuts the price of the 55K tokens but not the selection errors; one-line descriptions make selection worse, because search and selection both read them; prose definitions aren't callable tools at all.

landscape.q: A team argues they no longer need to benchmark new model releases because 'the frontier models are all basically the same now, 1M+ context, similar quality.' The strongest technical rebuttal:
o: Leaderboards still show 10–15 point gaps between frontier models on hard reasoning tasks, and the gaps widen further on long-horizon agentic benchmarks, so they are plainly not all the same caliber
1M+ windows are commoditized, but 100× cost spreads to fill the same window make context volume a first-class routing decision, and harness quality swamps model deltas on agentic tasks
Benchmark contamination makes frontier scores unreliable, so any apparent similarity between models could just reflect memorized public test sets
Open-weight models have now closed the gap so far that which closed frontier model you happen to pick barely matters for real-world quality
landscape.exp: The cost-spread argument (roughly 100× between the cheapest and priciest way to fill 1M tokens, even inside one vendor's lineup) is the practical rebuttal to 'they're all the same': same window size does not mean same economics. And the harness-sensitivity data (the same model scoring 36 points apart under different scaffolding) means that for agentic work, model choice is often the second-order variable anyway. The leaderboard-gap option is partly true but argues capability, which compresses on real traffic; contamination and open-weight parity are real but softer points that don't address the team's actual argument.

landscape.q: Filling the same 1M-token window costs $0.20 on one model and $20 on another from the same vendor. The correct architectural takeaway:
o: Standardize on the single cheapest 1M model so that long context becomes affordable everywhere by default
Context volume is a first-class cost decision: tier and route by task instead of defaulting to one model
Cap every production context at 128K tokens until per-token prices across the frontier finally converge
Treat the premium models as mispriced and assume the 100× spread will mostly close within a single quarter
landscape.exp: A spread of roughly 100× is a routing signal, not a verdict on any single model: cheap tiers for high-volume easy work, premium for the hard slice. Standardizing on the cheapest ignores quality differences; a blanket 128K cap solves cost by capping capability; betting on price convergence is hope, not architecture.

landscape.q: A team selected its production model because it tops a public leaderboard. The most substantive senior-level objection:
o: Public leaderboards lag actual model releases by several months, so the headline ranking you chose from is already stale by the time you ship
Arena-style rankings overweight chat style and formatting polish over genuine correctness on real tasks
Public benchmarks are contaminated; the top models have effectively memorized the published test sets
Leaderboard deltas compress on your real traffic, and on agentic tasks harness quality swamps model deltas, validate on your own evals
landscape.exp: Style bias in arena rankings and benchmark contamination are real, partial issues, and leaderboard lag is overstated (trackers add new models within days), but the decision-grade objection is distribution: yours isn't the benchmark's, the deltas shrink on the easy middle of real traffic, and the published 78/42 same-model result shows scaffolding can outweigh model choice entirely.

landscape.q: What actually makes model-switching cost approach zero?
o: Restricting all usage to OpenAI-compatible API surfaces so that any provider can be dropped in unchanged
A gateway abstraction plus versioned prompts plus a standing eval suite to validate the swap
Avoiding every provider-specific feature (caching, tool use, structured output) from day one for portability
Negotiating multi-vendor contracts up front with explicit capability-parity clauses across the providers
landscape.exp: Wire compatibility gets requests flowing but says nothing about behavior: the eval suite is what tells you the swap is safe, and the gateway makes it a config change. Avoiding provider features buys portability by forfeiting the platform's best capabilities; multi-vendor contracts don't move code.

landscape.q: Open-weight models (DeepSeek V4, Qwen3.8, GLM-5.3) earn a place in your stack when:
o: You need the absolute best quality on hard multi-step reasoning, where every last point of accuracy matters
Sub-100ms latency requirements rule out hosted API round-trips, forcing inference onto your own boxes
High-volume cost-sensitive or data-residency-bound workloads justify funding real self-hosting MLOps
Your security team enforces a blanket policy against sending any data to third-party APIs, full stop
landscape.exp: The honest case is unit economics at volume and hard residency requirements, bought with real serving infrastructure and on-call. Absolute best quality on hard reasoning is still the closed frontier's edge; sub-100ms needs are usually solvable with hosted regional endpoints and smaller models; a blanket no-third-party policy forces the choice rather than earning it (and enterprise API tiers usually satisfy security teams).

landscape.q: A notice arrives: the model behind your highest-traffic route retires in 60 days. Which setup turns this into a routine change rather than a fire drill?
o: A gateway with pinned model IDs plus a standing eval suite, so the replacement is a measured config swap
A contract clause obliging the vendor to extend retirement dates for its strategic enterprise customers
Moving every route to the newest model on release day, so a retirement never catches the team behind
Reusing the old model's prompts and settings unchanged, since a same-family replacement behaves alike
landscape.exp: Retirement notices come with a fixed clock (Anthropic gives at least 60 days for publicly released models), and the replacement often changes API behavior too (Claude Opus 5.5 rejects forced tool_choice and defaults to medium effort). Pinned IDs behind a gateway make the swap a config change, and the eval suite tells you it's safe. Negotiating an extension only delays the work; chasing every release trades one fire drill for constant churn; unchanged prompts and settings are exactly what breaks on upgrade.

rag.q: RAG answers are mediocre and the team is on its third generation-prompt rewrite. What do you check FIRST?
o: Run a faithfulness eval to see whether the generation step is contradicting the passages it was actually given
Raise top-k so more candidate passages reach the model, on the theory that more context lifts answer quality
Measure retrieval recall@k on a golden set, is the right passage even being retrieved before the model sees it?
Swap to the newest embedding model and rebuild the index, assuming better vectors will surface better passages
rag.exp: Retrieval ceiling-caps the system: if the right chunk isn't in context, no prompt fixes it, and typical unmeasured pipelines miss 30–50% of the time. A faithfulness eval comes after you know the inputs are good; raising top-k and swapping in a new embedding model are changes made blind without the recall number.

rag.q: Users searching exact part numbers ('XR-4421') get irrelevant results from a vector-only pipeline. The targeted fix:
o: Add BM25/keyword search fused with the dense results, exact identifiers are lexical search's home turf
Increase chunk overlap at ingestion so part numbers never get split across a chunk boundary and lost
Fine-tune the embedding model on your part-number vocabulary so identifiers embed into distinct neighborhoods
Normalize identifiers into a single canonical form at both ingestion and query time so the strings line up
rag.exp: Dense vectors blur exact strings by design; hybrid retrieval is the standard fix. More chunk overlap addresses a different failure (split chunks); fine-tuning the embedder can help eventually but is weeks of work for what fusion fixes today; normalizing identifiers helps matching consistency but doesn't make a semantic index respect exact tokens.

rag.q: A pipeline feeds raw top-10 vector hits straight into the prompt. The cheapest upgrade with the largest precision gain:
o: Decompose each query into sub-queries and retrieve for every one of them in parallel, then merge the hits
Apply HyDE-style query expansion before retrieval so a hypothetical answer pulls in closer-matching passages
Raise top-k to 30 and rely on the model to read past the irrelevant passages and answer from the good ones
Run a cross-encoder reranker over the top 50–100 candidates and keep only the best 5–10 for the prompt
rag.exp: Reranking is the classic underused stage: one component, ~100ms, large precision win, the cross-encoder's joint attention re-scores what the coarse bi-encoder fetched. Query decomposition and HyDE are real but heavier techniques; raising k to 30 without a reranker imports noise and pays for it twice.

rag.q: Your RAG assistant answers questions about documents the asking user has no permission to open. The correct fix:
o: Add an output filter that redacts content sourced from restricted documents before it is shown to the user
Enforce document ACLs inside the retrieval query so restricted chunks never reach the context in the first place
Instruct the model in the system prompt to check each source's permissions before using it in an answer
Maintain separate indexes per sensitivity tier and route each query to one based on the user's clearance level
rag.exp: Authorization belongs in the retrieval layer, filter by the requesting user's permissions at query time. Output redaction means the leak already happened in-context; permission checks in the system prompt make the model a security boundary, which it isn't; per-tier indexes can work but are a heavyweight redesign of what a query filter solves.

rag.q: What distinguishes agentic search (agentic RAG) from a classic retrieve-then-generate pipeline?
o: Retrieved passages are checked by a separate judge model for relevance before they are allowed into the context
Queries are decomposed offline by a planner model into a fixed retrieval plan that runs the same way every time
Multiple specialized indexes are always queried together in parallel and their results fused into one ranked list
The model treats search as a tool, deciding when and what to query, evaluating the results, and iterating as needed
rag.exp: The defining shift is retrieval moving into the loop under the model's control, adaptive, multi-query, self-evaluating. A separate relevance judge is a guardrail you can add to either pattern; an offline planner's fixed retrieval plan is still a pre-step (the opposite of adaptive); always querying several indexes in parallel is federation, which is orthogonal.

rag.q: Your RAG pipeline shows recall@10 = 69% on a golden set but recall@50 = 94%. An engineer proposes sending all 50 chunks to the model. The correct response:
o: Approve it, 94% recall is a big jump and feeding all 50 chunks should directly raise the answer quality here
Acceptable for short documents where the 50 chunks fit the context window comfortably without crowding it out
Reject: context pollution degrades generation; add a cross-encoder reranker to keep the best 5–8 of the top 50
Approve it, but first add a diversity filter to drop the near-identical chunks so the 50 carry less redundancy
rag.exp: recall@50 = 94% confirms the relevant chunk is in the index, the bottleneck is ranking, not coverage. Passing 50 raw chunks pollutes the context window and pays token costs for noise. A reranker extracts signal and passes only what the model needs, this is precisely the gap the reranker stage exists to fill. Approving all 50, with or without a diversity filter, accepts the wrong fix; the 'fine for short documents' answer trades one scaling problem for a different one.

rag.q: Users query with internal abbreviations ('OOO policy', 'PTO reqs') but your HR document corpus consistently uses expanded phrases ('out-of-office policy', 'paid time off requirements'). Results from a semantic-only pipeline are poor. The cheapest targeted fix:
o: Fine-tune the embedding model on internal HR vocabulary so abbreviations embed near their expanded forms
Rewrite the user query to expand abbreviations before embedding, a single cheap LLM call at query time
Add BM25 to the hybrid stack on the theory that abbreviations are lexical patterns BM25 handles natively
Maintain a separate keyword index for short queries under 5 tokens, where most abbreviations tend to appear
rag.exp: Query expansion is the targeted fix: a cheap LLM call rewrites 'OOO policy' to 'out-of-office policy' before embedding, so the query lands in the same vector neighborhood as the corpus. Adding BM25 doesn't help here because the corpus uses the expanded form, 'OOO' and 'out-of-office' are different strings in both lexical and dense spaces; BM25 excels at exact token matches, not abbreviation-to-expansion bridging. Fine-tuning the embedder teaches the model the vocabulary eventually, but it's weeks of work for a problem a one-line rewrite prompt solves today. A separate keyword index for short queries has the same limitation as BM25, the abbreviation still doesn't match the expanded term. The diagnosis here is semantic drift from vocabulary mismatch, and expansion fixes it at the source.

rag.q: An append-only RAG index has been running 18 months. When policies update, new chunks are added but old ones are never deleted. Retrieval precision dropped from 61% to 44%. The most likely cause:
o: The embedding model's representation quality degrades as the corpus grows past a certain scale, weakening matches
ANN index fragmentation from continuous appends reduces recall, especially on the oldest entries in the graph
Semantic dilution: updated content coexists with its stale version, splitting retrieval votes between them
Top-k was quietly reduced during a cost-cutting sprint, so fewer relevant chunks now make it into each result
rag.exp: Append-only indexes accumulate semantic pollution: when a policy changes, old chunks stay and new ones are added, retrieval now surfaces both versions without knowing which is current. At 18 months, version coexistence dominates the precision loss. Index maintenance, staleness pruning, version supersession, deduplication, is the structural fix. ANN tuning and model swaps can't remedy data-layer contamination.

rag.q: Your RAG chatbot answers 'What is our standard refund policy?' correctly 93% of the time but 'What is the refund policy for international orders during a promotional sale?' only 38% of the time. The most likely structural cause:
o: The embedding model cannot reliably represent a query that combines several distinct concepts in one vector at once
The complete answer spans multiple sections, no single chunk holds the full intersection, so top-k returns fragments
The reranker is systematically down-weighting any chunk that happens to mention promotional or sale-related terminology
top-k is set too low to cover these compound queries, so the extra conditions push relevant chunks out of the results
rag.exp: Simple queries resolve against one chunk; compound queries require content spread across multiple chunks that rarely co-retrieve together in top-k. The fix is multi-query decomposition (retrieve separately for 'international refund' and 'promotional sale refund' then merge) or parent-document chunking that provides broader co-text. Neither the reranker nor top-k setting explains the specificity of this failure pattern.

rag.q: A RAG eval shows: when recall@5 succeeds (71% of queries), generation faithfulness is 84%. When retrieval fails, faithfulness drops to 28% as the model hallucinates into gaps. What is the effective faithful answer rate across ALL queries?
o: ~84%, since that's the faithfulness number on successful-retrieval queries
~68%, weighting faithfulness by the retrieval success and failure rates
~71%, since the faithful answer rate just tracks the retrieval recall rate
~78%, splitting the difference between the high and low faithfulness rates
rag.exp: Weight by retrieval outcome: (0.71 × 0.84) + (0.29 × 0.28) = 0.60 + 0.08 ≈ 68%. Reporting faithfulness only on successful-retrieval queries ignores 29% of real traffic where the model fills gaps with hallucination, the most dangerous category. Retrieval recall and generation faithfulness are compounding failure modes, which is why you must measure both components separately to diagnose the system.

rag.q: Support leadership asks: 'What are the recurring complaint themes across this quarter's 40,000 tickets?' Your hybrid + rerank pipeline returns eight vivid but unrepresentative tickets. The technique built for this kind of question:
o: GraphRAG-style indexing: extract entities, cluster them into communities, and summarize each one up front
A deeper reranking pass over the top 200 candidates, so the most representative tickets rise into context
Late-interaction embeddings, so every token of every ticket is matched against the question with MaxSim
Raising top-k to 500 and asking the model to summarize the themes from everything the retriever returns
rag.exp: This is a corpus-wide question: any top-k of chunks is a sample, however well ranked (a deeper rerank) or finely matched (late interaction), and a bigger k is a pricier sample, not the population. GraphRAG pays its indexing bill (an LLM pass over every chunk plus community summaries) precisely so 'what are the themes' questions have precomputed answers. Benchmark it against the cheap baseline first: cluster the ticket embeddings and summarize each cluster.

embed.q: After a routine embedding-model upgrade, search quality quietly collapsed, no errors anywhere. The cause:
o: The new model emits a different dimension count and the index silently truncated the extra values
The two models follow different vector-normalization conventions, quietly skewing every cosine score the ranker computes
Queries now embed in the new model's space while the corpus sits in the old one, cross-model similarity is meaningless
The new model expects input_type hints (query vs document) that the existing pipeline never sends
embed.exp: An upgraded model's vector space has an unrelated basis; comparing across the two produces plausible-looking nonsense with zero errors. A dimension change would typically throw a mismatch error rather than degrade silently; normalization differences and missing input_type hints cause milder degradation, not collapse. Re-embed the corpus or roll back the query side.

embed.q: You must cut vector storage cost ~4× with minimal, measured quality loss. The modern first move:
o: Deduplicate near-identical chunks before embedding so the corpus, and its vector count, shrinks
Move the vectors for cold, rarely-touched documents over to keyword-only search to drop their storage
Re-embed the whole corpus with a smaller model that outputs fewer dimensions per vector to save space
Truncate Matryoshka dimensions or quantize, validating recall at each step
embed.exp: Matryoshka truncation and quantization are designed for exactly this, graceful, measurable degradation without re-embedding or model risk. Dedup helps but rarely 4×; moving cold docs to keyword-only changes retrieval behavior for those docs; re-embedding with a smaller model is a full migration with unknown quality, not a tuning knob.

embed.q: Legal-domain retrieval underperforms despite using a top-5 MTEB embedding model. The highest-leverage fix:
o: Chunk by the legal document's own structure (sections, clauses) instead of generic fixed-size boundaries
Fine-tune the embedding model on a few thousand in-domain query–passage pairs
Add a legal-domain reranker on top to compensate for misses coming out of first-stage retrieval
Expand each query with legal synonyms and citation forms at retrieval time to widen the match set
embed.exp: All four are real techniques, that's the trap. But MTEB rank ≠ jargon-heavy domain performance, and embedding fine-tuning attacks the root cause (the model's representation of legal language) for the largest recall gains. Structural chunking, a legal reranker, and query expansion layer well on top, but they compensate rather than fix.

embed.q: Why do input_type hints (query vs document) measurably improve retrieval?
o: They route short queries to a smaller, faster encoder that's tuned specifically for brief text inputs
They normalize text length before pooling so that very short queries aren't unfairly penalized in scoring
Queries and documents are asymmetric text types; hinted models encode each appropriately
They make vectors from different model versions compatible, so old and new embeddings can be compared
embed.exp: A five-word question and a 500-word passage are different distributions; models trained with the distinction encode them into better-aligned spaces. The smaller-encoder and length-normalization options invent mechanisms; the version-compatibility option is false, hints don't bridge model spaces (only a family deliberately trained into one shared space, like Voyage 4, is comparable).

embed.q: Beyond retrieval, which is a production-proven embedding application?
o: Lossless compression of long contexts into vectors before sending them on to the model to save tokens
Semantic caching: recognizing a new request as a paraphrase of an answered one and skipping the LLM call
Replacing cross-encoder rerankers outright at the same precision while costing meaningfully less to run
Encrypting stored documents in a form that still preserves the ability to search them semantically
embed.exp: Semantic cache is a workhorse cost lever on repetitive traffic. Lossless context compression is impossible (embeddings are lossy by definition); replacing cross-encoders inverts the architecture, bi-encoders are the coarse stage, cross-encoders the precise one; encrypted-but-searchable storage is searchable encryption, a different field entirely.

vecdb.q: A startup with 300K vectors already runs Postgres. The team wants a dedicated managed vector DB 'for growth headroom.' Your call:
o: Approve the managed DB, migrating later at 10M vectors will be far more painful than just starting on it now
Move to OpenSearch, since their logs already live there and it does vector search alongside the text it indexes
pgvector with HNSW, at this scale it removes a system while keeping joins, transactions, and ACLs
Run embedded FAISS inside the app with nightly snapshots, keeping the whole search path simple and in-process
vecdb.exp: Below ~5–10M vectors, the bolt-on wins on operational simplicity, and 'growth headroom' is speculative complexity, migration later is a real but bounded cost, paid only if growth materializes. OpenSearch is plausible if it's already core infra, but adds an index tier they don't need; embedded FAISS trades durability and ops maturity for less than pgvector offers.

vecdb.q: ANN search with a selective tenant filter sometimes returns zero results although matches exist. The classic cause:
o: ef_search is set too low relative to the filter's selectivity, so raise it until the matching results appear
The engine post-filters: it fetches the top-k first, then applies the filter, which can eliminate all k
Tombstoned vectors from prior deletes are still being excluded, quietly shrinking the candidate set below k
The metadata index has drifted out of sync with the vector segments, so filter values no longer line up
vecdb.exp: Post-filtering is the textbook failure: selective filters annihilate an unfiltered top-k. Raising ef_search is the seductive wrong answer, it papers over the architecture problem expensively and incompletely; the fix is pre-filter/filtered-ANN semantics (in pgvector, iterative scans). Tombstones and metadata drift are real operational issues with different signatures (gradual, not filter-correlated).

vecdb.q: Nobody has ever measured the ANN index's recall against exact search. The risk you're carrying:
o: Minimal risk, modern HNSW defaults reliably hold above 99% recall across essentially any production workload
Recall only becomes a concern above ~100M vectors, where the graph starts to fragment and lose neighbors
Silent relevance loss: speed-tuned parameters can quietly cap recall at 70–80%, bounding the whole RAG stack
No risk that matters, the downstream reranker recovers anything the index happens to miss before scoring it
vecdb.exp: ANN trades recall for speed by design, and tuning drift is silent, no errors, just worse answers. The '>99% always' option is exactly the assumption that bites; trusting the reranker misunderstands the pipeline: a reranker can only re-order what retrieval surfaced. Measure against brute force on a sample, monthly.

vecdb.q: Why should the vector index NOT serve as your source of truth?
o: Vector databases universally lack ACID guarantees, which makes them fundamentally unsafe to hold any system of record
Embeddings cannot be inverted back into their source text, so once you've stored only vectors the original data is unrecoverable
Storage and retention costs grow quadratically with corpus size in graph indexes, so keeping truth there gets far too expensive
It's a rebuildable derivative: embeddings change with model versions and ANN structures need rebuilds, truth belongs upstream
vecdb.exp: The index is disposable infrastructure with a rebuild path from a durable store, that's the architecture, regardless of any engine's ACID story (the 'universally lack ACID' option overgeneralizes; some offer strong guarantees). The 'cannot be inverted' option is shaky (inversion attacks recover approximate text, a privacy risk, not a backup) and beside the point when you store source text anyway. Quadratic storage growth is invented.

vecdb.q: A tenant reports seeing another tenant's content in vector search results. The most likely design flaw:
o: Isolation relied on a soft metadata filter (or prompt instruction) instead of enforced namespaces/partitions at the index layer
Embedding collisions, where semantically similar content across two tenants maps to nearly identical vectors and then co-retrieves
A shared semantic cache is handing back another tenant's previously cached answer when two queries look close enough to match
HNSW graph edges are crossing tenant boundaries during traversal, letting one search wander into the wrong tenant's partition
vecdb.exp: Filters-by-convention fail exactly once and it's an incident; isolation must be enforced where the query executes. Embedding collisions are normal embedding behavior, not leakage; a shared semantic cache is a real adjacent risk but the report says search results; graph edges "crossing" tenants anthropomorphizes the graph, traversal respects whatever isolation you actually enforced, which is the point.

memory.q: 'Our agent's memory is the last 50 messages.' The senior critique:
o: Fifty messages is too few, real personalization needs at least a few hundred turns of history to work from
That's working history, not memory: nothing is extracted, persisted, or selectively retrieved across sessions
Raw messages should be summarized before they're stored, otherwise the buffer wastes tokens carrying noise
The buffer should be bounded by token count rather than message count, so its context cost stays predictable
memory.exp: A buffer evaporates when the session ends and bloats context while it lives. Memory means extracted durable facts with provenance, retrieved selectively. Growing the buffer, summarizing it, or bounding it by tokens all accept the buffer-as-memory premise and tune it, the premise is the error.

memory.q: A user corrected their dietary preference months ago; the assistant still serves the old one. Both facts are in the memory store. The ROOT design flaw:
o: Retrieval is ranking the older memory above the newer one, so adding recency boosting at read time would fix it
The extraction step failed to register how significant the correction was, so a stronger extractor model is needed
Append-only memory: contradictions must supersede prior facts at write time, not coexist
Preference-class memories carry no TTL, so stale facts persist indefinitely instead of expiring on their own
memory.exp: Recency boosting and TTLs are patches that leave the contradiction in the store: read-time recency is fragile, and TTLs expire true facts too. The principled fix is at write: detect contradiction, supersede with history preserved. A stronger extractor misdiagnoses, the correction WAS captured; both facts exist.

memory.q: Why did file-based memory (progress files, MEMORY.md) win for long-running agents in 2026 harnesses?
o: Files let you avoid the embedding and vector-store costs that a semantic memory layer would otherwise add
Filesystem reads are faster than database reads from inside the agent sandbox, so lookups stay low-latency
Git history of the files doubles as provenance, making a separate provenance-tracking system unnecessary
Artifacts are durable, inspectable, survive compaction and crashes, and any session or harness can read them
memory.exp: The killer property is bridging amnesia: durable, human-auditable state that the next context window boots from. Cost and speed are incidental; git-as-provenance is a genuine bonus but a side effect of the design, not the reason for it.

memory.q: The agent's memory contains 'user authorized purchases up to $500', extracted from a session where the user READ A PHISHING EMAIL ALOUD to ask if it was a scam. Weeks later the agent auto-approves a purchase. The core failure:
o: The extraction model was too small to grasp the conversational nuance, and a larger one would have prevented this whole thing
Authorization-class memories should require an exact-phrase match at retrieval time before they are ever allowed to be acted on
Memory poisoning: no provenance/speech-act check at write (quoted ≠ asserted), and memory content was trusted as instruction at read
The purchase tool was missing a per-transaction amount limit, so nothing capped what any single auto-approval could end up spending
memory.exp: Two layers failed: the write path stored reported speech as a user assertion, and the read path let memory function as a privileged instruction. Per-transaction limits and approval gates are necessary defense-in-depth but don't fix the poisoned store; blaming the extractor's size misses that this is an architecture gap, not a model-size gap.

memory.q: Which design choice is simultaneously a trust feature AND a correctness feature for user-facing memory?
o: A cryptographic audit log proving that no memory was tampered with after it was first written to the store
User-visible, editable memory, users correct wrong facts, and transparency builds calibrated trust
Automatic expiry of every memory after 30 days, so stale facts are bounded and can't quietly outlive their truth
Admin-only memory editing, so a controlled set of operators can guarantee the integrity of what's stored
memory.exp: Visibility gives you free error correction (correctness) and consent (trust) in one feature. Audit logs prove integrity of possibly-wrong data; blanket 30-day expiry deletes true facts on schedule; admin-only editing optimizes integrity while blocking the person who actually knows the truth.

memory.q: Your coding agent runs on the Claude API inside your own harness. It must remember project conventions and past decisions across sessions, and engineers must be able to read and correct what it stored. The best-fitting starting point:
o: Claude's memory tool, backed by per-project files you store and version, with path checks on every call
An extract-then-store vector database of facts, retrieved by embedding similarity at the start of each turn
A sliding window of the last 200 messages kept in context, compacted into a summary when it nears the limit
A hosted memory store in a managed agent runtime, which first means moving the agent off your own harness
memory.exp: Conventions and decisions are durable, human-auditable project state, which is what file-based memory gives, and the memory tool is its API primitive: the model reads and writes files under /memories while your handler owns storage and rejects path traversal. A fact vector store fits many small user facts retrieved by similarity, not documents engineers edit; a 200-message window is history, not memory; a managed runtime's store fits if you move to that runtime anyway, but nothing here requires it.

agents.q: A process has 6 well-defined steps that never vary. The team built an autonomous agent for it. Your assessment:
o: Acceptable as long as the loop carries solid iteration caps and budget bounds to keep the runtime cost of path-choosing contained
Make it a workflow: enumerable paths get predictable, debuggable, cheap orchestration, agents are for paths you can't enumerate
Reasonable: an agent future-proofs the design for the day the six fixed steps eventually start varying and need runtime flexibility
Keep the agent but pin it with a plan-then-execute pattern so it reliably commits to following the same six steps in order every run
agents.exp: Runtime path-choosing is pure cost when the path is known: new failure modes, harder debugging, more tokens, for zero flexibility benefit. Iteration caps bound the waste without removing it; 'future-proofing' pays today for hypothetical variance; pinning a plan-then-execute pattern re-implements a workflow inside an agent, the worst of both.

agents.q: An agent with 95% per-step reliability runs a 20-step task. Expected end-to-end success, roughly:
o: ~80%, most step failures are locally recoverable, so the task absorbs them without ever sinking
~36%, per-step error compounds multiplicatively across all 20 steps (0.95^20), with no recovery
~60%, compounding applies but built-in verification absorbs roughly half of the failures
~95%, reliability is measured per step and that same figure carries cleanly end-to-end
agents.exp: 0.95^20 ≈ 0.36. The distractors describe what people WISH were true: local recovery and 'verification absorbs half' only exist if you build verification gates, and the ~95% option forgets that per-step reliability multiplies. That's precisely why the math makes gates, fewer steps, and sharper tools the three levers that matter.

agents.q: Your agent periodically declares a half-finished task complete. The most effective fix:
o: A second reviewer agent inspects and approves the first agent's completion claims before they land
Strengthen the prompt with firm wording: 'be exhaustive; never stop before absolutely everything is done'
A harness-verified completion contract, tests or a structured checklist that code, not the model, validates
Raise the effort setting so the agent reasons longer before it declares the task complete
agents.exp: Premature victory needs external ground truth. The reviewer agent is the tempting one, but it swaps one model's self-report for another model's opinion, still ungrounded; useful as a layer, not as the foundation. Firmer prompt wording and a higher effort setting change how hard the model tries, not whether anything checks the result.

agents.q: Which action class should ALWAYS carry a human approval gate in a production agent?
o: Any tool call that issues an external network request to a system outside your boundary
Any operation that reads or touches a customer's personal data in the course of the task
Irreversible or destructive operations: sends, deletes, payments, production deploys
Every state mutation the agent performs, regardless of whether the change is reversible
agents.exp: The gate criterion is irreversibility, one-way doors get humans. Gating every PII-touching operation is the tempting over-trigger: plenty of those reads are routine, gating them all kills the agent's usefulness, and access control belongs at the tool layer. Gating every network call or every state mutation gates by mechanism rather than consequence.

agents.q: The fastest path to improving a struggling production agent is usually:
o: Swap in the newest flagship model and re-run the full evaluation suite to measure the lift
Add a critic agent that reviews and signs off on each step before it is allowed to execute
Double the iteration budget so the agent has room to recover from its missteps mid-task
Sharpen the tools: clearer descriptions, instructive errors, narrower scopes, and a pruned tool list
agents.exp: Most 'agent stupidity' is tool-design debt, the model reads your descriptions every call and debugs from your error messages. A model swap rides someone else's roadmap; a critic agent adds cost and latency on top of the unfixed root cause; a doubled iteration budget funds more flailing.

agents.q: Your agent averages 18 steps per task at $0.02/step, running 20,000 tasks/month. A harness refactor costs $15,000 in engineering time and would cut average steps to 11. Payback period:
o: ~2.1 months
~3.4 months
~5.4 months
Never, at this step count, a better model is a higher-leverage investment
agents.exp: Baseline: 20,000 × 18 × $0.02 = $7,200/month. After refactor: 20,000 × 11 × $0.02 = $4,400/month. Monthly savings: $2,800. Payback: $15,000 ÷ $2,800 ≈ 5.4 months. ~2.1 months divides the refactor cost by baseline spend ($15,000 ÷ $7,200), counting all spend as savings, which it isn't; ~3.4 months divides by post-refactor spend ($15,000 ÷ $4,400), the same error in the other direction. The better-model option dodges the arithmetic: step count drives this bill, and a model swap mainly changes per-step price and quality while the refactor attacks step count directly. Harness investment reduces steps; model upgrades improve per-step quality. They're different levers.

agents.q: An agent tasked with researching 7 competitors spends 47 tool calls covering only 2 of them before hitting the iteration cap. The ARCHITECTURAL fix:
o: Double the iteration cap so the single agent eventually reaches coverage of all 7 competitors
Add a critic agent that monitors coverage in flight and redirects the worker after each competitor
Decompose: a planner emits 7 sub-tasks; a worker agent handles each competitor with its own tool-call budget
Expand the context window so all 7 competitors' research can be gathered within a single pass
agents.exp: Without per-unit allocation, the agent spends its full budget however it wants, and fixating on two competitors is rational local behavior with no global constraint. Decomposition makes coverage an architectural guarantee: the orchestrator can't succeed unless all 7 workers return results. Doubling the cap gives the agent more money to spend unevenly; a coverage critic detects the problem late without structurally preventing it; a bigger window changes how much fits, not how the budget gets spent.

agents.q: Production agent logs show it sometimes calls cancel_order() before verify_payment_received(), causing incorrect cancellations. The system prompt already says 'always verify payment before cancelling.' The correct fix:
o: Strengthen the system prompt with an explicit worked example showing the correct verify-then-cancel sequence
Enforce tool availability at the harness level, cancel_order is only exposed after verify_payment_received returns success
Add a human approval gate on cancel_order so a person signs off before any cancellation executes
Switch to a reasoning model that plans the full sequence of tool calls upfront before acting on any
agents.exp: Prompt instructions compete with task pressure and fail exactly in the high-stakes cases where they matter most. Making the wrong call sequence architecturally impossible, by gating cancel_order behind a successful payment verification result, removes the failure class entirely. A human approval gate is good defense-in-depth, but the agent can still call things in the wrong order and the reviewer inherits the mistake; a worked example is still just a prompt; a reasoning model plans better, but nothing enforces the plan. Architectural constraints beat behavioral instructions for safety-critical sequences.

agents.q: A multi-session coding agent restarts from scratch each session, ignoring progress from prior sessions. Root cause and fix:
o: The context window is too short, so raise the max token limit and let each session simply run longer before it runs out of room
No durable state: write a structured progress artifact (files changed, approach taken, remaining work) at session end and read it back at session start
Compaction is silently deleting prior progress, so raise the compaction threshold so it fires later and keeps earlier work in the window
The agent needs a vector embedding store that persists a semantic memory of everything it did across all of the prior coding sessions
agents.exp: Each new session is amnesiac by design, the prior transcript is gone. Durable files are the proven fix: structured state the next session reads at boot, independent of context length or compaction settings. A higher token limit or a later compaction threshold only delays the problem inside one session. An embedding store retrieves semantic content but can't restore structured progress state, or track which commits were made, as reliably as a file the agent wrote and can read directly.

agents.q: An agent generates 2,100 tokens of verbose reasoning narration per action turn but only 180 tokens constitute the actual action output. At 10,000 tasks/month with 6 action turns each, and output priced at $15/M tokens, what is the monthly overhead cost of the narration?
o: ~$290/month
agents.exp: Narration overhead per turn: 2,100 − 180 = 1,920 tokens. Per month: 10,000 × 6 × 1,920 = 115.2M tokens × $15/M = $1,728, so ~$1,725. ~$1,890 bills the whole 2,100-token turn as overhead, but the 180 action tokens are the work you want; ~$2,050 adds the action tokens instead of subtracting them (2,280 per turn); ~$290 forgets the 6 turns per task. The fix is terse action turns: a bare tool call with no free-text narration field, and lower effort on routine steps. Moving the narration into a hidden scratchpad field or a thinking block doesn't help, because every generated token bills as output.

agents.q: An expense agent must pause for a manager's approval that can take up to three days, across several deploys. Today it checkpoints messages to a file and keeps its loop process alive while it waits. The fix:
o: Keep the loop process alive and poll the approval API once a minute until the manager finally responds
Move it onto a durable-execution engine: journaled steps, the approval as a durable wait with a timeout
Checkpoint more often, so that a deploy during the wait loses less of the conversation when it restarts
Have the agent re-plan from scratch after each restart, since the approval state lives in the other system
agents.exp: A multi-day wait shouldn't hold a process at all. A durable-execution engine journals every model output and tool result, parks the run on a durable timer, and resumes by replaying the record when the approval, or the timeout and its escalation, arrives. Polling keeps a process and a budget open for days; more frequent checkpoints shrink what a deploy loses but still need a live process and give you no timer or escalation; re-planning from scratch re-asks the model, which can take a different path and repeat side effects.

tools.q: The model keeps calling search_orders when search_invoices is correct. Fix FIRST:
o: Rewrite both descriptions with explicit use-when / don't-use-when guidance and examples
Add an intent classifier that forces tool_choice for the model before it ever sees the raw request
Merge the two into one search tool with a 'type' parameter that the model has to set on each call
Collect a corpus of selection traces and fine-tune the model on the correct tool choice for each
tools.exp: Descriptions are the model's only documentation, re-read every call, ambiguity there is the usual culprit and the five-minute fix. An intent classifier forcing tool_choice is legitimate, but it adds a component to compensate for fixable docs (and Anthropic's newest models reject forced choice anyway); merging into one tool trades a selection error for a parameter error; fine-tuning is weeks of work for a documentation bug.

tools.q: A tool returns 'Error 400' on bad input and the agent flails. The better design:
o: Retry the call server-side with backoff a few times before surfacing any failure back to the model
Return instructive errors, 'date must be YYYY-MM-DD, got 6/10/26', so the model can self-correct
Return an empty result set so the agent loop keeps moving past the failure instead of stalling on it
Halt the loop the moment a tool errors and escalate straight to a human to handle the bad input
tools.exp: Error text re-enters context as the model's debugging information, write it like coaching. Server-side retries help for transient faults, but a malformed date will fail forever; an empty result set teaches the model the data doesn't exist, which is worse than an error; halting turns every recoverable mistake into an escalation.

tools.q: A tool accepts user_id as a model-supplied parameter for fetching private data. Verdict:
o: Acceptable as long as the tool is strictly read-only and every response it returns is written to an audit log
Acceptable if the server first validates that the supplied user_id exists and is well-formed before it acts on it
Privilege escalation by design: identity must come from server-side session context, never from model-generated arguments
Acceptable with strict tool use on, since grammar-constrained decoding keeps the ID inside the declared schema
tools.exp: Format validation is the trap: it confirms the ID is real, not that the model may act for it. The model is not a principal: anything it generates is untrusted, including identities, and injection can steer it. Read-only plus audit logs softens the impact, not the violation; strict mode guarantees a well-formed ID, not an authorized one.

tools.q: The problem MCP (Model Context Protocol) actually solves:
o: A standard authentication and authorization layer that governs how AI systems get access to tools
Tool integrations written once, usable by any compliant model or harness, ending per-app bespoke integrations
A versioned schema-negotiation handshake so different model providers can agree on tool formats
Faster structured-output decoding by letting the model use schemas registered ahead of time
tools.exp: MCP is the interop standard, the USB-C move: servers expose tools/resources once; Claude, IDEs, and other harnesses all consume them. Authorization is part of the spec (OAuth for remote servers) and schemas are part of the plumbing, but both serve the interop goal rather than being it; MCP does nothing to speed up decoding.

tools.q: Answering one query requires three independent lookups; the agent runs them one per turn. The improvement:
o: Cache all three results so any later query needing the same data can skip the lookups entirely
Merge the three lookups into one composite tool, guaranteeing the whole answer takes a single round trip
Acceptable as-is, since serial execution preserves ordering and keeps the trace simpler to follow
Emit them as parallel tool calls in a single turn, independent calls batch, cutting latency ~3×
tools.exp: Modern models batch independent calls natively; serial-only loops are a silent latency tax. Caching helps repeat traffic, not the first user; a composite tool couples unrelated operations and bloats its own contract; 'ordering' is exactly what independence means you don't need.

tools.q: A remote MCP server built for the 2025 spec kept each user's open cart in per-connection memory. After moving to the 2026-07-28 revision behind a plain load balancer, carts vanish between calls. The right redesign:
o: Pin each client to one replica with sticky sessions so its in-memory cart stays where its traffic lands
Return an explicit cart handle from the first tool call and require it as an argument on every later call
Restore the initialize handshake and send a session id in an Mcp-Session-Id header on every request
Keep the cart in the model's context and have it resend the full cart contents with every tool call
tools.exp: The 2026-07-28 revision is stateless: no initialize handshake, no protocol sessions, no Mcp-Session-Id header. A server that needs state mints an explicit handle and the model passes it back as an argument, so any replica can serve any request. Sticky sessions fight the design and break on scale-in; the handshake and session header no longer exist; making the model carry the cart costs tokens on every call and lets it edit state it shouldn't own.

tools.q: A remote MCP server must call your ticketing API on the user's behalf. An engineer proposes forwarding the OAuth token the MCP client sent to the server. Your verdict:
o: Fine if the token is short-lived and scoped narrowly to read-only access on the ticketing system
Fine as long as the MCP server validates the token's signature before forwarding it downstream
Forbidden: that token is bound to the MCP server's audience; get a separate delegated token for the API
Fine if every forwarded call lands in an audit log that ties it back to the original user session
tools.exp: The MCP spec says a server MUST validate that tokens were issued for it and MUST NOT pass the client's token through. Forwarding it breaks audience binding, defeats per-service scoping and audit, and turns the server into a confused deputy. The server acts as its own OAuth client to the ticketing API, with the user's delegated scopes. Short lifetimes, signature checks and audit logs are all good hygiene, but none of them fixes the audience violation.

tools.q: An agent's refund tool times out; the harness retries, and after a crash a durable engine may replay the step. How should the tool's idempotency key be generated?
o: A fresh UUID on every call, so each attempt is uniquely traceable in the provider's logs
Derived from the run and step (run_id:step_id), so retries and replays reuse one key
Derived from the amount and customer, so any two identical refunds collapse into one
Skip keys and cap retries at one, since a single retry rarely double-pays anyone in practice
tools.exp: The key must name the intended effect, not the attempt: run plus step stays the same across retries and replays, so the provider returns the first refund instead of issuing a second. A fresh UUID per call defeats deduplication exactly when it matters; keying on amount and customer collapses two legitimate refunds into one; capping retries trades duplicates for silently dropped refunds. If the downstream ignores keys, look the refund up before retrying.

harness.q: CORE-Bench evaluations showed Claude Opus 4.5 scoring 78% in Claude Code's harness and 42% in a generic scaffold, a 36-point gap from the same model. The defensible conclusion:
o: The benchmark itself is flawed, a result that unstable across harnesses shouldn't inform any decision
Multi-step capability is a model+harness property; scaffolding quality can outweigh model choice
The weaker harness was simply misconfigured; set up properly, that 36-point gap would mostly close
Benchmarks should mandate one reference harness so models can be compared fairly in isolation
harness.exp: Same model, 36-point spread, the scaffolding (context management, verification, recovery) IS capability on agentic work. 'The weaker harness was misconfigured' assumes away the finding, since that misconfiguration is the harness quality difference; mandating one reference harness is a reasonable methodology wish that dodges the engineering lesson; calling the benchmark flawed shoots the messenger.

harness.q: In the harness-as-operating-system analogy, context curation corresponds to:
o: The boot sequence, which initializes the system prompt and registers the session's hooks at startup, before any tool runs or work begins
Device drivers, the standardized interfaces through which the agent reaches its tools and its installed skills regardless of their backend
RAM management, deciding what's loaded in the window, what's paged out by compaction, and what's fetched on demand later
The scheduler, allocating turns across the main agent loop and the spawned sub-agents so each piece of work gets its slice of execution
harness.exp: All four mappings are real parts of the analogy, that's the point of it. Context curation specifically is memory management: loading, eviction (compaction), and demand paging (JIT retrieval). Boot = prompt/hooks setup; drivers = tool interfaces; scheduler = loop/sub-agent orchestration.

harness.q: A long-running coding agent keeps 'one-shotting', attempting the whole app, dying mid-context with undocumented state. Anthropic's proven fix:
o: A thorough planning phase that fully outlines every feature, interface, and data model before any single line of the application code is ever written down
Automatic checkpointing that snapshots the entire conversation transcript every N tool calls so the agent can roll back to any earlier point in the run
An initializer agent builds the environment (init script, JSON feature checklist, initial commit), then each session completes ONE verified feature
A much larger context window so the agent can fit a complete, multi-feature implementation inside one continuous session without ever running out of room
harness.exp: The published pattern pairs environment setup with incremental, verified, artifact-logged progress, each amnesiac session boots from durable state. A planning phase alone still one-shots the execution; transcript snapshots preserve the mess rather than structure the work; a bigger window delays the wall and worsens the crash.

harness.q: Why did Anthropic use JSON for the agent's feature checklist, with instructions to only flip a 'passes' field, instead of Markdown?
o: JSON parses reliably every single time, which lets the harness render a live progress dashboard straight from the checklist file on each run
Models are less likely to inappropriately rewrite structured JSON, and constrained edits stop the agent deleting requirements to 'pass'
JSON tokenizes far more compactly than the equivalent Markdown, shaving real context cost off of every single read of the checklist file
Git diffs on JSON stay line-stable across edits, which makes the session-over-session progress review much easier for a human to follow
harness.exp: It's a guardrail against the agent gaming its own success criteria: models are less likely to inappropriately rewrite structured JSON than Markdown, and the flip-one-field rule constrains the temptation. Reliable parsing, compact tokenization, and line-stable diffs all sound like real engineering perks; none is the published reason.

harness.q: Each new session of a multi-window agent should BEGIN by:
o: Resuming precisely where the previous transcript left off, replaying its tool calls to preserve momentum across the session gap
Running the full project test suite end to end, top to bottom, before reading any of the existing project state or progress notes
Asking the orchestrator or user for an entirely fresh brief each time, to avoid inheriting any stale assumptions from the prior run
Orienting: read progress notes and git log, run the init check, verify basic state, then select ONE work item
harness.exp: Boot-sequence discipline catches yesterday's undocumented breakage before building on it. Replaying the previous transcript assumes context the amnesiac session doesn't meaningfully have; a full test suite before reading any state costs time the targeted boot-check covers; asking for a fresh brief discards the durable state that exists precisely to answer that question.

harness.q: Your team proposes hand-rolling the agent loop 'in a sprint, it's just a while loop.' The experienced counter:
o: A hand-rolled loop simply can't reach key provider features like parallel tool calls and prompt-prefix caching, so it hard-caps your performance ceiling
The loop is the easy 10%; proven harnesses embody years of compaction, permissions, resume, and verification engineering you'd rebuild badly under deadline
An in-house agent loop creates unbounded legal liability around its actions that the compliance team will eventually step in and permanently block
Provider SDKs are contractually mandated for any production tool use, so rolling your own loop is barred outright by the very terms you already agreed to
harness.exp: It IS just a while loop, for the demo. Production is the forty failure modes around it: context exhaustion, premature victory, crash recovery, permission gates. The feature-ceiling, legal-liability, and contract-mandate arguments are false as stated; the real argument is engineering economics, same as not hand-rolling a web framework.

harness.q: A junior engineer asks why Claude Code keeps a MEMORY.md index file separate from CLAUDE.md instead of putting all memory in one file. The accurate explanation:
o: MEMORY.md is always loaded into context on every single turn, while CLAUDE.md is pulled in only when the model explicitly requests it for the task at hand
MEMORY.md is the index of Claude's own auto-memory notes, loaded each session while topic files load on demand; CLAUDE.md holds your instructions for every session

CLAUDE.md begins to measurably degrade context performance once it grows past roughly 500 lines, so any overflow memories beyond that hard line are automatically split off into a separate MEMORY.md file
MEMORY.md is synced to the cloud so the whole team shares one copy, while CLAUDE.md stays a strictly local-only file that is never allowed to leave the machine
harness.exp: The split is a context-management decision. CLAUDE.md is instructions you write (build commands, conventions, architecture), loaded every session. Auto memory is notes Claude writes for itself: only the MEMORY.md index (its first 200 lines or 25KB) loads at session start, and Claude opens a topic file only when an index line says it's relevant. That's JIT retrieval applied to agent memory.

harness.q: An agent session fails at step 23 of a 30-step plan with a tool error. The next session reads the progress artifact and resumes at step 24, but reintroduces a bug fixed in step 17. What progress artifact design flaw caused this?
o: The artifact tracked completed steps but not the decisions, constraints, and rationale that informed each step
The session crashed at step 23 before it ever managed to flush the in-progress artifact safely to disk at all
Step 24 should have automatically re-run steps 17 through 23 again as a full verification pass before it proceeded
The progress artifact should have been committed straight to git instead of being kept as a flat local working file
harness.exp: A checklist of completed steps ≠ the context of how they were completed. Step 17 fixed a bug, the fix was a decision the next session needed to inherit, but only the 'completed' flag was recorded. A robust progress artifact captures key discoveries, architectural decisions, and non-obvious constraints, not just done/not-done flags. The session at step 24 had no way to know about the step-17 constraint.

harness.q: Your harness compacts context when it reaches 80% of the 200K window. Post-compaction resets the window to 8K tokens. Each work unit generates approximately 3,000 tokens. How many work units complete between the first and second compaction events?
o: ~53 units
~50 units
~51 units
~64 units
harness.exp: After the first compaction the window holds 8K tokens; the second compaction fires at 160K (80% of 200K). Room to grow: 160K − 8K = 152K. Units: 152K ÷ 3K ≈ 50.7, so ~50 complete before the threshold trips partway through the 51st. ~51 rounds 50.7 up; ~53 forgets the 8K that survives compaction (160K ÷ 3K); ~64 ignores the 80% trigger and fills the whole window ((200K − 8K) ÷ 3K). Knowing this math lets you size work units so task boundaries line up with compaction events.

harness.q: A developer wants to use 'Bypass Permissions' mode during interactive development to reduce approval prompts on a large refactor. The correct guidance:
o: Yes, if those same prompts were already verified in a prior session, then re-prompting on this refactor adds no real safety value and only slows you down badly
Yes for internal tooling and one-off scripts that don't touch any user-facing surfaces or production code paths at all, where one stray action stays fully contained
No: bypass belongs only in isolated containers or VMs; on a dev machine, cut prompt fatigue with allow rules, the Bash sandbox, or auto mode, which keep checks running
Yes, provided a peer reviewer will audit every single file change the refactor produces afterward, since that later review reliably catches anything the agent got wrong
harness.exp: Claude Code's docs scope bypassPermissions to isolated containers and VMs: it runs everything without asking, and only deny rules and a few built-in checks still bite. Prompts during interactive work surface unexpected behavior, the moment oversight matters most, and a large refactor is exactly when you want them. To cut the noise, pre-approve safe commands with allow rules, turn on the Bash sandbox's auto-allow mode, or use auto mode, where a classifier reviews each action instead of you; in CI, the documented pattern is dontAsk with an explicit tool allowlist. A later peer review catches mistakes after the fact; prompts and classifiers catch them before.

harness.q: CORE-Bench showed one model scoring 78% in Claude Code's harness and 42% in a generic one. Your team's agent scores 59% on your own task suite with your harness. What gain should you expect from harness engineering alone?
o: Little: diminishing returns set in hard past 50%, so above your 59% the scaffolding gives back only a few points
Roughly 75–90%: the same 36-point lift applies to you, since harness quality outweighs model choice on agentic work
At most 5–10 points: that delta came from Claude Code's internal infrastructure and won't transfer to your harness
No figure transfers: the result proves the headroom can be large, so size yours by working your own failure taxonomy
harness.exp: A same-model gap on CORE-Bench proves harness headroom exists and can be large; it can't tell you the size of yours, because tasks, tools, and failure modes differ. The 75–90% option borrows someone else's lift wholesale; the 5–10-point and diminishing-returns options are equally confident guesses in the other direction. Classify your own failures (context exhaustion, premature victory, broken handoffs, tool errors), fix the biggest bucket, and re-measure: compaction, verification gates, and progress artifacts are the usual levers.

harness.q: Your team's agent loads a library of 200 skills, and a teammate worries it will flood the context window on every request. What actually happens with Agent Skills?
o: All 200 SKILL.md files load at startup, so the library must be pruned to the dozen skills used most
Only each skill's name and description load up front; its SKILL.md and files load when a task matches
Skills are embedded in a vector index, and the top three are retrieved into the prompt for each request
The harness compiles all 200 skills into the system prompt once and lets prompt caching absorb the cost
harness.exp: Progressive disclosure: discovery loads only names and descriptions (roughly 100 tokens per skill, so about 20K tokens for 200 skills), activation loads the full SKILL.md when a task matches, and scripts or reference files load only when used. Pruning is still good hygiene for selection accuracy, but context size doesn't force it; skills aren't retrieved from a vector index; and a cached monolithic prompt still occupies the window.

computer.q: A nightly job must pull 2,000 order statuses from a vendor portal that also offers a documented REST API. The team proposes a computer-use agent "because it works on any system." Your call:
o: Call the REST API: the GUI route adds steps, flaky clicks and an injection surface for no gain
Use computer use, but raise effort and add a verification screenshot after every status read
Use the browser toolset with element references so that the portal reads stay reliable at volume
Use computer use, but cache the screenshots so 2,000 nightly reads stay inside the budget
computer.exp: The ladder runs top-down: an API that covers the task beats any screen-driving agent on reliability, cost, latency and attack surface. The browser-toolset option is the right second rung, but only when no API exists; higher effort and cached screenshots tune a design that shouldn't exist. Computer use is for systems with no integration at all.

computer.q: Your harness asks a human to approve each assistant turn after its batch of browser actions has run. In testing, a 'Place order' click went through unreviewed. Why?
o: Batches execute concurrently, so the order click raced ahead of the approval prompt
One turn can click, type and submit, so the check has to run before each block executes
The API auto-confirms purchases unless a tool_choice setting forces one action per turn
Approval prompts expire the prompt cache, so the harness skipped them to contain cost
computer.exp: A single assistant turn can carry a whole click-type-submit sequence, which your executor runs in order; checking afterward approves a purchase that already happened. The gate belongs in the executor, before each consequential block. Batches run sequentially, not concurrently; the API never confirms anything, because your code executes every action; and a long approval wait costs a cache re-write, not a skipped check.

computer.q: On a Mac, every click your computer-use agent makes lands up and to the left of its target, by a consistent margin. The most likely cause:
o: Coordinates come back in screenshot pixels but get applied to a screen at a different scale
The model's effort is too low to localize targets, so it needs a higher setting for clicks
Zoom is disabled, so the model can't inspect small targets at full resolution before clicking
The screenshot history is too long, so the model keeps clicking against an outdated frame
computer.exp: A consistent offset is a coordinate-space mismatch: Claude answers in the pixel space of the screenshot it saw, so a 2× Retina capture or a resized screenshot needs each coordinate scaled by screen size ÷ screenshot size. Effort and zoom help near misses on small targets, not a uniform shift; an outdated frame produces wrong targets, not a steady offset.

computer.q: A browser agent must place orders on one supplier portal that requires a login. Which credential design holds up best against a page that tries to hijack it?
o: Put the login in the system prompt inside tags so the agent signs in only when it must
Store the login in a file inside the VM that the agent opens when it reaches the sign-in page
Pre-authenticate a dedicated low-privilege account and have a human confirm account changes
Run the agent in the procurement lead's own browser profile, where the portal is signed in
computer.exp: The model should never hold a secret it could be talked into typing elsewhere. A pre-authenticated session for a dedicated low-privilege account limits what a hijack can spend, and the human gate covers account changes. Prompt-held and file-held logins put the password within reach of injected instructions (Anthropic's docs show the prompt pattern and warn that it raises injection risk); a person's everyday profile hands over every session they have.

computer.q: A research agent browses arbitrary vendor sites and also holds the user's email session so it can send summaries. Which change most reliably removes the exfiltration path?
o: Add a system-prompt rule that page text is data and must never be treated as an instruction
Enable the vendor's injection classifier and log every page it flags for a weekly review
Browse in an unauthenticated profile, and send summaries in a separate human-reviewed step
Raise the effort setting so the model reasons harder about suspicious instructions on pages
computer.exp: Untrusted pages plus private data plus a way to send is the lethal trifecta, and cutting a leg is structural: with no email session in the browsing profile and sending moved behind a human, an injection has nothing to send through. The system-prompt rule and the classifier are useful layers that an adaptive attacker can get past (about 1% of the time in Anthropic's own November 2025 testing); more effort makes the model think harder, not safe by construction.

computer.q: The navigate handler allows a URL if it starts with 'https://portal.example.com'. A red-teamer still gets the agent onto their own site. The likely bypass and the fix:
o: Mixed-case URLs slip through; lowercase every URL before running the same prefix check
portal.example.com.evil.example passes; parse the host and re-check it after redirects
Known-bad domains aren't listed; add a blocklist regex for suspicious-looking host names
The model ignores the rule; restate the approved domains clearly in the system prompt
computer.exp: A prefix check matches portal.example.com.evil.example (and portal.example.com@evil.example), and redirects land anywhere after the check. So parse the URL, compare the host exactly, refuse non-http(s) schemes, re-check the landed URL, and enforce the same list at the egress proxy. Lowercasing fixes nothing here, blocklists lose to fresh domains, and the system prompt is a request, not a control.

computer.q: On Sonnet 5.5, a team deletes all but the last three screenshots from the message history before every request. Cache hits collapse and some requests are rejected. The fix:
o: Keep history append-only and drop old screenshots with server-side tool-result clearing
Re-encode the older screenshots as low-quality JPEGs instead of deleting them each turn
Disable thinking for the whole run so there are no signed blocks left to invalidate
Move the screenshots into the system prompt, where the cached prefix stays stable
computer.exp: Client-side edits to earlier turns change the prefix on every request (no cache hits) and, on Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, invalidate the signed thinking blocks that follow; Anthropic's docs say to keep history append-only and clear old results server-side, where context editing never invalidates thinking. Re-encoding is still an edit, thinking can't be disabled on Sonnet 5.5 (its lowest setting is between_tools), and the system prompt is not where tool results live.

computer.q: A 20-step browser task returns one 1280×720 screenshot per step (46 × 26 = 1,196 visual tokens each) and keeps every screenshot in history. At $2 per million input tokens, roughly what do the screenshots cost per attempt?
o: About $0.50
About $0.05
About $0.96
About $0.14
computer.exp: Step n re-sends n screenshots: 1,196 × (1 + 2 + … + 20) = 1,196 × 210 = 251,160 tokens × $2/M ≈ $0.50. About $0.05 counts each screenshot once (20 × 1,196), forgetting that history is re-sent; about $0.96 charges all 20 screenshots on every step (20 × 20 × 1,196); about $0.14 prices a different policy, keeping only the last three (1,196 × 57 = 68,172 tokens). That gap is why clearing old frames matters on long runs.

computer.q: Before shipping a browser agent that files expense reports, which evaluation gives you a number you can trust?
o: An LLM judge scores the agent's final summary of each run against the task description
Replay recorded tasks k times in a resettable copy of the app; code checks the end state
Track the model's published OSWorld score and ship once it clears your target threshold
Run each task once in production with a person watching, then sign off on the results
