Outside such a family, changing the embedding model is a full migration: re-embed every chunk in the corpus, rebuild the index from scratch, rerun retrieval evals on the golden query set, then make an atomic alias cutover. This is a blue-green migration, not an in-place upgrade. At 1M chunks of ~512 tokens with text-embedding-3-small, re-embedding costs roughly $10 at $0.02/M tokens and about 17 hours of batched embedding calls at 500K tokens a minute, and it scales linearly from there, manageable, but it must be planned like a database schema migration, not deployed on a Friday. The metadata requirement follows directly: store embedding model ID, version, and embedding date in every chunk's index metadata, and raise a hard error at query time if the live query embedder doesn't match, silent cross-model mismatches are worse than errors because they degrade quality without producing any signal.
trade: Fixed-size vs semantic chunking
Engineering simplicity vs semantic coherence
Tables split at byte boundaries return half a row; clauses split mid-sentence lose their legal meaning, the degradation is invisible until you measure recall@k
Contextual headers vs plain chunks
Retrieval quality vs ingestion cost

Deterministic headers (document title + section path) cost nothing at ingestion; LLM-written context, Anthropic's contextual retrieval, costs one LLM call per chunk, 1M calls at 1M chunks (prompt caching the parent document cuts that sharply), so measure the recall gain on your corpus before paying for it
One embedding model vs best-per-domain
Operational simplicity vs domain recall quality
General embedders lose 10–20 recall points on legal, medical, or technical jargon, a cheap fine-tune on 2,000 in-domain pairs recovers most of it
Text-layer extraction vs vision for PDFs
Cost and latency vs correctness on mixed docs
Text extraction on image-PDFs returns garbage; vision on digital-native PDFs wastes $0.01+ per page on something pdfminer does for free
Incremental update vs full reindex on model change
Deployment velocity vs index consistency
Stale chunks from the old embedder coexisting with new-model chunks, the quality degradation is silent and proportional to how much of the corpus has been updated
Scheduled re-ingest vs change data capture
Simplicity vs freshness and reliable deletes

A nightly full re-ingest is simple but serves edits up to a day late and only notices deletes by diffing; CDC makes edits and deletes searchable in minutes, at the cost of running a connector and an idempotent indexer plus a periodic full diff for missed events
scale: Re-embedding 1M chunks: at $0.02/M tokens with text-embedding-3-small and 512 tokens/chunk, cost is ~$10; at 500K tokens/minute of embedding throughput, time is ~17 hours, plan this like a database migration with a maintenance window

Index freshness SLA: time from document edit to searchable is typically 1–30 minutes for incremental pipelines, define it, measure it, and treat permission tightening (delete propagation) as a security SLA with a tighter target

ACL propagation: access control changes on source documents must reach all derived chunks within the security SLA or you have a data-residency gap between the permission model and what retrieval returns

The data flywheel is the compounding mechanism: production failures sampled weekly and labeled turn your eval set into a living document of what the system gets wrong, teams that run this improve over time; teams that don't stay at their launch recall numbers
sec: Embedding model ID and version must be stored as index metadata, mismatch between query embedder and indexed chunks produces silent garbage, not an error message, and the quality degradation is proportional to semantic distance between model versions

ACL filtering at query time is non-negotiable: the index does not enforce access permissions, the query path does, every chunk retrieval must check the requesting user's entitlements against the source document's ACLs

PII in source documents flows into chunks, into vectors, and is retrievable via similarity search, scrub or redact PII before embedding, not after; vectors are copies of your sensitive data in another basis

Data flywheel pipelines that automatically sample production failures into a labeling queue must have a human review gate before samples enter training data, poisoned production logs become poisoned training data silently
dataeng.interview: Data quality is the highest-leverage investment in any retrieval system and the least visible, the quality ceiling is set during ingestion and chunking, before the first embedding call, and it's invisible in metrics until you measure recall directly. The mechanisms that compound: semantic chunking on natural language boundaries instead of byte counts, contextual headers prepended to every chunk so bi-encoders can match without needing section structure in the query, and strict embedding lifecycle management. Changing embedding models is a full migration, re-embed everything, rebuild the index, eval on the golden query set, atomic alias swap, not an in-place upgrade, because vector spaces from independently trained models are incompatible bases (a shared-space family like Voyage 4 is the deliberate exception). I store the model ID and version in index metadata and raise a hard error on mismatch rather than serving silently degraded results. The data flywheel is what separates teams that improve over time from teams stuck at their launch recall: production failures sampled weekly, labeled, and added to the eval set turn each incident into a permanent regression test. And freshness is an event, not a schedule: change data capture from the source's transaction log, an idempotent indexer that treats deletes as seriously as edits, and a periodic full diff for whatever the stream missed.

multimodal.mech:
Vision-language models process images by dividing them into a grid of fixed-size patches and mapping each patch through a vision encoder (a ViT) into a vector. Those patch vectors become visual tokens in the model's context window, processed by the same attention layers as text. What you are billed follows each provider's published formula: Claude charges ⌈width/28⌉×⌈height/28⌉ visual tokens, so a 1024×1024 image is 1,369 tokens, and oversized images are downscaled to a per-model cap (1,568 tokens on standard models, 4,784 on the high-resolution tier that began with Claude 4.7). OpenAI and Gemini expose a detail or media-resolution setting instead, and a low setting cuts the count sharply. Image tokens bill at the same per-token rate as text; the premium is the count. A 10-page PDF sent as images at 1,000×1,333 pixels/page is ~17,000 visual tokens on Claude (1,728 a page), about what a 10,000-word document costs, for content whose text layer was free to extract.

The critical distinction is text layer presence. A digital-native PDF stores the actual Unicode characters in the PDF stream, extractable for free in milliseconds by pdfminer, with paragraph structure, heading hierarchy, and in many cases table boundaries. Sending that same document to a vision model pays several times more (about 5× at this module's per-page anchors) to have the model 'read' pixels that represent characters it could have received directly as text. Native PDF input doesn't dodge this: Claude, for one, processes each PDF page as extracted text plus a page image and bills both. The quality can even be lower on structured content, because generative extraction can hallucinate table values and misread column alignment, while a table-structure model returns exact cell geometry and generates no text.

The cases where vision genuinely wins: (1) image-only PDFs, scanned, no text layer at all; (2) charts, diagrams, and figures where the visual structure carries meaning that text cannot represent; (3) forms with handwriting or non-standard layouts that text extractors cannot parse; (4) documents where visual layout (sidebars, callout boxes, color coding) carries semantic meaning beyond the text. The routing decision reduces to two questions: does a text layer exist? and does the query reference visual content? Those two signals route most of a typical corpus (60–80% in many enterprise collections) away from vision processing at no quality cost.
trade: Vision for everything vs routing
Simplicity vs cost
In many enterprise corpora 60–80% of documents have a text layer; sending them to vision pays ~5× per page (this module's anchors) for lower accuracy on structured content
High vs low image resolution in vision calls
Extraction quality vs token cost

Low-detail settings cut image tokens sharply and high-resolution input multiplies them: on Claude's high-resolution tier a 4K screenshot costs ~3.7× a 1000×1000 page (4,784 vs 1,296 tokens), so measure whether quality actually improves before paying for resolution
Vision-native extraction vs OCR+layout tools
Coverage on hard cases vs cost on structured data

A table-structure model gives exact cell geometry and generates no numbers, so it cannot hallucinate one, at a fraction of a VLM call; frontier VLMs have closed much of the quality gap on tables, so benchmark both on your documents; vision clearly wins on charts and irregular layouts
Synchronous vs async vision processing
Latency simplicity vs throughput
Vision API calls run 2–8 seconds; async processing with polling keeps user-facing latency low without blocking threads on slow document batches
Cache by document hash vs re-process every time
Cost vs freshness
A SHA-256 hash cache eliminates repeat vision calls entirely, in B2B contexts with repeat supplier documents, cache hit rates of 30–50% are normal
Native PDF input vs extracted text
Convenience vs token cost

Claude, for one, turns each PDF page into extracted text plus a page image and bills both: roughly 1,500–3,000 text tokens a page plus about 1,728 image tokens if the page image is 1000×1333, so 1.6–2.2× the tokens of the text alone. Pay that for layout, charts or scans; send the extracted text when the text layer is clean
scale: Vision API cost math: 1M pages/month at $0.01/page = $10K/month; routing 70% to text extraction at $0.002/page drops this to $4.4K/month (700K × $0.002 + 300K × $0.01), saving $5.6K a month, so a classifier that takes a couple of days to build pays for itself within weeks
Image preprocessing is the hidden latency: resize and compress to the provider's optimal tile size before the API call to avoid paying for auto-tiling overhead
Cache by document hash: in B2B workflows, suppliers resubmit the same documents monthly, a DynamoDB table keyed by SHA-256 hash eliminates that fraction of vision cost with no quality trade-off

For audio at scale: transcribe first (self-hosted Whisper or a hosted speech-to-text API, with diarization on that path); only route to audio-native models when the task genuinely requires prosody, emotion, or realtime speech-to-speech

Generation jobs are slow and spiky: queue them, cap concurrency per tenant, budget video per second of output, and reuse outputs for repeated identical requests (standard voices, stock illustrations) instead of paying to regenerate them
sec: Vision models can read embedded PII in images, faces, handwritten SSNs, medical images, check numbers, that text extraction would miss; scope what the model is allowed to 'see' before enabling vision on a document type
Document hash caches must be tenant-scoped: a cache hit on another tenant's extracted document is a data leak, especially in multi-tenant B2B contexts where documents are commercially sensitive

Vision model outputs on structured content hallucinate numbers and amounts, faithfulness gates are more important on vision-extracted content than text-extracted content; the confidence of the output does not correlate with accuracy on tables

Medical and financial document images may fall under stricter regulatory scope than their text equivalents, treat image inputs containing PHI or PCI data as regulated regardless of whether you're extracting them with vision or OCR

Generated media carries likeness and rights risk: block real people's faces and voices without documented consent, keep provider safety filters on, and log prompt, model and output hash for every generation so you can answer 'did our system make this?'
multimodal.interview: The most common mistake in multimodal systems is vision-washing, routing every document through a vision model because it handles all types, then discovering the bill. Image tokens bill at the same rate as text, but a vision extraction pays for the page image, the transcribed output and a model call the text path never needed: about 5× the text path per page in this module's anchors. On structured content like tables, generative extraction can also hallucinate values a table-structure model never invents. The architecture that holds in production is a routing layer: text-layer detection first (pdfminer returning >500 chars signals digital-native), then query-intent detection (does the query reference a chart or figure?), with vision reserved for image-only documents and visual-query overrides. That routing classifies most of a typical corpus (60–80% in many enterprise collections) as text-extractable at no quality cost. The cost math is blunt: 1.08M pages a month (180K claims × 6 pages), and routing cut the blended cost from $0.01 to $0.003 a page, about $91K a year. The routing logic is 80 lines of Python. On the generation side the rule is symmetric: wrap the vendor behind your own interface because these endpoints churn, and mark every output twice, signed content credentials plus an invisible watermark, because metadata alone does not survive the internet.

voice.mech:
A cascaded turn is a relay of streams. Audio arrives in 20 ms frames; a VAD marks speech and silence; streaming STT emits interim words, then a final transcript; endpointing decides the caller is done (a silence timeout, a semantic turn model, or both); the LLM streams tokens; a sentence chunker hands each finished sentence to TTS, whose audio streams back through the transport. People leave gaps of around 200 ms between turns because listeners predict the end of a sentence instead of waiting for silence, which is what semantic endpointing imitates. Every stage must start before the previous one finishes. Generation runs far ahead of speech, so the tail of a reply is free once the first sentence plays, but reasoning before the first token is pure dead air: keep effort low on the voice route.

The subtle part is the gap between sent and heard. TTS and speech-to-speech models produce audio faster than real time, so seconds of it can sit in the client's playback buffer or the phone provider's media stream. A correct barge-in therefore has three moves: confirm it is speech (a minimum duration or a few transcribed words, not a cough or the agent's own echo); cancel generation and flush the downstream buffer (Twilio media streams take a clear message); then reconcile context. OpenAI's realtime API does the last step server-side with conversation.item.truncate, which deletes the text the caller never heard. In a cascaded stack you track played milliseconds, map them to words with TTS timestamps, and append a note of what was heard instead of rewriting the stored reply: on accounts created on or after August 31, 2026, Claude Sonnet 5.5 returns a 400 when a replayed thinking block follows an edit to earlier history.
trade: Cascaded vs speech-to-speech
Control, transcripts and model choice vs latency and prosody
Cascaded without end-to-end streaming feels like a walkie-talkie; speech-to-speech on a regulated flow leaves you guarding audio you can't inspect mid-sentence
Silence timeout vs semantic end-of-turn
Responsiveness vs cutting callers off
A 300 ms timeout interrupts people reading out account numbers; a 1,000 ms one adds a second of dead air to every turn
Barge-in sensitivity
Interruptibility vs false stops
Too eager: the agent stops for coughs, 'mm-hmm' and its own echo; too lazy: it talks over the caller for seconds
Orchestrator audio vs model-written filler during tools
Determinism vs naturalness
Silence past a couple of seconds sounds like a dropped call; model-improvised fillers vary, repeat and cost a model call
Frontier vs small model on the voice route
Answer quality vs time to first token and cost per minute
A frontier model thinking before every turn burns the latency budget; a small model alone fumbles the hard cases, so delegate them
scale: Cost per minute = telephony + STT + TTS + LLM tokens (or audio tokens); in this module's example audio services are about two-thirds of $0.043 a minute, so price them before optimizing the model
History re-sent every turn makes input tokens grow with the square of the turn count: cache the stable prefix, cap or summarize history, and price your longest calls, not your average one

Concurrency is the capacity unit: each live call holds a streaming STT session, a TTS stream and a model connection for its whole length, so provider concurrency limits and regional capacity cap your peak hour
Set the SLO on p95 voice-to-voice from per-turn timestamps; summing stage p95s (1,750 ms in this module's example) overstates it because stage tails rarely land on the same turn
sec: Spoken input is user input: a caller can say 'ignore your instructions', so tool permissions and identity checks live in code, never in the transcript's say-so; verify identity with a one-time code to the number on file, not caller ID or a familiar voice
Voices are forgeable: cloning defeats voice-as-password and enables impersonation; clone only with the voice owner's documented consent and never from call recordings

Recordings and transcripts are sensitive data: announce recording, keep payment digits out of them (DTMF into a payment-scoped component), redact before they reach traces or eval sets, and set retention per jurisdiction
Outbound calling has its own rules: in the US, robocall consent rules treat AI-generated voices as artificial voices; in the EU, the Article 50 disclosure applies to every call
voice.interview: I treat a voice agent as a real-time system first and an LLM feature second. I pick cascaded or speech-to-speech per route on evals: cascaded buys transcripts, guardrails and model choice; speech-to-speech buys latency and prosody. I budget voice-to-voice per stage, stream everything, start TTS on the first sentence, and keep reasoning off the critical path, delegating hard work to a background model while orchestrator-owned audio covers the wait. Barge-in is three moves: stop generation, flush what's queued downstream, and make the context match what the caller actually heard. I set the SLO on measured p95 voice-to-voice, test with simulated callers over real phone audio, and put the AI disclosure in the first sentence. Cost is per minute and grows with call length, so I cache the prefix and cap history.

agents.mech:
An agent is mechanically simple: a messages array, a while loop, and tool dispatch. Each iteration sends the conversation + tool schemas to the model; if the response contains tool calls, your code executes them, appends results, and loops; if it's a final answer (or a stop condition fires), you exit. Everything interesting lives in the loop's engineering. Stop conditions: max iterations, token/dollar budget, wall-clock timeout, goal-test satisfied, all four, because agents fail by both quitting early and never quitting. Verification gates are code, not prompts: after the agent claims completion, the harness runs the checklist, tests pass? schema valid? required sections present? and rejects with targeted feedback if not. Checkpointing serializes loop state (messages, plan, artifacts) so a crash at step 40 resumes at step 40. A durable-execution engine generalizes this for runs that outlive a process: every model call and tool call is a recorded step, resume replays the record, and an approval becomes a durable timer instead of a sleeping process.

The compounding math is the planning tool: per-step success p over n steps ≈ pⁿ end-to-end (to measure reliability across repeated runs, use pass^k from Evaluation & Eval Harnesses). At p=0.95, 20 steps → 36%. The three levers fall straight out of the formula: raise p (sharper tools, instructive errors), lower n (consolidate tools, better plans), and insert verification points that catch-and-repair so errors stop compounding, a mid-run gate converts multiplicative decay into a recoverable bump. Plan-then-execute vs ReAct (interleaved think/act) is a real architectural choice: planning up front lowers n and aids review; reactive handles surprise better. Production agents usually plan first, react within steps.

agents.interview: An agent is an LLM in a while-loop with tools, and reliability is a harness property, not a model property. The governing math is compounding: 95% per-step over 20 steps is 36%, so I raise per-step reliability with sharp tools and instructive errors, reduce step count through planning, and insert verification gates that catch-and-repair so errors stop multiplying. Completion is never self-reported, the harness checks tests or contracts. Bounds (iterations, budget, time), checkpoints for resume, full traces, and human gates on irreversible actions are the difference between a demo and production. Runs that outlive a process go on a durable-execution engine that replays the record, not the model. And my default is still a workflow, agents have to earn the autonomy.

tools.mech:
Under the hood, tool calling is structured generation: your tool schemas are rendered into the model's context, and the model, fine-tuned on function-calling data, emits a structured tool-call block (name + JSON args) instead of prose. Turn on strict mode (strict: true) and grammar-constrained sampling guarantees the arguments match your schema; without it they're usually, not always, valid. The model never executes anything; it asks. Your code validates, executes, and appends the result as a tool message, and the model continues with that observation. tool_choice can force a call on models that allow it (Anthropic's Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1 return a 400, so structured outputs are the dependable extractor there); independent calls can be emitted in parallel within one turn, multiple blocks, one round trip.

This is why descriptions are load-bearing: they are the only documentation the model has, re-read on every single call. Selection accuracy degrades measurably as tool count grows and descriptions blur (Anthropic's docs put the drop at roughly 30–50 tools), most 'dumb agent' bugs are documentation bugs. Error returns close the loop: whatever your tool returns on failure becomes the model's debugging information, so 'expected YYYY-MM-DD, got 6/10/26' enables self-correction while 'Error 400' guarantees flailing. MCP standardizes the whole surface: servers expose tools/resources/prompts over a defined protocol (stdio locally, Streamable HTTP remotely, with OAuth-based authorization), clients discover them at runtime, write the integration once, every compliant harness can use it. That's why it became the USB-C of the ecosystem, and since the 2026-07-28 revision its core is stateless, so a remote server scales behind an ordinary load balancer with no session affinity. Side effects need identity: agents and durable engines retry and replay, so a mutating tool takes an idempotency key derived from the task step and the downstream honours it; that one rule is what makes a retry or a replay safe.

tools.interview: Tool calling is structured generation: schemas go in, the model emits a tool-call block (grammar-constrained once strict mode is on), my code validates and executes, the model only ever asks. Descriptions are load-bearing because they're the model's entire documentation, re-read every call; most agent bugs are description bugs. Error returns are part of the prompt loop, so they're written to teach self-correction. Security model: the model is not a principal, identity from session context, server-side validation, idempotency on mutations, approval gates on consequential calls. And MCP turned tool integration into a write-once ecosystem play, with the supply-chain caution that implies: in production that means audience-bound OAuth with no token passthrough, pinned servers, and an idempotency key on every mutating tool.

harness.mech:
A production harness is an assembly line around the model call. Prompt assembly: system prompt + skill names and descriptions (full skills load on demand) + tool schemas + retrieved memory + compacted history, in cache-optimal stable→volatile order. The loop with hooks: pre-tool-call hooks enforce permissions and budgets (this is where 'needs human approval' actually executes); post-tool hooks truncate output, scrub secrets, update traces. Compaction fires at a utilization threshold, summarize old turns, pin critical decisions, drop stale tool dumps. Sub-agent spawning creates a fresh context with a scoped brief and tool set, returning a structured conclusion. Persistence: transcripts and checkpoints make sessions resumable; the permission engine defines autonomy tiers per tool class; sandboxing (filesystem/network isolation) lets the agent act boldly inside a hard boundary.

The initializer/coding pattern shows why this architecture wins on long work: session one writes init.sh, expands the goal into a 200+ feature JSON checklist (all failing), commits. Every later session boots identically, read progress file, read git log, run init, verify the app end-to-end, then implements exactly ONE feature, verifies it as a user would, flips its passes flag only after verification, commits, updates the progress file. Each session is amnesiac; the artifacts are the memory. The 78/42 CORE-Bench gap (Claude Opus 4.5, measured by Princeton's HAL team) isn't magic, it's this: one harness systematically removes failure modes (one-shotting, premature victory, broken handoffs, wasted boot time) that the other leaves open. Capability is the model × the failure modes your scaffolding eliminates.

harness.interview: The harness is the operating system around the model: prompt assembly, the loop with permission hooks, compaction, sub-agent scheduling, persistence, sandboxing. The published 78-vs-42 same-model result is the cleanest evidence that agentic capability is a model+harness property, the harness wins by systematically eliminating failure modes: durable artifacts and boot-sequence orientation kill broken handoffs, one-feature increments kill one-shotting, externally verified checklists kill premature victory. My defaults: adopt a proven harness over hand-rolling, durable state over compaction trust, verification gates over self-report, and sandbox-plus-gates so the agent can be bold inside hard walls. computer.mech:
Mechanically, this is the agent loop with a camera. You declare one toolset entry (computer_toolset_20260801 or browser_toolset_20260801, GA, no beta header) and the API adds the member definitions and a tool-use system prompt, about 4,500 and 6,600 input tokens respectively. Claude replies with a batch of member tool_use blocks tagged with toolset_name. Your executor runs them in order against the VM or browser, stops at the first failure, answers every block (skipped ones get the documented halt text; leave one unanswered and the next request is rejected) and returns images only for screenshot and zoom. There is no display-size parameter: coordinates live in the pixel space of the screenshots you send, and the API rejects an oversized toolset image instead of shrinking it, so you pick one size inside the model's limits and scale clicks back. Current Claude models open each response with thinking blocks signed over earlier turns, so the transcript is append-only and old screenshots leave through server-side tool-result clearing.

The security mechanics explain why this is the riskiest agent shape. The context is assembled from pixels and page text that strangers wrote, some of it invisible to the humans supervising. Classifiers help (Anthropic scans screenshots and page text and steers Claude to check with the user; Gemini's computer-use tool has an optional injection-detection flag), but nothing inside the model is a boundary: Anthropic's November 2025 testing still saw about 1% attack success against its hardened browser agent. The boundaries sit outside: the sandbox (what the box can touch), the egress allow-list (where data can go), credential design (what a session can spend) and the executor gate (what happens without a human yes). The Agents Rule of Two is the design test: an agent that reads untrusted pages may hold sensitive access or the power to act externally, not both, unless a human approves each action.

computer.interview: Computer use is the bottom rung of the action-surface ladder: I try an API or MCP server, then DOM-level browser automation through the accessibility tree, and only then pixels, and I write down why each step down was needed. The loop is observe, run the batch in order with a halt on the first failure, then observe and verify, with coordinates in screenshot space. Cost grows with the square of steps if screenshot history is kept, so I fix one screenshot size, cache the toolset prefix and clear old frames server-side. The real job is containment: every page is untrusted, so the agent gets a throwaway sandbox, an egress allow-list at the network layer, no credentials, and an executor-side human gate before anything irreversible. I evaluate on resettable environments, graded on end state, several runs per task.

multi.mech:
Orchestrator–worker mechanics: the orchestrator decomposes the goal into briefs, each a contract with objective, boundaries ('don't cover pricing; worker 3 owns it'), output format, and quality bar. Workers spawn as independent sessions with fresh contexts and scoped tools, burn their messy intermediate tokens privately, and return structured conclusions, never transcripts, because returning raw output re-imports the pollution the spawn existed to quarantine. The orchestrator synthesizes, optionally spawning follow-ups for gaps. Parallelism is real: wall-clock ≈ the slowest worker, not the sum.

Shared state goes through artifacts (files) rather than message passing, durable, inspectable, and survivable, with explicit ownership rules or merge points, because concurrent writes are last-write-wins data loss. Failure handling: per-worker timeouts and budgets, retry-once-then-degrade, synthesis proceeding with partial results flagged. Topology matters: star (orchestrator-centric) beat free-form agent 'conversations' in practice because every hop between agents is a lossy text serialization, fewer hops, less drift. The known scaling facts: in Anthropic's research system, agents used ~4× the tokens of a chat and multi-agent ~15× (token spend alone explained 80% of the performance variance on their BrowseComp eval), and quality hinges on brief-writing, the same skill as delegating to humans, with the same failure mode: vague briefs produce confident, overlapping, drifted work.

The architecture that survived contact with production is orchestrator-worker: briefs as contracts, fresh-context workers returning conclusions not transcripts, artifacts with ownership rules for shared state, star topology because every inter-agent hop is lossy serialization. It costs roughly 4× a single agent's tokens (~15× a chat), so the parallel wall-clock or context-hygiene gain has to be priced and justified. Brief quality is the ceiling of the whole system, which is delegation skill, and it transfers directly to managing humans. design.mech:
Follow the request path, because each box is a mechanism you own. Input rails: a fast pass, regex + small-model classifier, screening injection patterns, redacting PII, filtering topics; single-digit milliseconds and fractions of a cent. Cache stack, in order: exact-match (hash of normalized request), semantic (embedding similarity above a calibrated threshold), then provider prefix caching on the model call itself. Gateway: routing tables (route → model tier), health checks feeding a circuit breaker (closed → open on error-rate threshold → half-open probes → close on recovery), retries with exponential backoff + jitter, idempotency keys so retries are safe, per-route rate limits and budget meters. Output rails: schema validation, faithfulness gate on grounded routes, safety filters. Around it all: every call emits a trace (prompt hash, params, tokens, latency, cost, route), a sampled fraction flows to async judge scoring, and drift alerts watch the score time-series.

Release mechanics tie it together: prompt + model ID + tool schemas + eval-set version travel as one pinned, versioned bundle. A change to any of them is a release, eval-gated in CI, staged rollout, instant rollback. That single discipline is what makes 'the model updated and everything changed' an impossible class of incident instead of a quarterly surprise.

Batch-shaped work never pays synchronous prices, and degraded mode is designed, not improvised.

evals.mech:
Building the stack, mechanically. Dataset: sample production traffic stratified by route and difficulty, oversample failures and complaints, label with a written protocol (two labelers on a subset, if humans don't agree, the judge can't), version it like code. Scorers, cheapest first: exact/programmatic checks (schema, regex, numbers), embedding similarity for paraphrase tolerance, NLI entailment for groundedness, LLM-judge for rubric qualities. Judge construction: one binary criterion per call ('Does the answer rely only on the provided sources? YES/NO'), a different model family than the generator (self-preference), both answer orders for pairwise comparisons (position bias), and calibration, run the judge over ~50 human-labeled cases and report agreement separately on human passes and human fails (a judge that says PASS to everything scores 90% raw agreement on a 90%-pass set, and Cohen's κ of 0); below ~85–90% on either, fix the rubric, not the threshold. Binary beats scalar because 1–10 scales have inconsistent internal anchors; yes/no forces a decision boundary.

Wiring: CI runs the suite on any PR touching prompts/models/schemas, diffs per-criterion scores against baseline, and blocks on regression, eval latency under ~10 minutes or engineers route around it. Online: an async queue samples N% of production, scores with a cheap judge, and feeds time-series drift alerts. Agent trajectories add step-level scoring (sensible tool choice? recovered from the error? stopped appropriately?) plus end-state verification (tests pass, artifact correct), process and outcome, because either alone lies. Agents are nondeterministic, so run each task k times and report pass^k: an agent that succeeds 90% of the time per run clears three runs in a row only 73% of the time.

Agent eval harnesses make the fixture an environment. Each trial resets a seeded sandbox (repo snapshot, database fixture, mock APIs, a simulated user for conversational tasks), runs the agent under its production harness and effort setting, then grades the end state with code first (tests, record checks, a log of forbidden calls) and a calibrated judge only for trajectory qualities. Report pass^k next to cost and steps per solved task. Read vendor agentic benchmarks (Terminal-Bench, SWE-bench Pro, BrowseComp) the same way: they score a harness plus a model, and one 2026 model card reports different BrowseComp results with and without context compaction, so rerun candidates on your own harness before you trust a delta.

evals.interview: Evals are the test suite for behavior: golden datasets as fixtures, scorers as assertions, CI as the gate, no eval, no deploy. The craft is in the details: datasets grown weekly from real failures beat synthetic volume; judges are binary per-criterion, a different model than the generator, calibrated against human labels with agreement reported next to every score. Component evals localize blame, retrieval recall separate from faithfulness, while end-to-end tells the user's truth. Production is the real distribution, so sampled online scoring with drift alerts closes the loop. For agents, score trajectories and verify end-states, because process and outcome each lie alone.

halluc.mech:
Hallucination is a property of the objective: training rewards the most plausible continuation, and plausibility is computed from pattern-fit, not truth. The model has no internal fact/fiction boundary and no calibrated 'I don't know' unless one was trained or designed in, so fabrication concentrates exactly where pattern-fit outruns knowledge: niche facts, citations, numbers, recent events. You don't fix this in the model; you build a verification system around it.

The workhorse is the faithfulness gate: split the answer into atomic claims (cheap model pass), check each claim for entailment against its cited source (NLI model or judge call), and apply a decision policy, all claims supported → serve; unsupported claims → flag, regenerate with stricter grounding, or route to 'couldn't verify' UX. Cost: fractions of a cent per answer. Citation verification is its sibling: cited IDs must exist, and the cited span must actually support the sentence. Provider-native citations (Claude's Citations API guarantees each citation points at a real span of the documents you passed) make the existence check free; the support check is still yours. Prompt injection is mechanically deeper than it looks: in token space there is no instruction/data boundary, the model sees one stream, so delimiting and 'treat this as data' framing reduce but cannot eliminate the attack. Real defense is layered: input screens (classifier + heuristics), content marking, least-privilege tools, and the decisive control, privileged actions gated on checks independent of any content the model read. The email can say anything it wants; the refund still requires an approval that no token stream can grant.

Track gate hit rates: rising unsupported-claim rates are an early-warning drift signal
Incident runbooks for hallucination events: what was served, to whom, eval case added, gate adjusted
sec: Map your surface to the OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 (2026 edition): LLM01:2026 Prompt Injection, LLM03:2026 Excessive Agency and LLM10:2026 Improper Output Handling cover most real incidents
Injection arrives through every external channel: documents, email, web pages, memory, tool results, enumerate and screen each
Data exfiltration via outputs ('summarize and send to…') needs output rails and egress controls
The deciding control: privileged tool calls validated independently of model-read content, always
halluc.interview: Hallucination is intrinsic, the objective rewards plausibility, not truth, so I engineer trust as a system property: ground answers in retrieved sources, verify claims with entailment gates before display, constrain outputs with schemas and allowed values, and design abstention as a first-class path because punishing 'I don't know' manufactures confident nonsense. Injection gets the same systems treatment: there's no instruction/data boundary in token space, so delimiting helps but the real control is layered rails plus privileged actions gated independently of anything the model read. The metric that matters: verified-claim rate on consequential routes, trending up.

lead.mech:
Staff-level leadership runs on a few concrete mechanisms. Decision classification: every significant choice gets tagged two-way or one-way door (the test: cost and time to reverse, and who bears it). Two-way doors, prompts, models behind a gateway, rerankers, move at team speed with eval gates. One-way doors, data rights, vendor lock-in, trust-sensitive launches, get the slow treatment: a written decision memo (context, options, differentiation test, reversibility analysis, kill criteria), circulated for red-team before commitment. Writing is the mechanism, not the artifact: a one-page memo surfaces the disagreement a meeting papers over.

Operating cadence: monthly business reviews carry AI-native metrics, task success rate (from evals, not vibes), unit economics per feature (cost/task vs value/task), incident counts by failure class, eval coverage of shipped surface. Quarterly: re-benchmark models on the standing suite, revisit build/buy/wait calls (wait answers expire), prune the portfolio against pre-agreed kill criteria. Team capability is built the same way: hiring loops use work-samples (design an eval for this feature; critique this architecture) over framework trivia, because frameworks churn quarterly and judgment compounds. And the narrative discipline: every capability claim to executives ships with its failure modes and a counterfactual ('this gate would have caught the March incident'), credibility is the staff engineer's compounding asset, and it's built by being the person whose claims survive contact with production.

Compliance is a build list, not a slide. Decide your role per feature first: providers carry more duties than deployers, and substantially modifying a model or selling it under your name can turn a deployer into a provider. Then ship the controls the duties imply: an AI-interaction disclosure at the start of every chat or call, machine-readable marks on generated media and text (some vendors now watermark outputs for you; make sure your pipeline doesn't strip them), audit logs that tie each output to model ID, prompt version, redacted inputs and any human approval, override hooks on consequential decisions, and an incident runbook with the reporting clock your counsel specifies. In the EU, transparency duties already apply, and the 2026 Digital Omnibus pushed high-risk duties out to December 2027 (stand-alone systems) and August 2028 (systems embedded in regulated products).
trade: Platform AI team vs embedded engineers
Leverage + consistency vs product intimacy
Central teams becoming ticket queues; embedded teams rebuilding five gateways
Speed vs governance, per decision class
Velocity vs blast radius
One process for everything: either bureaucracy on prompts or yolo on data rights
Build careers vs buy expertise
Compounding capability vs time-to-impact
Contractors leaving with the judgment; or quarters lost to ramp
Demo-driven vs eval-driven roadmaps
Excitement + funding vs deliverable truth
Roadmaps built on happy-path demos slipping 3–10×
Centralized vs delegated model choices
Cost discipline vs team autonomy
Shadow AI spend; or a bottleneck committee for every swap
Build compliance controls now vs at the deadline
Small design-time cost vs launch speed
Retrofitting disclosure, logging and oversight into a shipped product on a regulator's clock
scale: Portfolio view: run/build/explore budget split, reviewed quarterly, with kill criteria agreed before projects start, not negotiated after sunk cost
Unit economics per feature monthly: kill what never closes; scale what compounds
Eval coverage as a tracked org metric: % of shipped AI surface with CI-gated evals
Succession on judgment: document decision memos so the reasoning outlives the decider
Measure AI-assisted development like any process change: cycle time, defect escape rate and review load per change, before and after rollout; self-reported speed-ups are not data
sec: Governance designed in: data rights in contracts, audit trails, human override on consequential decisions, AI-content disclosure where required

Build the compliance controls, don't just cite the law: AI-interaction disclosure, machine-readable marking of generated content, log retention and record-keeping, human-override controls, incident-report clocks. EU AI Act transparency duties already apply (Anthropic's text watermark, for example, ships on Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1); high-risk duties phase in through 2027–28
Incident comms rehearsed: hallucination and injection incidents are when credibility is spent or banked
lead.interview: My job at staff level is portfolio management of irreversibility: classify every decision as a one-way or two-way door, let teams move fast through the two-way ones behind eval gates, and slow down hard on data rights, lock-in, and trust. The operating system is written decision memos with kill criteria, monthly unit-economics reviews, quarterly re-benchmarks and build/buy/wait revisits, and eval coverage tracked as an org metric. I buy commodity, build differentiation, our evals, data, and UX, and I translate capability to executives as risk, cost, and revenue with failure modes attached, because claims that survive production are the only currency that compounds.

PLAIN.llm: An LLM (large language model) is a program that's extremely good at predicting the next word. You send it text, it sends text back, and that's the whole interaction. It doesn't remember you between calls, it isn't wired into anything, and it sometimes gets things wrong while sounding completely sure of itself. This module is about that text-in/text-out machine: what it costs, how fast it is, and how to pick the right one.
PLAIN.prompt: A prompt is the text you send to the model: your instructions plus whatever the user asked. Writing a good one is like briefing a very capable temp worker who has never seen your company before. Clear rules, a few examples, and a defined output format change everything. This module is about doing that systematically instead of by trial and error.
PLAIN.context: The 'context window' is everything the model can see right now. Think of it as the model's desk: anything not on the desk doesn't exist to it. This module is about deciding what goes on that desk, which documents, how much chat history, and what to summarize away once it fills up. It sounds mundane. It's actually most of the job.
PLAIN.landscape: There are a handful of major AI models, from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and others. They leapfrog each other every few weeks and vary enormously in price. This module covers who the players are right now and, more durably, how to choose between them without getting swept up in launch-day hype.
PLAIN.rag: RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) means that before the model answers, your system looks up relevant passages from YOUR documents and pastes them into the prompt. The model then answers from your material instead of its general memory. This is how you build an AI that knows your company's docs, policies, or products, and can cite where each answer came from.
PLAIN.embed: An embedding turns a piece of text into a long list of numbers, designed so that texts with similar MEANING get similar numbers. That lets a computer measure 'how alike are these two sentences?' mathematically, which is the trick underneath search-by-meaning, recommendations, and most of RAG. This module explains how that works and where it breaks.
PLAIN.vecdb: Once you've turned millions of text snippets into number-lists (embeddings), you need a way to find the closest matches to a question in milliseconds. A vector database is a search engine built for exactly that. This module covers how they work, when you need a dedicated one, and when a regular database does the job fine.
PLAIN.memory: Out of the box, an AI assistant forgets everything the moment a conversation ends. Any product where it 'remembers' you (your preferences, past conversations, ongoing projects) has an engineered memory system behind it: code that decides what to save, where, and what to bring back later. This module is how those systems are built and how they go wrong.
PLAIN.agents: An agent is an AI that acts instead of just answering. It can search, read files, call APIs, and take several steps toward a goal, deciding what to do as it goes. That autonomy cuts both ways. Tiny per-step error rates snowball across many steps. This module covers when agents earn their keep and what makes them reliable.
PLAIN.tools: Tools are how an AI gets things done in the world. You describe a set of actions to the model ('search_flights', 'send_email'), like buttons with documentation, and the model asks your code to press them. The model never runs anything itself. It requests, and your code decides. Designing those buttons well matters more than almost anything else in agent quality.
PLAIN.harness: If the model is an engine, the harness is the rest of the car: steering, brakes, dashboard, seatbelts. It's all the software wrapped around the model in an agent system. What the model sees each turn, which tools it gets, when a human has to approve, how progress survives a crash. Same engine, different car, wildly different results. That's why this layer is where AI engineering happens in 2026.
PLAIN.computer: A computer-use agent operates software the way you do: it looks at a screenshot, decides where to click or what to type, does it, and looks again. A browser agent does the same inside web pages. They help when a system has no API, but they are slow, make mistakes, and can be tricked by text hidden on a page. So they run in a sealed sandbox, without passwords, and a human approves anything important.
PLAIN.multi: Sometimes one AI splits work across several AIs: one coordinating, others researching different subtopics in parallel, each with its own working memory. Like hiring a team instead of a single person, it pays off for genuinely parallel work and just adds cost and miscommunication everywhere else. This module is about telling those situations apart.
PLAIN.design: A working AI demo and a reliable AI product are separated by a lot of unglamorous plumbing. What happens when the AI provider goes down? How do you stop costs from exploding? How do you notice quality dropped before customers do? This module is that plumbing: the production engineering around the model call.
PLAIN.evals: You can't test AI like normal code. The same input can produce different outputs, and 'correct' is often a judgment call. Evals are the answer: a curated set of test questions with known good answers, run automatically against every change, so you KNOW whether the new version is better instead of feeling it. No single discipline separates serious AI teams from everyone else more clearly than this one.
PLAIN.halluc: AI models sometimes state false things with total confidence: invented facts, fake citations, wrong numbers. This isn't a bug to be patched. It's a side effect of how they work, since they're trained to sound plausible rather than to be true. This module covers the systems built around the model to catch fabrications before users see them, plus the related attack where someone hides malicious instructions in content the AI reads.
PLAIN.lead: Past a certain level, your value isn't writing the code. It's making the calls: build it or buy it, which risks are acceptable, what to tell executives, how to keep a team's skills current in a field that reinvents itself quarterly. This module is the judgment layer on top of everything technical you've learned.
PLAIN.finetune: Fine-tuning is additional training that specializes a model on your data. Done right, it can slash inference costs and tighten consistency on narrow tasks. It's also expensive, it can quietly break things the model used to handle well, and it's almost never the first tool to reach for. This module covers when the economics actually work, how to run the training without contaminating your results, how to train against an automatic grader or distill a big model into a small one, and how to verify you haven't traded one problem for three others.
PLAIN.serving: Self-hosting means running an open-weight model on GPUs you rent or own instead of paying a provider per token. You pay for the GPUs by the hour whether they're busy or idle, and the model's memory needs, not just its size, decide how many people it can serve at once. This module covers that memory math, the serving software, the shortcuts that make models smaller, and the unit cost that tells you whether it beats an API.
PLAIN.aisec: Every AI feature you ship is a new attack surface. Users can hide instructions inside documents, emails, and web pages that hijack what your model does, and unlike traditional security bugs, these attacks turn the model's own intelligence against you. This module covers the specific threat classes that LLM-powered systems face, how to design systems that hold under adversarial pressure, and which security controls actually work versus the ones that look good on paper and fail in an afternoon.
PLAIN.mlops: An AI system that works in demos can be quietly failing in production: returning wrong answers that look right, degrading week by week as the model drifts, running up costs with no alerts. Standard infrastructure dashboards can't see any of it. This module covers the extra instrumentation layer AI systems need, namely distributed traces with AI-specific attributes, quality metrics on live traffic, the drift alerts that catch problems before users do, and the audit trail that proves what an agent did and who approved it.
PLAIN.dataeng: The retrieval system is only as good as the data pipeline feeding it. Bad chunking, stale indexes, mixed embedding versions, and missing access control propagation quietly cap quality at 60–70% before you write a single prompt. This module covers how to design the pipeline so the retrieval system improves automatically, with the quality ceiling set by the content rather than the plumbing.
PLAIN.multimodal: Not all documents are text. Scanned PDFs, tables, charts, and audio recordings carry information that text-only pipelines miss entirely, but routing everything through an expensive vision model is a fast way to a very large bill. This module covers when vision or audio processing actually adds value, when it's just expensive theater, and how to build routing logic that sends each document type through the right pipeline at the right cost. It also covers the output side: generating images, video and speech, and marking what you generate so it can be identified as AI-made.
PLAIN.voice: A voice agent is an AI you talk to out loud, on a phone line or in an app. It listens, decides when you've finished, thinks, and speaks back, all within about a second, or the conversation feels broken. It also has to stop talking when you interrupt and remember only what you actually heard. This module covers how voice agents are built, timed, tested, and honestly disclosed to callers.

GLOSSARY: The AI engine behind ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, a program trained on enormous amounts of text to predict the next word, which turns out to make it capable of writing, reasoning, and coding.
The chunk of text a model actually processes, roughly ¾ of a word in English. Everything (price, limits, speed) is measured in tokens.
The maximum amount of text a model can see in one request, its working memory. Everything you want it to know right now must fit here.
The text you send to the model: instructions, examples, background, and the actual question.
The standing instructions that define the AI's role and rules, set by the developer and weighted heavily by the model.
The text the model sends back.
Running a trained model to get answers (as opposed to training it). When you call an API, you're doing inference.
The months-long, GPU-heavy process where a model learns from data. As an AI engineer you almost never do this, you use models others trained.
Additional training on your own examples to specialize a model. Powerful but often unnecessary, prompting and RAG usually get there first.
The billions of numbers inside a model that store what it learned. 'Open weights' means these are downloadable so you can run the model yourself.

A dial for randomness: 0 = consistent and boring, higher = varied and creative. Doesn't guarantee identical outputs even at 0. Most current flagship models fix it and reject changes, so you steer them with prompts and effort instead.
When a model confidently states something false, invented facts, fake citations. Intrinsic to how LLMs work; managed with systems, not scolding.
Looking up relevant passages from your documents and including them in the prompt so the model answers from your material, with citations.
Text converted to a list of numbers such that similar meanings produce similar numbers, the math behind search-by-meaning.
That list of numbers. 'Vector search' = finding the nearest vectors to your query's vector.
A search engine specialized in finding similar vectors among millions, fast.
Splitting documents into passage-sized pieces before embedding them, so search can find the relevant paragraph instead of the whole file.
A second, more careful pass that re-sorts the top search results so the best few go to the model. Cheap and very effective.
Classic exact-word search. Complements vector search, which can miss exact codes and names.
Using keyword AND vector search together, the production default.
Prepending a short, LLM-written description of where a chunk sits in its document before embedding and keyword-indexing it, so orphaned chunks stay findable.
Retrieval over an LLM-built graph of entities, relationships and community summaries; strong on corpus-wide 'what are the themes' questions, expensive to build and refresh.
Keeping one vector per token (ColBERT) or per page-image patch (ColPali) and scoring query against document token by token: sharper matches than one vector per chunk, at many times the storage.
An AI that takes multi-step actions using tools to pursue a goal, deciding its own path as it goes.
A fixed sequence of steps with AI calls inside, the simpler, cheaper alternative to an agent when the path is known in advance.
Running an agent on an engine that records every step, so a crash, a deploy or a days-long wait resumes from the record instead of starting over.
The mechanism letting a model request actions (search, send, look up) that YOUR code then executes. The model asks; your code acts.
The open standard (governed by the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation) for exposing tools, data and prompts to any AI app: write the integration once, every compliant assistant can use it.
A value that names an intended action (for example run + step) so the receiving service applies it once, however many times the request is retried or replayed.
All the software wrapped around the model in an agent system: context management, tool registry, safety gates, progress tracking. Where reliability comes from.
An open format for packaging know-how for agents: a folder with a SKILL.md (name, description, instructions) plus optional scripts, loaded only when a task needs it.
Summarizing older conversation history to free up context window space. Lossy, important state must be saved elsewhere.
A helper AI spawned with a fresh context to do one noisy task (like a big search) and report back just the conclusion.
The lead agent in a multi-agent system: breaks down the task, briefs workers, assembles results.
An automated quality test for AI: a set of inputs with known good outcomes, scored on every change. The AI equivalent of a test suite.
Your curated collection of real test cases, the fixture library your evals run against.
Using one AI model to grade another's answers against a rubric. Standard practice, with rules to keep it honest.
The share of tasks an agent completes on every one of k repeated runs: the reliability number for agents, unlike pass@k, which counts any single success.
An automated check on what goes into or comes out of the model: blocking attacks, redacting personal data, validating answers.
An attack where malicious instructions are hidden inside content the AI reads (an email, a webpage) to hijack its behavior.
Forcing answers to be based on provided sources rather than the model's general memory, usually with citations.
Whether an answer's claims are actually supported by the sources it cites. Checked automatically in serious systems.
A model's tendency to agree with or flatter the user instead of being accurate. Optimizing for thumbs-up ratings makes it worse.
A single routing layer all AI traffic flows through, enabling fallbacks, cost tracking, caching, and easy model swaps.
Provider feature that makes repeated prompt prefixes (like your system prompt) about 90% cheaper to re-read, more on some models.
Half-price processing for work that can wait hours instead of seconds, bulk jobs, nightly evals.
Sending the answer word-by-word as it's generated, so users see progress immediately.
How long before the first word of the answer appears, the latency users feel most.
Models whose internals are downloadable (DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, Gemma, Llama) so you can run them on your own hardware, cheaper at scale, more work.

A model that 'thinks' through hidden working steps before answering, better on hard problems, slower and pricier. On current flagships it's an effort setting on one model, and thinking tokens bill as output.
Forcing the model's answer into an exact format (like JSON matching a schema) so software can parse it reliably.
Including a few worked examples in the prompt so the model copies the pattern. Usually beats lengthy instructions.
Recognizing that a new question is a rephrase of one you've answered before, and reusing the answer instead of paying for a new one.
Several AI agents cooperating on one task, usually one orchestrator plus parallel workers.
An open protocol for one agent to discover another organization's agent through its Agent Card and delegate tasks to it without seeing inside it.
The hardware AI models run on. Relevant to you mainly if you self-host open-weight models.
API: the web interface you call to use a model. SDK: the code library that makes calling it convenient.
The per-request setting (low to max) that controls how much a model thinks before answering. Higher effort helps hard problems and costs more output tokens and latency.
Letting a model operate a computer through screenshots plus mouse and keyboard actions that your code executes in a sandbox. The last resort when no API or DOM-level tool exists.
An agent that navigates and acts on web pages, ideally through the page structure (accessibility tree, element references) rather than pixels. Every page it reads is untrusted input.

The structured view of a UI (roles, names, states) that browsers and operating systems expose for assistive technology. Agents read it to target elements reliably, often with fewer tokens than a screenshot.

The two main roles the EU AI Act assigns duties to: the provider develops an AI system or model and places it on the market under its name; the deployer uses one in its own operations. Substantially modifying a model can make you a provider.
Fine-tuning that freezes the base model and trains two small low-rank matrices per adapted layer, typically 0.1–1% of the parameters; the result is a small adapter file you can swap in or merge.
Fine-tuning on pairs of preferred and rejected answers, with no reward model and no rollouts: the simple way to shift behavior the model can already produce.
Fine-tuning by reinforcement learning against a grader (unit tests, exact match, a rubric model) instead of example answers; the product name for RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR).
Training a small student model on a larger teacher model's outputs, often including its reasoning: cheap to serve, capped by the teacher's quality and bound by the teacher's terms of use.

The keys and values a model has already computed for every token in a conversation, kept in GPU memory so each new token doesn't recompute them. It grows with context length × conversations in flight, and it is usually what limits how many users one GPU can serve.

Serving-engine scheduling that adds and removes requests from the running batch at every generation step, so a finished request's slot is refilled immediately instead of waiting for the slowest request in the batch.
Storing a model's weights (or its KV cache) in fewer bits, such as FP8 or a 4-bit format instead of 16-bit, to cut memory and speed up generation, at a quality cost you check with your own evals.

The server software that runs an open-weight model on GPUs and exposes it as an API, handling batching, KV-cache memory, quantized formats and adapters. vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM and llama.cpp are examples; most speak the OpenAI API format.

An agent that combines access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and a way to communicate externally. With all three, assume an injected instruction can exfiltrate data; the fix is cutting a leg or gating it per action, not adding a filter.

An input crafted to make a model ignore its safety training or policy (role-play framing, multi-turn escalation, encodings, many-shot priming). Unlike prompt injection, the attacker is usually the user.
Hiding instructions in a tool's description or schema, which an agent reads as trusted; a rug pull is the variant where a tool changes after you approved it.
Attacking your own AI system before others do: a threat model, creative human probing and automated attack suites, with every finding kept as a permanent regression test.

A trace records one request's path through your system; each step in it (a model call, a retrieval, a tool call) is a span with timing and attributes such as model, token counts and cost. The basic unit of LLM observability.
A service-level objective on answer quality rather than uptime, such as a 7-day rolling faithfulness rate of at least 82% from sampled online evals, with an alert threshold and an error budget.

An append-only, tamper-evident record of consequential actions (who asked, which model and prompt version ran, which tools fired, who approved), kept as evidence for as long as retention rules require; unlike debug traces, it is complete rather than sampled.
A loop that turns production failures into labeled eval cases (and eventually training data), so the system measurably improves every week instead of staying at its launch quality.
Streaming every insert, update and delete from a source system's change log (for example with Debezium) so downstream indexes update in minutes instead of waiting for a batch re-ingest.

Embedding a whole document with a long-context model first, then pooling each chunk's vector from those full-context token representations, so a chunk keeps the meaning of references that live elsewhere in the document.
A model that reads images (and often video or audio) alongside text in one context by turning image patches into tokens; billed per visual token, so resolution is a cost dial.
The machine-readable characters stored inside a digital-native PDF. If it exists, extraction is free and exact; if not (a scan), you need OCR or a vision model.
A signed manifest attached to a media file recording which tool or model made it and how it was edited, under the open C2PA standard; easy to strip, so pair it with an invisible watermark.

A model that takes spoken audio in and produces spoken audio out directly, with no separate transcription or text-to-speech step. Lower latency and it hears tone, but less control than a cascaded pipeline.
A small, fast model that labels each slice of audio as speech or silence. Voice agents use it to notice when someone starts or stops talking.
Deciding that a speaker has finished their turn, by waiting for a stretch of silence, by judging whether the sentence sounds complete, or both. Too eager cuts people off; too patient adds dead air.
A caller starting to talk while a voice agent is speaking. Handling it means stopping playback fast and keeping the agent's memory to what the caller actually heard.

llm.intro: The tiered router is the first thing to build in any LLM codebase: every call goes through one function that picks the model and effort, caps the output, and logs the economics.
llm.code:
import time

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TIERS = {  # model, output cap, and effort are per-route decisions
  "triage":    {"model": "claude-haiku-4-5",  "max_tokens": 200},   # Haiku 4.5 takes no effort param
  "workhorse": {"model": "claude-sonnet-5-5", "max_tokens": 4000,  "effort": "medium"},
  "hard":      {"model": "claude-opus-5-5",   "max_tokens": 16000, "effort": "high"},  # stream past ~16K
}

def call(task_tier, system, user, request_id):
    cfg = TIERS[task_tier]
    extra = {"output_config": {"effort": cfg["effort"]}} if "effort" in cfg else {}
    t0 = time.time()
    resp = client.messages.create(
        model=cfg["model"],
        max_tokens=cfg["max_tokens"],                     # caps thinking + answer
        system=[{"type": "text", "text": system,          # static block FIRST,
                 "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}],# marked cacheable
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user}],     # volatile data LAST
        **extra,
    )
    u = resp.usage
    log.info("llm_call", request_id=request_id, tier=task_tier,
        in_tok=u.input_tokens, out_tok=u.output_tokens,   # out_tok includes thinking
        cached=u.cache_read_input_tokens,                 # watch this number
        stop=resp.stop_reason,                            # "max_tokens" = cut off
        ms=int((time.time()-t0)*1000),
        usd=cost(cfg["model"], u))                        # cost per call, always
    return resp
notes: Every route declares a tier, defaulting to the flagship becomes impossible by construction.

The system block is cache-marked and placed first; per-request content last. Check cache_read_input_tokens in logs: if it's 0, your prefix isn't stable or is shorter than the model's caching minimum (4,096 tokens on Haiku 4.5, 512 on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5).

Effort is a per-tier cost lever: it sets how much thinking the model buys, and max_tokens caps the expensive token class, thinking included (Haiku 4.5 rejects the effort parameter, so its tier omits it). Output budget is a product decision, not an accident.
The log line is the foundation of cost attribution: per-request, per-tier, with cache visibility and the stop reason.
debug: Bill rising, traffic flat
Output length creep, a model or effort change that raised thinking, or a cache hit rate that fell after a prompt edit
Plot out_tok and cached over time, per route
Same input, different outputs
Normal: no provider guarantees bitwise reproducibility, and most current flagships don't take a temperature setting
Need determinism? Cache by input hash at the app layer
p95 latency spikes
Long outputs or heavy thinking (decode is serial), or missing streaming
Check out_tok at p95 vs p50; lower effort or stream interactive routes
Answers cut off mid-sentence
max_tokens also caps thinking on adaptive-thinking models
Alert on stop=max_tokens in the log; raise the cap or lower effort

prompt.intro: Prompts live in files under version control, deploy through CI, and produce schema-enforced output. This is the minimal shape of that discipline.
prompt.code:
# prompts/support_classify.yaml  (versioned, code-reviewed, eval-gated)
version: 3
owner: support-ai
evals: evals/support_classify.yaml     # CI runs this suite on every change
system: |
  You are a support-ticket classifier for Acme.
  Categories: billing, technical, account, other.
  If the ticket is ambiguous, pick "other" - never guess billing.
  <examples>
  ticket: "card charged twice"            -> {"category": "billing",   "urgent": true}
  ticket: "love the product!"             -> {"category": "other",     "urgent": false}
  ticket: "site down for our whole team"  -> {"category": "technical", "urgent": true}
  </examples>

# app code: schema-enforced output - off-schema JSON is unsamplable
resp = client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024,          # headroom: thinking counts toward the cap
    system=load_prompt("support_classify", version=3),
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": ticket_text}],
    output_config={"format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"category": {"type": "string",
                                    "enum": ["billing", "technical", "account", "other"]},
                       "urgent":   {"type": "boolean"}},
        "required": ["category", "urgent"],
        "additionalProperties": False}}},
)
if resp.stop_reason in ("max_tokens", "refusal"):   # cut off or declined: JSON may be partial
    raise ClassifyError(resp.stop_reason)
result = json.loads(next(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text"))  # schema-valid dict
check_rules(result, ticket_text)   # schema guarantees shape, not truth: validate, retry once
notes: The prompt file carries version, owner, and the eval suite that gates changes to it, the metadata IS the process.

context.intro: An explicit context budget, enforced in code, with compaction that persists durable state before it summarizes. This skeleton is what 'context engineering' compiles down to.
context.code:
BUDGET = {"system": 2000, "tools": 3000, "docs": 6000,
          "memory": 1000, "history": 8000, "output_reserve": 8000}

def assemble(state):
    sections = [
        ("system",  state.system_prompt),        # stable -> cacheable prefix
        ("tools",   render_tools(state.tools)),
        ("memory",  format_as_data(state.memories)),  # marked untrusted
        ("docs",    state.retrieved),            # JIT-fetched, not preloaded
        ("history", state.history),              # volatile -> last
    ]
    for name, content in sections:
        used = count_tokens(content)
        metrics.gauge(f"ctx.{name}", used)       # profile it like memory
        if used > BUDGET[name]:
            log.warn("ctx_over_budget", section=name, used=used)
    return sections

def maybe_compact(state):
    if utilization(state) > 0.70:                # threshold, not crisis
        # 1. durable state FIRST - compaction is lossy
        append_progress_file(state.key_decisions, state.open_questions)
        # 2. then summarize old turns, pin recent ones
        old, recent = split_turns(state.history, keep_recent=10)
        summary = cheap_model_summarize(old)
        state.history = [pin("Earlier (summarized): " + summary)] + recent
        # 3. drop stale tool dumps entirely
        state.history = prune_tool_results(state.history, older_than_turns=5)
        # 4. a rewritten history breaks thinking blocks bound to their prefix
        #    (Claude Fable 5.1 / Opus 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5): drop them from kept turns
        state.history = strip_thinking_blocks(state.history)
notes: Budgets are declared and measured per section, the ctx.* gauges are the first dashboard to build for any agent.
Compaction order matters: durable artifacts BEFORE summarization, because the summary is lossy and the progress file is not.
Stale tool output is dropped, not summarized, it's the main source of context rot and rarely worth a summary.
Memory enters formatted as data, never as instructions, the injection defense starts at assembly.

Step 4 exists because the newest Claude models sign each thinking block over the history before it: after any rewrite, keeping those blocks gets them dropped or the request rejected. Strip them, or let the provider's server-side compaction do the rewrite.

In production, prefer the platform primitive where it fits: server-side compaction and context editing replace steps 2 and 3, and on-demand compaction keeps recent turns' thinking valid under its documented conditions.

landscape.intro: The quarterly re-benchmark is a script, not a meeting. With a gateway and a golden set, evaluating any new model is an afternoon.
landscape.code:
# benchmark.py - run on every notable release; quarterly at minimum
ROUTES = ["support_answer", "doc_summary", "code_review"]
CANDIDATES = {  # benchmark (model, effort) pairs: effort moves cost AND quality
    "incumbent":  ("claude-sonnet-5-5", "medium"),
    "challenger": ("new-model-x", "medium"),     # whatever just shipped, effort pinned
}

for route in ROUTES:
    golden = load_dataset(f"evals/{route}.jsonl")     # your 50-100 real cases
    for name, (model, effort) in CANDIDATES.items():
        results = []
        for case in golden:
            out = gateway.call(model=model, effort=effort, route=route, input=case.input)
            results.append({
                "pass": run_judges(out, case),        # binary criteria
                "usd": out.cost, "ms": out.latency,
            })
        report(route, name, model, effort,
            score=mean(r["pass"] for r in results),
            p95_ms=pct(results, "ms", 95),
            usd_per_task=mean(r["usd"] for r in results))

# Decision rule (pre-agreed, so launches don't become debates):
# swap a route iff: score >= incumbent - 1pt  AND  (cost -30% OR p95 -30%)
# or: score >= incumbent + 3pts at comparable cost
notes: The gateway makes 'add a candidate' a config line; the golden set makes 'is it better' a number.
Pre-agreed decision rules turn releases from debates into diffs, write the swap criteria before you need them.
Score, cost, AND p95 latency: a model that wins on quality and loses 3x on latency is a per-route decision, not a global one.
Run it per route, the new model can win route A and lose route B. Routing is the point.
Pin the effort level in every candidate: defaults differ (Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol default to medium, Claude Sonnet 5.5 to high), so an unpinned run compares defaults, not models.
